MD06 / GBA LCD, CURVED GLASS AND FRAME
GBA LCD, curved glass and frame
Name the actual modeled surface

The chapter title includes glass because a screen assembly must be discussed as a visual surface, but the inspected GBA factory does not create a separately named transmissive glass slab. It creates a bezel surround, charcoal bezel, LCD recess, and live LCD mesh. Do not infer thickness, refraction, or a transparent material merely from the word glass. The visible display uses MeshBasicMaterial with tone mapping disabled and both shadow flags false. Actual assembly (src/handheld.js:467).

That distinction protects the image pipeline. A live picture should not become brighter or darker merely because a room lamp illuminates its material. The factory's basic material provides an unlit display surface; the runtime later supplies the picture. This chapter analyzes the geometry and initial material, not the complete runtime texture lifecycle. The player test separately checks that native video directly supplies the material map rather than a host-side replacement CRT effect. Direct-video assertion (tests/browser/player.spec.mjs:265).
A curved outline is not a curved framebuffer mapping

createLcdGeometries(curved) fixes width at 4.05 and height at two thirds of width, giving 2.7 scene units. Flat mode uses a plane. Curved mode triangulates a specially authored shape with thirty-two curve segments. Both represent an image-bearing face in XY; the curved mode changes its boundary, not the Z curvature of a thick lens. LCD geometry factory (src/handheld.js:49).

The outline is a series of quadratic curves. Its bottom begins near (-.451w,-.483h) and bows through a control at y=-.521h; sides use controls near x=±.503w. These coefficients describe a fitted perimeter around the native CRT picture. They are not a physical lens equation or a universally correct CRT model. Like the shell's controls, curve control points are not guaranteed sampled extrema.

The decisive operation follows triangulation: every curved-screen UV becomes u=x/w+.5, v=y/h+.5. This preserves rectangular framebuffer coordinates across the clipped perimeter. It avoids applying another image warp after the native CRT shader has already shaped the picture. Geometry chooses where the image can be seen; UVs choose which image pixel appears there. Those are different responsibilities. Boundary and UV construction (src/handheld.js:34).
Figure MD06.1. The fitted boundary clips visibility while preserving the original image-coordinate mapping.
Stack the frame without burying the display

The surround is 4.47×3.39 with nominal depth .045; the charcoal bezel is 4.35×3.27 with nominal depth .055. Their centers share Y .1, while recess and screen share Y .22. Z centers progress from .65 and .685 to .748 and .782. These values are not interchangeable: changing the screen center without the recess changes alignment; changing the bevel can alter occlusion without changing any center.

The recess outline is enlarged by .12 in both width and height, then extruded with depth .015 and bevel .009. In flat mode it uses a rounded rectangle with corner argument .025; in curved mode it uses the matching CRT outline. Thus the surrounding frame follows the effective screen mode. An overly thick recess bevel could cover the image plane, a problem the reference record explicitly notes was corrected during earlier shape work. Recorded occlusion correction (TODO/07_REFERENCE_SHAPE.todo:43).

The source revision introducing curved geometry had smaller dimensions than the pinned implementation. Historical commit 72da407f03ddf872bdd7b3c19e4a9bba92445998 is evidence for the change from rectangular border to fitted boundary and explicit UV restoration. It is not the source of today's 4.05 width. Keep historical values beside their commit rather than copying them into current parameter tables. Scoped historical diff.
MD06-W01 Derive the no-second-warp invariant

At the screen center, x=0,y=0, so the mapping gives u=.5,v=.5. At an arbitrary point x=.25w,y=-.2h, it gives u=.75,v=.3. These coordinates are independent of whether the outer edge is rectangular or bowed. A native pixel at three quarters of framebuffer width is not moved again simply because the border is curved.

The following original browser-console recipe is runnable without brand loading or a ROM. It checks all vertices of both modes against the same formula. The expected maximum error is near float precision, below 1e-6; the recipe does not assert pixel content or rendered border quality.

Why check all vertices if the formula is already visible? The check catches future geometry replacements that inherit default shape UVs or change dimensions without updating viewport metadata. It is cheap and independent of screenshots. It still cannot detect clipping of native lit pixels: a perfectly linear UV mapping can sit on an outline that is too small.

For clipping, the existing browser case samples lit edges from the actual native output, raycasts corresponding positions onto the screen, and measures distance to a sampled perimeter. It requires more than two hundred samples, zero sampled clipping, maximum keyline distance below nine native pixels, and UV error below .00001. Those are separate invariants, not four names for the same visual judgment. Edge-fit assertions (tests/browser/scene.spec.mjs:1475).
Why shortest distance matters near a curved tangent

A horizontal gap from an image edge to a curved border can grow large near a nearly horizontal tangent even if the border is close in the normal direction. The test computes closest distance to each sampled line segment of the outline and takes the minimum. That quantity better matches “thin keyline” than a fixed-axis distance.

This remains a sampled approximation. The perimeter is discretized, rows are sampled at intervals, and lit pixels are selected by a brightness threshold. An all-black frame provides no useful image-edge sample. The historical LCD workstream explicitly limits its claim to a fitted outline for the pinned native shader. Do not generalize it into proof for every cartridge, shader parameter, output resolution, or browser. Recorded fit limits (TODO/13_CURVED_LCD_BORDER.todo:17).
MD06-R01 Retry when unfiltered corners disappear

Suppose CRT Geom looks correct, but switching to unfiltered output cuts off rectangular corners. The first hypothesis is stale curved geometry, not bad texture filtering. The player case checks that screenCurved is true only for crt-geom.glslp, while retaining the same native runtime identity across preset changes. That condition prevents a curved-only screen from becoming an unconditional model feature.

Retry with geometry inspection before image tuning. Record viewport dimensions, geometry type, curved-state flag, and the first raycast object at a corner-adjacent point. Then switch back and verify the corresponding border changes. If the mode updates but corners still vanish, inspect the recess envelope and material map; if the geometry does not update, changing anisotropy cannot solve the error.

The long CRT case is parked under CI in the pinned source because retained reload readiness remains unresolved. Its assertions are valuable specifications but not evidence of a current CI pass. A separate preset-loop case remains a different source of coverage. This distinction must survive future summaries, particularly when a chapter cites a test's thresholds. Skip condition (tests/browser/scene.spec.mjs:1438).
Figure MD06.2. Missing corners are investigated through mode, geometry, occlusion, mapping, and only then actual pixel output.
Separate image sharpness from perimeter density

Increasing the number of boundary segments adds triangles around the curved perimeter. It does not add native game pixels. If the image looks blurred throughout its interior, inspect texture filtering, source resolution, display scaling, and the renderer rather than increasing shape tessellation. If the perimeter looks faceted while interior pixels remain crisp, boundary sampling is a more plausible cause. These symptoms point to different representations.

The reverse mistake is to sharpen the image while ignoring geometric clipping. A nearest-sampled texture can still lose its corners if the outline is too tight. A high-resolution source can still sit behind an overly thick recess. The worked UV check, center raycast, and native edge fit form a useful diagnostic ladder precisely because each isolates a different property.

When comparing screen modes, hold the native output and camera as stable as the experiment permits. A moving game scene can change which edge pixels are lit, so a difference in sampled keyline distance may reflect content rather than geometry. The existing original-demo case uses a specific running environment; this chapter does not generalize its threshold into an arbitrary-content theorem.
Treat viewport metadata as a geometric promise

The screen geometry stores width and height in userData.viewport. The edge test uses that metadata to map framebuffer pixels into local coordinates. If an extension changes the geometry's scale by modifying vertex positions but leaves metadata unchanged, the test's rays can sample the wrong physical location even though its arithmetic still looks correct.

A safe extension updates the outline parameters, UV mapping, and viewport metadata as one coherent operation. If only the mesh object scale changes, make clear whether viewport dimensions remain local or describe the scaled result. Mixing those meanings produces subtle errors in picking and pixel measurements. The pinned factory's metadata describes its unscaled local screen.

Finally, do not interpret a dark border as missing alpha without inspecting material and source content. Native CRT output may include black pixels outside its visible curved picture, while the mesh itself remains fully opaque. Transparent glass, opaque black picture pixels, and absent geometry create different raycast and compositing behavior. A debugging receipt should name which of those quantities was actually measured.
MD06-Q01 Add a genuinely transparent glass layer

A future agent proposes a reflective transparent sheet above the live LCD. Explain why this is an extension, what new coordinate and material decisions it introduces, and why the existing “LCD center hit is Live LCD” assertion may need a carefully justified replacement rather than deletion.
MD06-A01 Preserve display ownership while adding optics

It is an extension because the inspected factory has no separate glass slab. The new layer needs its own Z envelope, thickness policy, outline, material, shadow behavior, and ownership. If placed above the display, it may become the first raycast hit at the center even when the image is still correctly visible. A transparent surface is not automatically ignored by picking.

The existing assertion protects against an opaque bezel burying the image. Replace its literal first-object expectation only with an equally strong observation: for example, require an approved glass object first, then an unobstructed LCD intersection behind it, and verify actual image visibility. Otherwise a test “fix” could accept a new occluding panel.

Reflection should not be confused with image emission. Keep the image on its direct unlit material; let the optical layer contribute bounded reflection rather than multiply room lighting into game pixels. Current Three.js material guidance can inform a proposed design, but it cannot prove the original project used that design. The old pixels chapter explains the native-picture boundary, while the asset loader clarifies that supplied brand images are not the live framebuffer. Earlier pipeline account (docs/book/chapters/05-pixels-and-light/README.md:5); brand inputs (src/brand.js:6).

MD07 / GBA CONTROLS, GRIPS AND TACTILE DETAILS
GBA controls, grips and tactile details
Tactility begins with clearance

A button cannot convincingly move into a case if the case is a solid lid beneath it. The factory therefore separates openings, receiving floors, moving caps, and cap-relative markings. This is a geometric contract before it is an animation effect. The historical aperture correction replaces intersecting raised socket surfaces with actual holes in the front face and lower dark floors. That change is visible in commit 706563fe0355d6455a3c1ba1ff8fd9bafd3fa2a4, not inferred from a current screenshot. Historical change.

A and B use opening radius .315 and cap radius .29, leaving a nominal radial gap .025 before detailed bevel and pose effects. Start and Select use .18 openings around .155 caps, the same nominal gap. The source also stores target size separately: .65 for action buttons and .38 for Start/Select. Target dimensions are interaction metadata, not measurements of cap diameter. Control parameter table (src/handheld.js:444).

These are scene-unit clearances. They are not molding tolerances or guarantees against all animated intersections. A cap's curved profile, face bevel, and rocking motion can change the visible gap. The correct question is whether the complete surface remains coherent at rest and through its supported motion envelope, not whether one radius subtraction is positive.
The D-pad is one body with four directional anchors

The cross outline uses arm extent .61 and half-arm width .205. Its opening is the same cross scaled by 1.09 and translated to (-3.2,.26). The visible pad face contains a circular center hole of radius .135, with a lower circular pivot-well surface. Its nominal depth .07 and bevel .015 create a short manufactured profile rather than a flat sticker. D-pad construction (src/handheld.js:563).

Four directional controls share that one mesh. Their anchors sit at offsets of .40 along the cardinal axes and local Z .055. Four small extruded arrows use rotated copies of a triangular path. This arrangement lets the pad rock as a body while preserving separate directional target locations. Creating four independent pads would change the physical model and could open cracks at their joins.

Material ownership adds a second layer of tactility. Rubber is cloned from a physical material initially used for silver-colored parts, then roughness rises to .68 and clearcoat drops to .06. Arrow marks use another clone with a different color. Shared mesh motion does not require every marking to share exactly the same material object; it requires deliberate parentage and bounded finish differences. Material clones (src/handheld.js:399).
Figure MD07.1. Openings and floors provide physical clearance; moving caps own relief and target anchors.
Recessed A/B letters are surface reconstruction

The action cap begins as a forty-segment lathe. For action buttons, center-closing triangles are removed while rim normals remain. The letter is then recovered from browser-rendered bold 95px Arial, projected into a .25×.28 footprint with Y offset -.005. A must produce two contours and B three, including their enclosed spaces. The extractor throws if that expectation fails. Glyph recovery contract (src/handheld.js:232).

The reconstructed top is a circular face with the glyph cut out and counter islands added back at cap height. Its dome follows z=.055-.003*r/(radius*.6). The glyph floor lies at .047; walls connect floor and dome along all outer and counter contours. This is why the result remains a recessed letter from an oblique angle. Lowering a dark letter plane under an intact cap would hide it rather than engrave it. Recess construction (src/handheld.js:324).

Normals deserve attention because the new center meets an existing lathe rim. The implementation assigns top normals using a normalized profile-related vector rather than recomputing a flat face normal everywhere. Walls receive computed normals from their explicit

triangles. This separates smoothly continued cap shading from the cavity's edge behavior. A visible circular seam after an edit suggests a normal-continuity problem before it suggests a material-color problem.

The old geometry chapter records why replacing the original font with hand-drawn rounded contours was rejected. The later contour recovery preserves browser-font dependence; it does not bundle or license Arial. A future reproducibility effort should record browser and font availability, or explicitly propose a licensed deterministic outline asset as an extension. Historical typography distinction (docs/book/chapters/04-handheld-geometry/README.md:55).
MD07-W01 Derive resting and pressed action-cap heights

An action cap's mesh center is .653. Its uncut center dome reaches approximately local .055, so its resting center height is about .708. Factory motion metadata gives ordinary action controls travel (0,0,-.075). At full nominal translation, the corresponding cap center surface is near .633. The visible face's outer envelope is near .620, so the cap approaches the opening while remaining slightly proud at that central location.

This is a local geometric derivation, not an assertion that the runtime always reaches exactly full travel or never intersects at every radial point. The groove floor is lower than the cap dome and moves with it. Its full-translation height would be .653+.047-.075=.625, which explains why tiny depth changes can matter to perceived occlusion. Motion and cap placement (src/handheld.js:553); button creation (src/handheld.js:584).

The following original browser-console recipe assumes a freshly created independent model from createHandheld(), after loadBrand(). It checks factory metadata without driving the live application. The observable outcomes are one shared D-pad mesh and .075 nominal action travel.

Next calculate why Start/Select should not inherit the same travel blindly. Their metadata uses .04 inward motion and their caps are smaller. Shoulder controls move along negative local Y by .12, not along Z. Uniformly changing every control's Z coordinate would violate these different mechanisms. Geometry and interaction share a parameter map, but the mechanism remains control-specific.
Shoulders and grips complete the tactile vocabulary

L/R are rounded boxes 1.3×.39×.7 at x=±3.45, Y 1.81, Z .15, with opposite small Z rotations. Their extruded L/R marks belong to the button. An anchor above the local surface locates the target independently of the button's center. Start/Select instead receive molded shell labels attached to the casing, so those words do not compress with the round caps.

The underside slider has five grip ridges; the battery cover has four thumb grips. Neither set is a generic “texture”: both are separate meshes whose depth can catch light. Grip spacing and ownership must follow the moving part they describe. A power ridge belongs to the slider; a battery grip belongs to the cover. The source's parent arguments encode that distinction directly.
MD07-R01 Retry when deeper motion makes a cap dark

An extension increases action travel and finds the pressed cap unexpectedly black. Do not repair this with emission or an unlit cap material. First verify that the opening still clears the cap and that the front face or another socket surface is not intercepting light. Then compare rest and pressed samples under the same light and camera. A geometry-induced shadow failure should be solved geometrically before changing finish.

The active aperture-lighting cases require resting probes above a brightness threshold and pressed probes above sixty percent of rest. A separate complete compression/release/unlit-response case is explicitly skipped in the pinned source. These are not interchangeable receipts. This writing inspected the assertions but did not run them. Aperture lighting assertions (tests/browser/scene.spec.mjs:946); parked response case (tests/browser/scene.spec.mjs:986).
Figure MD07.2. Increased travel can recreate occlusion; artificial cap emission would conceal rather than solve that construction error.
Distinguish travel, rocking, and visual compression

The factory metadata records travel vectors and rest quaternions, but it does not itself execute a press. That boundary matters when writing reusable instructions. A correct factory can be driven incorrectly by a host animation, and a forgiving animation can conceal a geometric collision. Diagnose the rest assembly first, then inspect the host's supported pose envelope as a separate task.

For the shared D-pad, four anchors do not imply four independent travel accumulators. If simultaneous directions are represented by repeatedly translating the same mesh once per control, the result can exceed the intended movement. The factory's shared motion object is evidence that the pad is one body. A future host should combine directional intent into one bounded pose rather than sum unrelated mesh displacements.

Visual compression should also not be implemented by scaling the cap unless a redesign explicitly calls for squash. Scaling changes the glyph width, rim profile, and socket clearance, whereas the source metadata describes translation and orientation around a preserved rest shape. The old book's stronger-feedback discussion distinguishes deeper motion from altered cap shape; current factory values establish the baseline being explained. Historical feedback account (docs/book/chapters/04-handheld-geometry/README.md:129).
Diagnose finish without confusing it with shape

A rougher cap spreads highlights and may make a shallow groove less legible under broad light. That does not mean the groove disappeared. Compare raycast depth and grazing illumination before changing its contour. Conversely, a high-contrast dark floor can make a tiny cavity seem deeper than it is. Neither appearance alone measures geometry.

A practical proposed study holds the cap mesh fixed and varies only light direction, then holds light fixed and varies only floor depth. The first reveals shading sensitivity; the second reveals geometric depth sensitivity. Keep screenshots labeled with the changed condition and retain the same camera. This simple experiment avoids treating material roughness, letter color, and cut depth as interchangeable controls named “softness.”
MD07-Q01 Make only the action-letter grooves deeper

A request asks for more pronounced A/B engraving while preserving the original cap silhouette, lettering footprint, and all other controls. Which parameters and surfaces belong to the change? What must not change, and why is darkening the material alone insufficient?
MD07-A01 Change the cavity, not the alphabet or cap

The change belongs to the A/B floor depth and walls connecting that floor to the unchanged dome. Preserve recovered contours, counter islands, cap radius, rim normals, and mesh position. Lowering the floor requires rebuilding the wall vertices consistently; otherwise the cavity may have a gap or walls ending at the old depth. Do not edit the shared molded alphabet, because it also supplies shell labels and shoulder marks.

Darkening the groove material changes contrast but not depth, ray intersections, or wall shadows. It may make letters look heavier without satisfying the geometric request. Conversely, deeper walls can make an unchanged font look sharper through occlusion. The historical record
documents that distinction, so a good retry includes front and grazing-angle comparisons while holding light fixed.

Recheck pressed clearance because a lower floor approaches the shell's visible depth. Verify actual floor hits and cap-height counters, not mesh names alone. The broader input suite confirms that physical controls reach the native core, but those integration assertions do not measure newly changed engraving depth. Input integration boundary (tests/browser/player.spec.mjs:693); asset initialization prerequisite (src/brand.js:6).

MD08 / CARTRIDGES, SMALL DETAILS AND MARKINGS
Cartridges, small details and markings
Small parts explain what the large shape is

The shell carries silhouette, but a cartridge slot, battery cover, screw sockets, and edge controls explain how the object is used. These details should be modeled according to their observable role. A screw slot needs a thin dark geometric cue; a deep rear logo needs an actual cut surface; a cartridge title can be a canvas-backed label. Treating every detail as an image loses depth, while extruding every pixel adds complexity without a corresponding observation requirement.

The pinned factory returns a cartridge reference alongside root, screen, recess, controls, LED, and bezel texture. That return contract makes the cartridge a manipulable component rather than an anonymous decoration. Its initial state is invisible; host behavior later makes it meaningful during loading. This chapter explains the factory structure, not the full insertion choreography. Returned model and loaded cartridge (src/handheld.js:622).
Figure MD08.1. Diagnostic cartridge factory render under neutral studio lighting, showing prop thickness, label layering, and grip cues; not a historical loading screenshot.
The reusable cartridge is deliberately simple

createCartridge(color,title,subtitle) returns a group. Its body is a rounded extruded box 1.48×1.13×.22 with corner argument .1. A cream label backing 1.17×.65×.025 sits at Y -.02, Z .15. Two transparent text planes sit at Z .21, one centered at Y .11, the other at -.12. Five box grips span the lower region at X -.53+i*.26, Y -.43, Z .14. Complete prop factory (src/handheld.js:645).

The body uses roughness .72; the label backing uses .85. These choices describe a matte prop, not a measured material sample. The text helper creates a standard lit material with transparency and disabled depth writing. That lets antialiased letter edges reveal the backing while avoiding writing the full rectangular plane into the depth buffer. It does not remove all transparent-ordering limitations.

No separate contacts, connector cavity, rear screw, or detailed molded seam is created in this factory. A future chapter must not describe a cartridge back render as evidence for geometry that the factory lacks. Its value is precisely that it reveals the simplified rear boundary. Adding contacts would be a proposed extension with new dimensions, materials, and tests, not an explanation of existing implementation.
MD08-W01 Fit the loaded cartridge to the top slot

The handheld creates a default prop with body color #666574, title BBA, and subtitle LOCAL CARTRIDGE. It scales X and Y by 1.9 while leaving Z at one, then positions the group at (0,1.52,-.3). Nominal body width becomes 1.48*1.9=2.812; nominal body height becomes 1.13*1.9=2.147. Thickness remains .22 before bevel effects. These calculations are dimensions of the base body, not the complete label-and-grip envelope.

The named slot is 3.05 wide, so comparing nominal widths leaves .238 total horizontal difference before bevel expansion and other geometry. This is a first check, not a collision guarantee. The factory's nonuniform scaling also changes corner proportions in the XY plane relative to depth; that is an authored prop-fitting choice, not a physical cartridge standard.

The following original recipe assumes a browser page with the project import map. It creates only the standalone prop, so it needs no brand decoding. It measures the full visible group after the same scale used by the handheld and compares that envelope with the nominal slot width.

The expected width is larger than the un-beveled 2.812 because the body helper adds bevel extent. Measuring all children also catches a future grip or label that protrudes sideways. The check assumes no rotation and does not prove the cartridge clears the tabletop throughout insertion. The scene tests sample actual motion and table clearance; a factory envelope is only one part of that integration story. Insertion sampling (tests/browser/scene.spec.mjs:229); motion assertions (tests/browser/scene.spec.mjs:283).
Figure MD08.2. Reusable cartridge geometry is distinct from instance fitting and runtime loading motion.
Rear cover engraving preserves the original rim

The rear cover is a rounded 3.65×2.9×.06 box at (0,-.2,-.57). Four small thumb grips are children of the cover. Its logo is not simply a plane pasted above the plastic. engraveRearLogo() reads the supplied image alpha through a 512×171 mask, projects contours into a 3.45-wide local region centered at Y -.35, and cuts a .024-deep engraving.

The algorithm computes the original cover's minimum geometry Z, removes triangles lying wholly on that rear cap, and retains side and bevel geometry. A subgroup at that surface rotates around Y by π so its front-facing shapes point backward. A replacement face contains the cut regions, colored floors sit inward, and explicit wall triangles connect the boundaries. Keeping the original outer bevel avoids replacing the entire cover with a visibly different object. Rear-cap replacement (src/handheld.js:285).

Nested contours preserve plastic islands inside transparent counters. Bounds accelerate containment selection, but an actual point-in-polygon test determines the relationship. Winding is adjusted by nesting parity. The floor UVs map back into the original artwork, so the colored logo survives as recessed color rather than becoming a uniformly dark silhouette. The floor's basic material is transparent, not tone-mapped, and does not cast or receive shadows; the plastic walls carry geometric shading.

Historical commit cf53ecc05ea27a9c26e60a87d0306de1bce78bc5 changes width from 2.95 to 3.45 and depth from .006 to .024. This supports the current enlargement and deeper cavity as an observed source change. It does not establish a measured real-world engraving depth or a new human approval. Scoped enlargement diff.
Figure MD08.3. Diagnostic rear factory render under neutral studio lighting, intended to reveal cover relief, grips, and screw cues rather than prove live-room illumination.
Molded marks and edge hardware use different ownership

The maker mark is a shell-owned group at (0,2.10,.625). It contains extruded polygon lettering and a chamfered outline. Start/Select labels use rounded outline rings and molded text, rotated together on the shell. These letters come from an explicit small polygon alphabet, unlike the recovered Arial action glyphs and canvas cartridge text. Reusing the wrong alphabet would change appearance and could fail for unsupported characters. Molded labels and maker mark (src/handheld.js:362).

Five screw positions each receive a dark socket, a smaller silver cylinder, and a thin dark slot box. These are visual hardware cues, not threaded fasteners. The link port is a box; the headphone socket uses an additionally rotated cylinder. Their simplified representations are adequate for the inspected exterior contract but do not describe internal electronics. Documenting that limit makes extension safer: a future agent knows which details are abstractions rather than missing pieces of an unseen CAD model.

The brand loader is responsible for decoding the PNGs before the rear mask is generated. A blank engraving can therefore originate at input loading, alpha extraction, region classification, or surface replacement. These boundaries should be investigated independently. Brand decoding (src/brand.js:6).
MD08-R01 Retry when a new logo loses thin features

Suppose a licensed replacement logo has fine translucent lines that disappear from the cavity while the colored floor still contains them. The mask is sampled at 512×171 and uses alpha threshold 16, while the color texture remains 1024×342. Geometry and color therefore have different sampling responsibilities. Inspect the mask before increasing depth or brightening the floor.

A line narrower than the mask's effective sampling can merge, vanish, or create unexpected contour connections. Increasing mask resolution is a proposed change with higher contour and wall cost. Lowering the threshold may recover faint pixels but also admit noise and detached regions. Neither is automatically correct. Compare contour count, nesting, and wall complexity against the intended licensed artwork, then inspect an oblique render for artifacts.

Do not silently edit the original PNG to suit a cavity algorithm. Preserve the source asset and derive a documented mask. The historical reference record explicitly distinguishes independently authored geometry from extracted assets, and the same provenance discipline applies to replacement marks. Provenance boundary (TODO/07_REFERENCE_SHAPE.todo:19).
Figure MD08.4. Rear-logo failures are traced from source alpha to the final cavity rather than treated as generic material problems.
Keep tiny detail readable without falsifying construction

Small parts face a sampling limit: a real geometric slot may project to less than one pixel in a distant view. Increasing its contrast can improve recognition, but enlarging the slot changes the model. Decide whether the contract is close inspection or distant readability before choosing a remedy. The same source can reasonably support a detailed inspection view and a simpler distant presentation, but this factory does not implement a separate level-of-detail system.

Screw slots illustrate the distinction. The thin dark box communicates orientation and recess-like contrast, yet it is not a modeled helical thread or a fully subtracted driver cavity. Describe the actual cue without promoting it into absent engineering detail. A future physically detailed fastener would require a new profile and an observation budget that makes those triangles useful.

For the rear engraving, detail scale is coupled to mask sampling rather than only camera distance. Enlarging the final mesh makes existing contour segments more visible but does not recover alpha detail discarded during extraction. Rebuilding the mask at a different resolution changes geometry; scaling the subgroup does not. This is another reason to record source resolution, projection width, and groove depth as separate parameters.

The cartridge title has a similar separation. A wider plane can stretch existing text without changing its raster input, while rerasterizing at a different aspect changes layout. Preserve readable naming by editing the intended stage rather than compensating with a transform somewhere else.
MD08-Q01 Add rear contacts to the cartridge

Design a bounded extension for visible cartridge contacts. What must be established before choosing a gold material and placing strips? Explain how to avoid claiming that a diagnostic back image already proves those contacts exist.
MD08-A01 Establish the missing geometry contract first

The current factory has no contacts, so the extension must define a connector region, strip count, spacing, recess, thickness, and rear-facing orientation from an authorized reference or an explicitly fictional design. A metallic color alone does not establish any of these. Keep dimensions in scene units unless calibrated evidence supports a physical conversion.

Attach contact geometry to the cartridge root or a named connector subgroup. Its rear-facing transform must be derived from the prop's frame, not copied from the handheld's battery-cover engraving. Preserve the existing label and grips, then measure the complete envelope again: a new rear protrusion may affect slot fitting or table clearance even if width is unchanged.

A back diagnostic of the old factory documents absence and simplification, not hidden detail. Produce separate baseline and extension observations and label them accordingly. Existing loading tests check motion and seating relationships; they would need additional contact visibility and clearance observations before covering the new geometry. The original book's relief-versus-color explanation provides a useful conceptual test, but it does not supply missing contact dimensions. Earlier geometry principle (docs/book/chapters/04-handheld-geometry/README.md:26).

MD09 / PROCEDURAL TEXTURES AND ASSET BOUNDARIES
Procedural textures and asset boundaries
Procedural does not mean asset-free

The project creates many textures at runtime, but their inputs differ. Wood grain is generated from seeded arithmetic. Cartridge text is rasterized by the browser. The bezel wordmark is derived from supplied artwork. Rear engraving turns supplied alpha into geometry while retaining image color on the cavity floor. Calling all of these “generated textures” hides important reproducibility and provenance boundaries.

The shared canvasTexture(width,height,paint) helper creates a canvas, obtains a 2D context, invokes a painter, and wraps the result in THREE.CanvasTexture. It throws an explicit error if drawing is unavailable. The texture is marked sRGB and assigned anisotropy 4. These are actual implementation settings; they do not prove every consuming material or renderer uses the same sampling behavior. Texture helper (src/handheld.js:68).

The current CanvasTexture documentation, consulted 2026-11-07, describes canvas-backed texture construction and inherited sampling defaults. Use it as explanatory guidance, not a version-pinned historical receipt. This project explicitly overrides color space and anisotropy, so copying generic defaults into a parameter table would be wrong.
Color data and coverage data have different jobs

sRGB marks how encoded color should be interpreted. Alpha describes coverage, not brightness. The bezel derivative uses source RGB to decide which pixels belong to neutral lettering, but ultimately preserves a reconstructed alpha silhouette and fills that silhouette with stylized color. The rear engraving uses alpha to create contours, while its floor samples the color image. A bright RGB pixel with zero alpha contributes no visible mark; a dim but opaque pixel may still be important to geometry.

This distinction explains why debugging should inspect channels separately. If a logo is missing, first determine whether the color is dark, alpha was removed, UVs point elsewhere, or another surface occludes it. Increasing light only addresses one of those possibilities. Disabling depth writing on a transparent label addresses a different problem again: whether the plane's rectangle prevents later geometry from drawing.

Text labels use a canvas height of 128 and width ceil(128*aspect), centered text alignment, middle baseline, and a maximum drawing width eighteen pixels smaller than the canvas. The world plane's width-to-height ratio supplies the aspect. Thus text size, canvas resolution, and world footprint are related but not identical. A font size in canvas pixels is not a world-space letter height. Text and label helpers (src/handheld.js:81).
Figure MD09.1. The same RGBA input can supply visible color or geometric coverage, but those outputs have different contracts.
The bezel wordmark is a derived asset

loadBrand() decodes logo.png, star.png, orbit.png, and glow.png. The handheld module imports brandImage; it does not use all four images directly. The full wordmark texture is drawn at 1024×342 for rear artwork. A separate bezel canvas is 1536×174, cropped from the supplied image and placed into a centered region occupying sixty percent of each canvas dimension. Preserve that distinction: the rear uses full artwork, while the front derives letter-only branding. Input loader (src/brand.js:1); initial derivative (src/handheld.js:475).

The derivative first computes the minimum RGB channel and uses it to attenuate alpha, rejecting saturated orbital accents while retaining neutral lettering and highlights. It then finds solid alpha cores using a seven-by-seven neighborhood. Those seeds flood into connected nonzero-alpha pixels. The seed test selects components; the flood reconstructs their original edge pixels rather than simply eroding the whole mark.

This algorithm has a concrete failure boundary: if no solid cores remain, it throws. A replacement artwork with thin lettering may therefore be unsupported even when it looks valid as a PNG. Broadening the threshold is not automatically safe because detached exterior contours may return. Inspect the retained components before changing the test. Core selection and flood (src/handheld.js:487).

Finally the canvas applies vertical chrome color bands with source-in, adds a horizontal iridescent tint with source-atop, and restores source-over. The resulting material uses roughness .4 and metalness .1. The colored bands are baked stylization, not physically traced reflections or a thin-film simulation. Their appearance can coexist with room lighting, but the gradient itself does not respond to camera movement. Compositing and material (src/handheld.js:529).
MD09-W01 Reproduce the wood generator's controlled variation

createWood() paints a 1024×1024 canvas. It starts from seed 41 and advances a 32-bit linear congruential generator using multiplier 1664525 and increment 1013904223. Eight bands of 128 pixels establish planks. Each receives low-alpha tonal variation, then 110 grain strokes whose paths combine sampled Y positions with sine displacement. Thin dark and light seams separate planks. The texture repeats twice along both axes. Complete wood painter (src/handheld.js:657).

The seed makes the arithmetic sequence repeatable. It does not promise identical raster pixels across every browser implementation, GPU, and operating system. Canvas line rasterization and color handling can differ. The useful invariant is stronger within one environment: two calls follow the same painter and seeded sequence, so their pixel results should agree there.

The following original browser-console recipe assumes the project's import map and a usable 2D canvas. It hashes canvas pixels, not GPU readback, and creates no scene. Expected results are equal hashes in the same execution environment and repeat values [2,2]. It is a diagnostic proposal, not a historical test.

Derive what changing seed versus repeat means. A seed change alters the generated grain arrangement while preserving canvas size and the eight-band structure. A repeat change alters how often the same image tiles over the receiving geometry; it does not repaint new planks. If a desk looks too repetitive, changing only seed cannot remove the fact that the same tile repeats twice. If grain appears stretched, inspect mesh UVs and aspect before repainting.

The function returns a texture, not a desk mesh or material. Its placement and physical scale belong to the consumer outside this part's scope. Recording that boundary prevents “wood model” from becoming an unsupported claim about desk dimensions or UV orientation.
MD09-R01 Retry when a replacement wordmark fails

Suppose a new licensed wordmark decodes correctly but the factory throws that it has no solid lettering. Begin with the derivative canvas, not the mesh. The crop constants refer to the current source artwork layout. A differently arranged image may place its letters outside that crop or make them too thin after resampling. Successful decode proves only that the image loaded.

Retry by inspecting crop coverage, alpha thresholds, and seed neighborhoods separately. First verify that the crop contains intended letters. Then inspect neutral-channel selection. Finally inspect whether any seven-by-seven solid regions survive. Changing all three at once can produce a plausible output while leaving the cause unknown. A replacement should carry its own explicit derivation parameters rather than silently inheriting assumptions about the old image.

The earlier geometry chapter records why threshold-only filtering damaged lettering and why component reconstruction was introduced. That historical explanation supports retaining component identity, but the exact current loop remains authoritative. It also distinguishes the
later colored finish from earlier neutral ink; do not describe both as simultaneous source behavior. Recorded derivative evolution (docs/book/chapters/04-handheld-geometry/README.md:95).
Figure MD09.2. Wordmark diagnosis follows each image-processing boundary instead of treating every missing pixel as an asset-loading error.
Asset delivery and legal provenance remain separate

The static allowlist copies top-level JS, SVG, and PNG files from src and assets, maps the inspection logo separately, and vendors selected Three files and license. A runtime-generated texture need not exist as an exported PNG to be reproducible. Conversely, a local asset outside the
allowlist is not automatically available at the same browser URL. Public delivery rules (scripts/site-files.mjs:4).

The root manifest's Three dependency establishes the geometry library; it does not establish rights to every supplied image or system font. The historical reference workstream explicitly avoids extracting unavailable model assets. Preserve that discipline when adding references: use authorized inputs, document derivation, and do not infer permission from technical accessibility. This chapter does not perform a new rights audit. Library declaration (package.json:7); historical provenance limit (TODO/07_REFERENCE_SHAPE.todo:19).
Own the lifetime of generated resources

Each helper call creates a new canvas and texture. The text contour routine disposes its temporary texture after reading pixels, and the rear-mask routine similarly disposes the mask. Those calls release texture resources; they do not imply that every scene object is automatically cleaned up when removed from a group. Temporary glyph resource (src/handheld.js:232); temporary rear mask (src/handheld.js:255).

An agent writing a repeated diagnostic should therefore distinguish temporary extraction inputs from textures retained by materials. Disposing a shared retained texture while another material still uses it can invalidate the display. Failing to release unique diagnostic resources can accumulate allocations across many specimens. Track ownership explicitly instead of assuming traversal and removal constitute disposal.

The same principle applies to caches. The brand loader returns early only when all four image exports are present; that is an input cache, not a cache of generated handheld geometries or wordmark textures. Calling the factory twice still constructs two model trees and derived canvases. A proposed factory cache would need rules for material mutation, texture reuse, and disposal, especially because cloned finishes and mutable control state belong to individual instances. Resource reuse is an extension design, not something established by the current loader's early return.
MD09-Q01 Make the book fully reproducible across fonts

An agent wants every A/B contour and cartridge title to match across machines. Is a fixed random seed enough? Propose a bounded extension and explain what existing behavior it would change. Include why matching the bezel bitmap would not solve the action glyph problem.
MD09-A01 Control the actual source of variability

A seed controls wood's arithmetic choices, not browser font rasterization. Action glyph geometry begins with Arial text rendered to a canvas, and cartridge labels use browser text as well. If the selected font differs, contours and line breaks can differ even with identical Three versions. The
bezel is derived from a supplied image, so matching its bitmap does not determine the separately rendered A/B letters.

A deterministic extension could supply appropriately licensed font data and await its loading before rasterization, or provide authorized fixed vector contours for the required glyphs. Each changes the input contract and should be labeled as a new design. The first retains rasterization dependence but controls font selection; the second removes raster contour recovery for those glyphs but introduces vector-asset maintenance and provenance responsibilities.

Verification should compare contour topology, footprint, counter preservation, and actual rendered readability, not only a file hash. Keep the existing baseline available so the extension is not misrepresented as recovered historical tooling. The player test's direct-video assertion further reminds us that decorative texture reproducibility must not replace the live framebuffer with a baked image. The model's labels, brand derivations, and game display are three different asset boundaries. Live-video boundary (tests/browser/player.spec.mjs:265).

MD10 / DS ASSEMBLY AND THE PARAMETER MAP
DS assembly and the parameter map
Read the assembly as a set of contracts

The DS is not one sculpted object. It is an assembly whose convincing appearance depends on separate transform spaces, layered solids, readable controls and a stable pixel surface. The reconstruction problem is therefore not “make a blue rectangle.” It is to preserve relationships while parts move: the upper display follows the lid, the lower display stays with the base, and the stylus remains available without stretching the camera envelope toward the pointer.

Implemented evidence. createDsHandheld() imports Three.js and three helpers from handheld.js; it constructs groups, extrusions, cylinders, lathed caps, planes and canvas textures. There is no model-file loader in this factory. The repository and installed package both identify Three.js 0.186.1. This chapter describes JavaScript procedural authoring, not a Blender, CAD or imported-mesh workflow. Read the factory entry and materials (src/ds-handheld.js:1) and dependency declaration (package.json:7).

Numbers below are model-space units, not measured millimetres. A screen width of 4.5 establishes a useful internal scale, but it does not establish a manufactured part's dimensions. Surface names are authoring labels, not a promise of mechanical equivalence to every Nintendo DS revision. Begin a reconstruction by recording those limits; otherwise seemingly precise arithmetic becomes misleading hardware documentation.
Figure MD10.1. Reconstruct in dependency order: silhouette and ownership precede decorative details and interactive targets.
Build a parameter ledger before changing geometry

The lower assembly contains a parting line, rear shell and control deck centered at local Y −2.43. Their common nominal width is 8.5 and height 4.75. The lid's nominal footprint is 8.5 by 4.65, centered at its own Y 2.43. The opposing signs place the joint near the root origin instead of at either shell's center. This origin choice makes articulation simpler: the lid rotates around its parent origin while its geometry is offset away from that origin.

These are nominal constructor inputs, not final beveled bounds. The DS wrapper supplies bevel min(.02, depth/3, radius/3) to the shared rounded-box helper. Extrusion bevels extend the outline and thickness; an 8.5-wide shape can therefore occupy more than 8.5 in its generated bounding box. The shell construction (src/ds-handheld.js:68) must be read with the centered extrusion helper (src/handheld.js:19). That combination explains why center-to-center spacing is insufficient for clearance work.

The lower rear shell uses depth .19 at Z −.135; the control deck uses depth .22 at Z .105. The parting line is much thinner, .025 at Z −.025. These layers establish visible seams without requiring a single watertight enclosure. Do not silently reinterpret them as a production injection-molding cross-section: intersecting layered meshes are acceptable here, but manufacturing wall thickness and internal fasteners are not being solved.
Assign transform ownership before assembly

The root owns the base, lower LCD, controls, card and stylus. The lid owns its shell layers, upper LCD, speaker details, bumpers and hinge leaves. The separate hinge group is root-owned; its barrel does not rotate merely because the lid rotates. This distinction prevents double articulation. Attaching the hinge under the lid and then rotating both would create a plausible-looking but structurally wrong joint.

The return object is the public assembly interface: root, lid, hinge, screens, screen, controls, led, power, cartridge, stylus references, branding and accent materials. screen aliases the second entry of screens, so downstream lower-touch logic can address the intended surface directly. The returned interface (src/ds-handheld.js:273) is more reliable than guessing targets from traversal order.

Research guidance, not pinned implementation evidence. Current Three.js Object3D documentation, consulted 2026-11-07, distinguishes local transforms, world matrices and radian rotations. Use that model to reason about parent-child composition. Do not adopt a newer documented property merely because it appears on the current page; this implementation uses group origins and offsets, not a newly introduced pivot API.

Figure MD10.2. Parent-supplied neutral-studio constructor diagnostic, intended for silhouette and layering inspection; it is not native gameplay, historical development evidence or a claim that every control is unobstructed in every pose.
Separate visual construction from application completion

A factory instance is not the finished application state. Its branding plane starts invisible and without the supplied logo map. DsController.initialize() loads the image, assigns an sRGB texture and reveals the plane. Its screens initially use unlit materials, but the controller constructor subsequently selects reflective powered-off glass. A bare-constructor diagnostic must therefore identify which initialization stages it includes.

The controller initialization (src/ds-controller.js:186) establishes this asset boundary. It is a supplied artwork texture on procedural geometry, not evidence that the whole console was imported. Likewise the scene puts the root into a desk or focused-play transform; a local positive Y coordinate is not automatically “up” in the room.

The scene pose constants (src/scene.js:18) use a rotated table quaternion and an identity default play quaternion. Keeping that distinction in the ledger prevents mistaken descriptions of the card's travel or the lower expansion slot. The modeled front/bottom expansion opening is separate from the rear DS game-card slot near the hinge; the factory names and places both.
MD10-W01 Audit a face-button clearance numerically

Consider the leftmost face button, Y, at X 2.75 with cap radius .195. Its recessed socket has radius .195 + .025 = .220, so the socket's leftmost nominal X is 2.75 − .220 = 2.530. The outer touchscreen bezel starts with width 4.88, giving half-width 2.440, but its .035 depth limits the DS wrapper bevel to .035/3 ≈ .011667. The outer bound is therefore approximately 2.451667. The nominal horizontal gap is about .078333.

That result explains two decisions. First, the socket, not just the smaller cap, is the limiting feature. Second, ignoring the bezel's extrusion bevel would overstate the available gap. The browser test requires greater than .05 between every cap/socket bound and the actual bezel, and greater than .1 toward the deck edge. Read the bound-based assertions (tests/browser/ds.spec.mjs:1309).

Original diagnostic pseudocode follows. Assumptions: a browser has constructed the model, matrices are current, and boundsInBase() transforms all eight geometry-box corners into root space. The expected result is positive margins, not an assertion that this recipe was executed here.

bezel = boundsInBase("Touch fine cyan bezel edge")
deck = boundsInBase("Metallic blue control deck")
for label in X, A, B, Y:
  for part in button, recessed_socket:
    box = boundsInBase(label, part)
    require box.minX - bezel.maxX > .05
    require deck.maxX - box.maxX > .10

For a beveled corner, an axis-aligned box is conservative: it can reject space that is geometrically empty near the rounded edge. That is useful for a readable diagram and predictable safety margin, but it is not exact mesh-to-mesh distance. Record which measurement you use rather than switching between them when a test fails.
MD10-R01 Retry after widening the screen surround

Suppose a proposed surround change increases its width by .12 without changing controls. Its right edge advances .06. The previously calculated .078333 gap becomes about .018333 and violates the .05 criterion. Moving only the Y legend does nothing; moving only its cap leaves the socket overlapping. Shrinking the LCD would change a separate display contract.

The corrected proposal must move the entire diamond or redesign the surround, then recalculate both inner and outer margins. Moving all four controls outward by .04 might recover the inner threshold but consumes .04 of the A button's deck-edge margin. Inspect both limits before choosing a value. Historical commit 89d905f moved the complete cluster outward by .2; that recorded correction supports the method, not permission to move it indefinitely.
Figure MD10.3. A parameter change is accepted only after checking both adjacent constraints; passing one side does not preserve the assembly.
Make parameter changes transactional

Proposed reconstruction practice. Keep a small change ledger with four columns: parameter, dependent geometry, dependent behavior and evidence to regenerate. For example, changing LCD width affects the plane, all three surround layers, illumination viewport metadata, control clearance and camera bounds. Changing only shell roughness affects appearance but should not change those dimensions. This classification keeps an agent from treating every visual complaint as a material problem.

Work from a reversible baseline. Change one relationship, rebuild the affected geometry and capture numerical bounds before interpreting a new image. A plane becoming wider without a matching viewport metadata change is an internal inconsistency even if the image still looks acceptable. A moved cap with an unmoved shell label may be visually inconsistent even though its input anchor follows correctly.

Resource lifetime is another dependency. The existing controller disposes replaced display materials and maps; proposed geometry replacement should similarly account for the old geometry rather than retaining every revision indefinitely. Do not copy that disposal strategy blindly onto shared objects: first determine whether another mesh still references the resource. The factory intentionally shares several materials, including the shell/rim relationship, so mutation has a wider scope than one named mesh.

Finally, save both the intended effect and the invariant that must remain unchanged. “Move the diamond outward while keeping screen size” is testable; “improve the controls” is not. This makes later debugging a comparison of contracts rather than a reconstruction of undocumented taste.
MD10-Q01 Exercise: choose the correct editable object

A diagnostic operator wants the top display to fold while the lower touchscreen, battery cover and branding remain fixed. They propose rotating root, then counter-rotating every lower component. Explain the ownership error, choose the minimal correct transform, and identify one downstream calculation that must be refreshed.
MD10-A01 Explained answer

Rotate lid.rotation.x, not the root. Counter-rotation replaces a clear hierarchy contract with many compensating transforms; every later base detail becomes another opportunity for a missed correction. The upper LCD already belongs to the lid and therefore follows automatically. The battery cover and underside branding remain root-owned. The hinge barrel also remains root-owned while the lid-owned leaves move with the shell.

Refresh articulated bounds and view matrices before trusting projected input. dsPoseBounds() evaluates separate root and lid transforms; a single cached flat rectangle cannot describe both poses. This is a geometric correctness requirement, not merely a camera convenience. The pose/bounds implementation (src/scene.js:502) supplies the actual application mechanism. This chapter read source and assertions; it did not rerun browser tests, render production images or establish owner approval.

MD11 / HINGES, LIDS AND ARTICULATION
Hinges, lids and articulation
A hinge is first a coordinate-system decision

An articulated object fails when its pivot is chosen after its geometry. A lid centered on its own origin spins like a signboard; it does not fold around its lower edge. This factory instead places the lid group's origin at the joint and offsets its visible shell to local Y 2.43. The group receives an initial X rotation of 70 degrees and a Z offset of .07. The upper screen and surrounding details are children, so one transform carries the complete upper assembly.

Implemented evidence. The lid creation (src/ds-handheld.js:71) precedes the separately created barrel group. That ordering makes the visual joint independent of the mathematical articulation. No torque, detent spring, hinge friction or collision-constrained rigid-body joint is implemented by these groups. The physical mechanism is approximated through recognizable geometry and bounded pose editing.
Figure MD11.1. Offset geometry creates the lever arm; rotation belongs to the joint frame rather than the shell center.
Construct the barrel without confusing its axis

Three.js cylinders are initially aligned along their local Y axis. The central barrel uses radius .255, width 6.90 and 48 radial segments, then rotates around Z by π/2 so its length lies along the hinge's X axis. A right lime cap at X 3.80 uses width .72. The left end is assembled from two half-cylinder sections at X −3.80 with angular starts −π/2 and π/2. Their names distinguish front and rear sections, but both use the same lime material at this cutoff.

Two collars sit at X ±3.43 with radius .258 and width .035. The slight radial increase creates a legible seam without making the joint look like disconnected cylinders. Lid-owned leaves at those X positions bridge the upper shell toward the barrel. The microphone, MIC legend and indicator recesses belong to the barrel frame, so they do not unexpectedly orbit the upper LCD. Inspect the complete joint details (src/ds-handheld.js:111).

The barrel is a visual approximation rather than a mechanically interlocking mesh. A continuous cylinder and narrow collars are inexpensive and readable at desk scale; modeling internal axles would add surfaces that the current interaction does not expose. If an extension requires an exploded mechanism, add that as a new documented model contract rather than claiming the existing continuous barrel already contains one.
Opening degrees and stored rotation are different quantities

The scene's getter reports 180 − radToDeg(lid.rotation.x). Its setter clamps an opening angle to 30–180 degrees and stores the complement in radians. Thus an opening of 180 corresponds to zero stored rotation, 145 corresponds to 35 degrees, and the factory's 70-degree rotation corresponds to a 110-degree opening. These conversions are not interchangeable descriptions of one raw number.

MD11-W01 Calculate a useful diagnostic pose

Use the lid center point (0, 2.43, 0) in the lid's local coordinates, ignoring shell thickness for this calculation. After an X rotation θ, the root-space point becomes approximately (0, 2.43 cos θ, .07 + 2.43 sin θ). At a 145-degree opening, θ is 35 degrees, giving Y about 1.9905 and Z about 1.4638. The center rises away from the lower assembly in root space while retaining the joint origin.

This is not yet a room-space prediction. If the root has the tabletop quaternion, multiply the result by that root transform before calling a direction world-up or world-forward. The useful diagnostic outcome is relative: the upper screen changes orientation and the lower screen's local transform does not. A root rotation would move both, exposing a hierarchy error immediately.

The following original browser-module recipe assumes a constructor-capable DOM and imported Three.js. It creates a new diagnostic instance, not a live application mutation. Expected result: a 145-degree opening under the scene convention, with updated world matrices. No production render is requested.

There is no hinge setter returned by the factory. The returned lid is the exact factory API for this operation. In the application, use view.setDsHinge(145) only after entering unlocked DS Inspect and waiting for the transition to finish; that method accepts opening degrees and also reframes the camera. Do not call setDsHinge(35) expecting a 35-degree stored rotation.
Preserve three pose purposes

Desk pose, Inspect pose and optional gameplay lock serve different jobs. The desk has a remembered placement and resting hinge. Inspect allows independent root rotation and hinge edits. Locking records a clone of the root quaternion plus the current lid rotation; it does not rewrite the saved desk arrangement. Unlocked gameplay defaults to the flat, front-facing configuration.

Historical commit e885636 introduced independent hinge controls and locked gameplay poses. The associated construction task (TODO/87_DS_HINGE_GAMEPLAY_POSE.todo:1) explicitly separates the desk's 110-degree resting opening from gameplay. Those records ground the feature's purpose; they are not a fresh execution or a substitute for reading the current setter.

The pose lock is session state, not permanent storage. Cloning the quaternion matters because keeping a mutable reference would allow later root edits to mutate the supposed saved pose. Clearing drag and pinch state at the lock boundary similarly prevents an earlier gesture from continuing through a new ownership rule.
Figure MD11.2. A gameplay lock captures a chosen pose without converting that pose into the console's remembered desk placement.
MD11-R01 Retry with a nearly folded lid

Change the opening from 145 to 30 degrees. The stored rotation becomes 150 degrees, placing much of the upper assembly over the lower half. A previously visible control may now be covered even if the whole console remains inside the camera frustum. The correct retry does not increase exposure, disable depth testing or keep invisible controls clickable.

Recompute articulated bounds and update matrices, then let occlusion decide availability. projectControls() checks facing, clip-space limits and lid intersections before exposing projected HTML buttons. Its projection path (src/ds-controller.js:684) explains why a folded control can disappear correctly. For touch, the first relevant root intersection must be the lower LCD, not simply any intersection farther down the ray.

Also recheck materials at an oblique angle. Shared rounded solids obtain their bevels through ExtrudeGeometry construction (src/handheld.js:19). A highlight vanishing on a grazing face is not automatically a missing normal; first determine whether the face points away from the lamp or is physically hidden.
Precision checks for a convincing joint

Recommended diagnostic procedure. Inspect the joint from front, rear and a grazing side direction while holding the root transform fixed. A front view checks continuity across barrel sections; a rear view checks whether the leaves remain attached to the shell; the side view reveals an offset pivot that a frontal image can conceal. These are complementary questions rather than three decorative views of the same proof.

Measure in the joint's local frame before measuring in world space. A collar radius .258 versus barrel radius .255 creates a radial difference of .003. That is a deliberate small geometric distinction in the source, not a reason to round every number to two decimals. A rounded diagnostic export could erase the distinction even though the original geometry retains it. Conversely, do not report the .003 as a manufacturing clearance: both are visual surfaces and are not an axle-and-bearing tolerance pair.

If a collar appears detached, inspect its width and axial position independently of radius. A larger radius repairs a radial silhouette gap but cannot repair an axial separation. If a leaf penetrates the barrel, first decide whether the overlap is intentional cover geometry or a visible discontinuity. A mechanical mesh requires different checks from an economical visual joint, and the current source promises the latter.

For a proposed alternate shell size, preserve the pivot origin and change the child offset deliberately. Moving the lid center without revisiting its nearest edge can create an exposed gap at the joint. Calculate the edge position from half-height, center offset and bevel extension, then inspect the resulting seam through the allowed opening range. Checking only the 145-degree diagnostic pose can miss a collision or gap near 30 degrees.

Finally distinguish geometry precision from input precision. A correctly rotating lid can still leave stale hit targets if the scene matrix refresh is omitted. Record the opening angle, stored radians, root quaternion and matrix-update stage together. That record turns an intermittent “hinge bug” into a reproducible question about either geometry, state guards or projection.
MD11-Q01 Exercise: diagnose a lid that translates while folding

A reconstruction rotates a shell mesh about its own center and then updates the lid group's position on each frame to make the lower edge “approximately stay put.” The barrel is also parented under that group. Why is the result fragile, and what should a replacement validation measure?
MD11-A01 Explained answer

The implementation has replaced one stable joint frame with two coupled approximations: rotation plus corrective translation. Small changes to shell dimensions invalidate the correction, and the barrel moves with the lid even though it should identify the fixed joint axis. Put the lid origin at the joint, offset shell geometry in the child frame, and keep the barrel root-owned. The replacement needs only one articulation transform.

Measure a joint-adjacent reference point over several openings and confirm it follows the intended hinge neighborhood rather than circling the shell center. Check that the lower LCD, battery cover and branding retain their root-local transforms. Then validate occlusion and actual input in the articulated pose. The browser's independent-hinge scenario (tests/browser/ds.spec.mjs:927) is read evidence for those application expectations, not a test rerun in this authoring task. A stationary hinge point alone cannot prove usable screens or correct projected input.
