MD19 / PEAR BOY: THE PARAMETRIC BODY
Pear Boy: the parametric body
Evidence boundary and construction objective

Implemented behavior. Pear Boy is authored by createPearBoy, not imported from a sculpting package. The factory assembles a lathed shell, projected facial geometry, simulated rope limbs, decorative stem and leaf, contact shadow, and interior lights. This chapter reconstructs the shell first because its sampled profile becomes the geometric authority for both facial depth and rope collision. The implementation baseline is commit 1e4ef518d6943ab1af39cef3b4d558f209a17891; measurements below are model units, not inferred manufacturing dimensions. See factory and profile (src/pear-boy.js:5).

Design interpretation. A broad lower body and narrower upper neck can read as soft, stable, and toy-like. That is an interpretation of the silhouette, not proof that a user approved it or that a physical silicone prototype exists. The useful procedural objective is more concrete: preserve a continuous, rotationally symmetric shell whose front surface can be sampled consistently by independent features.
Build the profile before the surface

The profile starts as ten radius-height pairs in the XY plane. The endpoints are (0,.16) and (0,6.85). Intermediate radii grow through 1.6, 2.5, and 2.85, then taper through 2.8, 2.5, 1.95, 1.6, and 1. The widest authored control point is therefore at height 1.3, not at the middle of a generic sphere. The control-point list is interpolated with CatmullRomCurve3, sampled with getPoints(96), converted to Vector2, and clamped to nonnegative radius. This produces 97 sampled profile points.

There are two distinct resolutions: 96 curve divisions describe the vertical silhouette; 64 lathe segments describe angular sampling. Increasing one cannot repair undersampling in the other direction. A coarsely sampled profile can produce a stepped shoulder despite a smooth circular cross-section. Conversely, a fine profile with too few radial segments can look polygonal from above. Do not silently replace getPoints with evenly spaced arc-length samples: that would change the correspondence used by the downstream height lookup. The actual choices appear together at shell construction (src/pear-boy.js:66).
Figure MD19.1. One sampled profile supplies the lathe and the later shell queries; those consumers must not drift into independent approximations.
Derive the shell coordinates

For explanatory purposes, let r(y) denote the radius interpolated between neighboring sampled profile points. A rotational shell can be described by x=r(y) sin(theta) and z=r(y) cos(theta). This is a derivation of the surface of revolution, not a transcription of Three.js's internal vertex ordering. Positive Z is the authored face direction. At each fixed height, the ideal cross-section satisfies x²+z²=r(y)².

The code does not solve the original spline analytically for height. radiusAt finds the first sample after index eight with height at least the requested value, then linearly interpolates its radius against the preceding sample. The index guard avoids the beginning of the rounded base. Its validity depends on the authored profile behaving sensibly over the queried heights. A proposed profile with loops or decreasing height needs a new lookup contract; the existing function is not a general spline inversion algorithm.

This distinction explains why a visually plausible replacement sphere is insufficient. The face and collision code would continue asking the old profile for radii. A faithful rebuild must retain one authority, or deliberately update every dependent consumer and its tests.
Topology, normals, and ownership

The body uses LatheGeometry(profile,64) and a MeshStandardMaterial. The factory does not manually recalculate its normals after construction. Do not describe the body as a subdivision surface, voxel remesh, or normal-map sculpt: none of those stages appears here. The mesh helper marks the object with userData.pearBoy, sets receiveShadow, and adds it to the root. The root owns model placement; the body geometry remains in local coordinates.

Researched guidance. Current Three.js BufferGeometry documentation distinguishes indexed shared vertices from non-indexed triangles and explains that normal recomputation behaves differently for each. That reference was consulted on 2026-11-07; it is not an immutable description of this repository's dependency internals. If a proposed extension edits lathe positions directly, inspect its actual index and normal attributes before deciding how to rebuild shading. Updating positions alone is not a complete geometry-editing policy.

The material's cream base, roughness .65, warm emissive color, and intensity 77 are factory defaults. They suggest a luminous toy surface but do not implement subsurface scattering or elastic shell deformation.
Keep decoration separate from shell authority

The brown stem is a curved tube through heights 6.8, 7.55, and 8.02, with radius .22. The leaf is a planar Bézier outline extruded .08, with .04 bevel size and thickness. Its root translation is (0,7.5,.2); the vein is another small tube. These parts extend the recognizable silhouette without changing radiusAt. See stem, leaf, and vein (src/pear-boy.js:285).

That separation matters in collision interpretation. A profile-radius query describes the pear shell, not the leaf or every decorative protrusion. Conversely, an object-wide box can include protrusions that are not intended as physical support. Neither representation replaces the other. The source uses several envelopes for different jobs; treating all of them as the literal surface would produce contradictory dimensions.
Figure MD19.2. Actual original-factory diagnostic under neutral studio lighting; useful for silhouette comparison, not proof of native-room illumination or animation.
MD19-W01 Reconstruct a cross-section consistently

Begin with the exact control points, create the 97-point profile, and select height 4.5, the facial anchor height. Locate the same bracketing samples that radiusAt uses. Compute t=(4.5-a.y)/(b.y-a.y) and then r=a.x+t(b.x-a.x). Do not substitute the radius of a neighboring control point: the sampled interpolant is the implemented surface authority.

Next choose a test horizontal coordinate .66, matching one calm eye center. Derive its shell depth as sqrt(r²-.66²) and add the feature's chosen offset. Repeat with negative .66. The two depths should match because the shell is rotationally symmetric. Their X coordinates differ; their Y and Z values should not. This checks both symmetry and the sign convention without needing a rendered screenshot.

Finally compare the derived point with the factory's front result and check that all coordinates are finite. A useful observable recipe is to create the factory in its normal browser environment, inspect the named black eyes, and compare their neutral local positions. The texture helper needs a document canvas, so do not claim a bare Node factory run works without a canvas adapter. The helper's actual environment requirement is visible at canvas creation (src/handheld.js:68).
MD19-R01 Widen the belly without breaking dependents

Proposed extension. Change the 2.85 control radius to 3.1 in an isolated experiment, retaining its height and the sampling counts. This retry changes geometry, not only material color. Rebuild the shell and derive radii at limb attachment heights and the face height. A local belly change can influence adjacent spline intervals; do not assume the effect ends exactly at the edited control point.

Diagnose three consequences separately. First inspect the silhouette for a new shoulder kink. Second compare projected facial depths using the new shared profile. Third settle the ropes against the new radius function. The rope constraint pushes points outward using body radius plus cord or tip radius, as implemented in body contact (src/pear-rope.js:140). A rope that intersects the widened shell is not repaired by increasing render order.

Also re-evaluate body movement bounds. PearMotion has a deliberately simplified box, not a runtime extraction of every new profile vertex. Widening beyond its half-width can invalidate collision expectations even when the visible mesh is excellent.
Movement and clearance are different contracts

The motion controller bounds Pear by (-3,0,-3) to (3,8.1,3), with root workspace from (-22,0,-11.5) to (24,25,7.5). Those values govern upright body motion; they are not a promise to enclose every hanging foot. See PearMotion configuration (src/pear-motion.js:150).

The factory additionally computes an object box and expands its horizontal reach to at least ±4.5. Scene clearance starts with that envelope and unions current children except the contact plane. That arrangement protects broader limb reach while avoiding a fake shadow becoming solid furniture. Scene envelope assembly (src/scene.js:797) and the separate placement solver (src/desk-clearance.js:3) explain why a new body shape needs integration checks, not merely a neutral-front capture.
Figure MD19.3. A silhouette edit propagates into three geometric contracts before the model can be considered safely placeable.
Preserve useful invariants during reconstruction

A practical reconstruction should record three independent measurements before experimenting: the shell's local vertical span, sampled radius at the face anchor, and full assembly bounds after settling. The first describes body geometry, the second supports attachment math, and the third describes scene participation. Combining them into one “size” number throws away the distinction that makes later failures diagnosable. The factory exposes both body and bounds, while motion supplies another explicitly configured envelope (src/pear-boy.js:375; src/pear-motion.js:150).

For a proposed lower-resolution version, reduce only one sampling direction at a time in an isolated copy. Compare front silhouette, top circularity, and projected face clearance under the same coordinates. A lower polygon count is not automatically a valid optimization if broad expression patches start intersecting a coarser shell. Likewise, a higher count is not evidence of a better design if it changes nothing visible at the intended desk scale. The relevant tradeoff is observable quality against geometry cost, with the attachment contract retained.

The existing rope tests offer a useful numerical counterpart to silhouette inspection: finite coordinates, pinned attachment, controlled length error, and correct edge support. Keep the tests' synthetic constant-radius fixture distinct from the actual pear profile. Passing that fixture validates solver mechanics, not every authored radius sample. A profile-specific extension should sample its own critical heights rather than copying the fixture's constant 2.8 as if it were the entire body's radius. The fixture and its assertions are explicit in (tests/unit/pear-rope.test.mjs:6).
MD19-Q01 Choose the right failure detector

A rebuilt Pear looks correct from the front, but its hand enters the shell after a lateral pickup. Should the first repair change shell roughness, add more radial lathe segments, or inspect the shared radius/contact contract? Explain what additional observation would distinguish a bad collision radius from an incorrectly transformed rope.
MD19-A01 Separate shape, contact, and coordinate failures

Inspect the radius/contact contract first. Roughness changes shading, and radial segments change the polygonal approximation; neither necessarily changes the constraint's requested clearance. Compare each rope point in world coordinates against the body-local radius evaluated at point.y-origin.y. Then check that painting subtracts the root position exactly once. A consistent radial shortfall suggests wrong radius or tip clearance; a displacement that follows root translation suggests a coordinate conversion error.

The failure boundary is important: the rope only collides with the pear and desk, not arbitrary scene props. Existing rope unit cases exercise body contact and stale-momentum removal, but do not prove a future profile is safe at every possible point. Use them as regression contracts, then add focused negative controls for the changed shape. This handbook is a reproducible reconstruction aid, not a recovered internal design memory.

MD20 / PROJECTING A FACE ONTO A CURVED SHELL
Projecting a face onto a curved shell
Why a flat face fails on a rounded body

Implemented behavior. The Pear face is real mesh geometry attached to a curved shell. It is not a texture decal and does not use a camera-facing billboard. Its placement function derives Z from the same sampled radius profile that builds the body. The important dependency is therefore geometric: a facial feature must remain outside a shell whose depth changes with both height and horizontal coordinate. See profile, front projection, and patches (src/pear-boy.js:66).

Design interpretation. Keeping the markings close to the surface can make them read as part of a soft lamp rather than floating accessories. That reading does not establish a physical printing process. The procedural problem is simply to balance surface clearance against conspicuous separation, including when the face moves.
Derive the front projection and its domain

At a chosen height, the ideal section satisfies x²+z²=r². Selecting the front half gives z=sqrt(r²-x²). The code adds a positive offset, named inset, although numerically it pushes the point outward along positive Z. Its default is .03. A literal inward normal displacement would have a different meaning; use the actual equation rather than interpreting the name as a physical direction.

The function clamps the square-root argument to zero. This prevents a negative radicand from generating NaN when |x|>r, but does not make such a point a correct surface attachment. It would sit beyond the valid circular section with depth equal to the offset. Nor does front include the explicit height guard present in radiusAt; an out-of-range height can fail while selecting its interpolation pair. Valid feature authoring must respect both domains.

For a broad patch, it is not enough to project only its corners. A triangle connects projected vertices with planar edges. Across a convex shell that flat chord can cut inward between samples, burying its interior even when the vertices are individually clear. This is the reason to examine tessellation before increasing offset.
Form expressions in two dimensions first

facePatch constructs a ShapeGeometry with curve-segment argument 16, converts it to non-indexed triangles, copies its positions into vectors, and disposes both intermediate geometries. It then performs two triangle subdivision passes. Each triangle becomes four by introducing edge midpoints. After two passes an original triangle contributes sixteen triangles. Only then are all vertices projected using front.

This ordering is the central lesson: shape placement happens in its XY description before projection. Translating an already projected patch vertically does not re-evaluate the shell radius at the new height. A mouth can consequently enter a region of greater shell depth and disappear behind the body; movement toward a narrower region can instead leave it floating. The implemented anger mark follows the safer pattern too: it adds .42 to the authored Y coordinate before calling front, rather than moving the finished tube afterward. See anger mark construction (src/pear-boy.js:215).
Figure MD20.1. Subdivision precedes projection so the filled interior follows the rounded shell rather than remaining a large cutting plane.
Tubes, patches, and small solid features

The calm eyes are scaled spheres at x=±.66, y=4.5, with scale (.18,.22,.09). The smile samples seventeen points from X -.5 to .5, using a sine depression of .32 from height 3.96, then forms a tube of radius .055. These solids have their own thickness; they are not equivalent to a zero-
thickness patch with the same center coordinate.

Expression eyes, cheeks, mouth fills, and tongue use different offsets. Typical patch clearance is .06; the white angry-eye interior and tongue use .085; rosy cheeks use .025. These layers should be understood relative to their projected surface, not as absolute world depths. The mesh helper initially adds meshes to the model root, after which adding them to a face group reparents them. Their coordinates were already authored in model space, and those face groups start with identity transforms.

Researched guidance. Current BufferGeometry documentation states that absent indices, successive triples form triangles. That supports the patch's setFromPoints construction. The returned patches do not explicitly compute normals or retain UV coordinates; their MeshBasicMaterial colors do not require the same lighting response as the standard-material shell.
Move around the body axis, not the face center

face.root is a group at the body origin, containing both expression groups and permanent freckles. Horizontal tracking rotates this group about Y. Because its geometry is already located near the shell's front, that operation moves features around the body axis. Rotating a group newly centered at the face anchor would instead turn markings around their own center, an entirely different trajectory.

Vertical tracking translates the group and scales X and Z by radiusAt(4.5+dy)/radiusAt(4.5). This is a shared center-height approximation, not a per-vertex reprojection at every feature height. It preserves a coherent face while accommodating the narrowing shell. The fixed anchor is a separate object attached directly to the model root, so pointer normalization does not chase the moving face. See anchor and transform update and gaze transform (src/pear-boy.js:248).
MD20-W01 Derive lateral motion of a marking

Take a neutral point (x,y,z) on the face. Let the horizontal normalized gaze be one, so the implemented yaw is .55 radians. Under the conventional Y rotation, its new horizontal coordinate is x cos(.55)+z sin(.55). This includes a contribution from shell depth. An eye can therefore move substantially farther than a simple .55-unit lateral translation would suggest. The angle is approximately 31.5 degrees; it is not a screen-pixel distance.

Now set upward gaze to one. The implemented Y offset is .75 model units, not .75 radians. Compute the radius ratio at heights 5.25 and 4.5. Apply that ratio to local X and Z before yaw. The exact numerical result must come from the sampled profile, not from assuming a spherical head.

For an observable reproduction, compare world positions of both named black eyes at neutral and extreme gaze after updateWorldMatrix(true,true). Keep the root position unchanged and separately project the fixed anchor. The browser regression requires upward eye movement over .65 world units and five screen pixels, with an unchanged anchor. It also checks smile and freckle movement. See pointer assertions.
MD20-R01 Move a broad mouth toward the shoulder

Proposed extension. Raise an expression mouth's XY control points by .3 before constructing its shape. Rebuild its triangulation and projection; do not translate the finished mesh. The changed condition is increased shell curvature and a smaller radius at the new height. Inspect the patch center as well as its perimeter, because corner-only tests miss chord penetration.

If the interior disappears, first verify subdivision and the resulting vertex depths. Increasing offset may restore visibility but can leave a floating outline in three-quarter views. Increasing tessellation better approximates curvature, at a geometry cost. Replacing the fill with a texture is another tradeoff, but it would introduce UV and texture-resolution contracts absent from the implemented expression pipeline.

Do not assume DoubleSide fixes buried geometry. It can expose back faces, but the shell can still occlude the patch. Current Raycaster documentation also distinguishes back-face behavior from closest-hit ordering. Diagnose the actual surface intersection instead of using material settings as a substitute for correct placement.
Visibility means foremost appearance

The freckle test casts toward each dot and selects the nearest intersection whose entire ancestor chain is visible. A dot's own visible=true is not sufficient if its parent is hidden. Nor does a visible flag prove the body or another eye is not in front of it. The test examines all nine gaze combinations for four expressions, requiring all six foremost names to be the freckle name. See visibility filtering.
Figure MD20.2. A geometric visibility check rejects hidden ancestors and intervening surfaces before accepting a facial marking.
Integration constraints beyond the face

The same model root also carries moving limbs and lights. Rope painting converts simulated world positions back to root-local coordinates; it must not inherit face-group yaw. Body motion is separate again, using DeskMotion integration rather than facial interpolation. These ownership boundaries are explicit in limb painting, rope origins (src/pear-rope.js:48), and body integration (src/pear-motion.js:59).

Scene pointer normalization projects the immutable anchor and clamps gaze to [-1,1], independent of the current markings (src/scene.js:1326). Texture color-space setup is centralized in the canvas helper (src/handheld.js:68), whereas face patches use direct basic colors. Those distinctions explain why changing emission or the canvas gradient is not a repair for a buried mouth.
Depth offsets are a layered budget

The patch and solid-feature offsets form a small but important depth budget. An angry eye's white interior at .085 sits farther forward than the black outline's default .06; the tongue uses the same larger offset against its mouth fill. Blush at .025 is intentionally closer to the shell than many ink features. These are source values, not universal safe distances. Their relative arrangement is visible in the expression constructors (src/pear-boy.js:136; src/pear-boy.js:202).

When adapting a feature, first identify which layer should be foremost and whether it is a tube, flattened sphere, or triangulated fill. A tube radius contributes additional geometric depth around its centerline, whereas a patch has no comparable thickness. Equal center offsets therefore do not imply equal front surfaces. This explains why moving every feature to the same Z offset can introduce new occlusion even if it removes shell penetration.

A useful proposed diagnostic is to cast separate rays toward the intended foreground layer, its surrounding outline, and a point just beyond the feature. Record object identity, not only hit distance, because two parts can be nearly coplanar while belonging to different expressions. Repeat after upward and horizontal gaze, then compare the same local layer ordering. This extends the existing freckle-center method without pretending it already tests every mouth pixel. If a repair requires disabling depth testing, stop and re-examine geometry: the current implementation's lesson is to construct surface-following features, not to draw facial colors over unrelated objects.
MD20-Q01 Diagnose a face that vanishes only upward

A new cheek fill is visible at neutral gaze but becomes partly hidden looking up. Its object and parent are visible, and its corner vertices are outside the shell. What should be measured next, and why is rotating the whole lamp an invalid repair?
MD20-A01 Inspect interior sampling and transform ownership

Measure interior triangle clearance at the changed height, then inspect the group's center-height scale approximation. Large planar triangles may penetrate between clear vertices; a shape extending far above the anchor may also exceed the approximation's useful range. Rebuild with more appropriate sampling or change its authored XY extent before projection.

Rotating the whole lamp changes body, ropes, lights, and desk collision relationships. It conceals the local error by changing the viewing condition. The failure boundary is that the current face transform is designed for the authored range, not arbitrary expressions spanning the entire pear. History records wider gaze and later upward travel, but those commits do not prove every proposed larger face is safe. Extend the geometric test grid and inspect actual appearance rather than converting historical qualification into universal approval.

MD21 / EXPRESSIONS, GAZE AND SIX VISIBLE FRECKLES
Expressions, gaze and six visible freckles
Separate where the face looks from what it expresses

Implemented behavior. createPearBoy builds four expression groups beneath one movable face root: calm, scared, angry, and sad. The public expression labels are curious, scared, angry, and sad; the final sad appearance is a squeezed-eye pout, not the earlier glossy worried face. Gaze moves the shared face root, while visibility selects the expression. This separation prevents each expression from implementing slightly different tracking. Face ownership (src/pear-boy.js:43) is the authoritative hierarchy.

Design interpretation. The compact eyes, short brows, blush, and puckered mouth can communicate a gentler reaction than large wedges. “Cuter” is a design interpretation and historical task vocabulary, not a measurable shader property. This chapter instead makes the mechanics reproducible: which geometry appears, what triggers it, how long it remains eligible, and which markings never belong to a temporary expression.
Permanent freckles are structural, not duplicated decoration

Each side creates three dots at positive-coordinate pairs (1.05,4.25), (1.16,4.03), and (.92,4.04), mirrored in X by the side sign. Each dot is a sphere of radius .055, with ten width and eight height segments, flattened in Z by .4. The material is orange MeshBasicMaterial with tone mapping disabled. All six are attached directly to face.root, not to calm or scared. See freckle creation (src/pear-boy.js:160).

This ownership makes six a persistent inventory invariant. Duplicating the dots into four groups would multiply maintenance points and could accidentally leave two sets visible. Attaching them outside the moving root would preserve their count but break whole-face tracking. Neither error is caught by simply counting named objects in the entire model; both hierarchy and actual foremost visibility must be checked.
Gaze math and a fixed reference

The scene projects an immutable anchor at the original face center, converts cursor displacement into fractions of twenty percent of viewport width and height, and clamps each axis to [-1,1]. Upward screen movement reverses the usual screen-Y direction. The anchor is separate from the animated face group, avoiding a feedback loop in which the target moves because the face already moved. See scene normalization (src/scene.js:1326).

The gaze interpolation blend is 1-exp(-12*delta), or one for reduced motion. For a constant target, the remaining error after elapsed time t behaves like exp(-12t) until the snap threshold is reached. The characteristic time is about .0833 seconds. A squared error below 1e-7 copies the target exactly, preventing perpetual microscopic changes.

Horizontal gaze produces Y-axis rotation up to .55 radians. Positive vertical gaze produces up to .75 model units of rise; negative gaze produces down to -.18. These are deliberately different dimensions. A radius ratio scales X and Z to follow the changing shell width. It is not a .75-radian pitch.
Figure MD21.1. Gaze is derived from a stationary reference and applied once to every expression and permanent dot.
Expression state and paint acknowledgment

showExpression switches group visibility, restores the wobbly scared mouth, hides the open scream mouth, resets elapsed time, and clears presented. setFaceLifted selects scared or curious unless an impact reaction currently owns the face. A reset or new lift clears that reaction. reactToImpact ignores speeds below ten and ignores another impact while already reacting. State setters (src/pear-boy.js:224) establish these rules.

While reacting, angry lasts at least .9 accumulated seconds and sad at least 1.25, but transitions additionally require presented=true. The scene sets that flag after submitting the main room render. Consequently a stalled renderer cannot silently consume the entire reaction sequence before any expression was submitted. This is a visibility contract layered over elapsed time, not a promise of exact wall-clock dwell on every device.

When lifted without a reaction, the two scream mouths alternate after .9 seconds only if the current mouth was presented. Reduced motion suppresses that alternation and forces the wobbly mouth if the open one was visible. Recovery can still progress through static expressions. See face update.
MD21-W01 Reproduce the mouth dwell without a stopwatch

Use the factory in its normal browser environment and explicitly call setFaceLifted(true). Acknowledge one presentation, then update with .6 seconds and zero gaze. The wobbly mouth remains selected. Add .31 seconds: the accumulated .91 crosses .9, so the open mouth becomes visible and presented resets.

Without another acknowledgment, advancing time does not authorize another switch. After acknowledgment, repeat the .6 and .31 pair. The deterministic browser test records [false,true,true,false,false], where the final false comes from a reduced-motion update forcing the closed variant. This recipe distinguishes state timing from automation latency and does not require loosening any screenshot deadline.

Then test a hard impact separately: set lifted false with reset, call reactToImpact(20), and inspect the expression label. Advance beyond .9 without acknowledging paint; angry should remain. Acknowledge, update, and observe sad. Repeat beyond 1.25 to return to curious if no longer lifted. The actual browser timing and visibility fixture provides an existing executable model for this separation.
MD21-R01 Retry under sparse rendering and reduced motion

Change conditions from regular paints to a long update with no paint acknowledgment. If all expressions disappear immediately into curious, inspect whether a caller set presented before rendering or bypassed the state setter. Do not conclude that large deltas inherently require skipping intermediate states. The implementation explicitly preserves them until presentation.

Next enable reduced motion. Gaze should snap rather than ease; mouth alternation should stop; impact recovery remains eligible after its timing and presentation conditions. Rope motion has a different accommodation: it settles constraints immediately instead of swinging. See reduced-motion limbs and the settling procedure (src/pear-rope.js:34). Reduced motion is therefore not a global instruction to freeze every state variable or teleport a dropped body home.

MD22 / LIMBS, ROPE AND SOFT MOTION
Limbs, rope and soft motion
What softness actually means here

Implemented behavior. Pear's shell does not squash. Soft motion comes from four separately simulated ropes, each ending in a rounded hand or foot. PearRope owns simulated points, prior points, segment lengths, collision queries, and sleep state. The factory owns their tube meshes and terminal geometry. Calling this a skinned character or finite-element silicone solver would invent an authoring pipeline absent from the source. Rope state (src/pear-rope.js:1) and factory limb creation (src/pear-boy.js:110) define that division.

Design interpretation. Inertial lag, rounded tips, and resting feet can suggest a small hanging toy. The measurable implementation contracts are stronger and less subjective: attachment stays pinned, segment lengths remain bounded, body and desk contact are respected, and the final tube follows finite simulated points without allocating a new mesh every frame.
Establish rest geometry and terminal dimensions

Each authored limb starts from a three-point Catmull–Rom curve. The factory uses getSpacedPoints(6), producing seven particles and six rest lengths. Arms start around (±2.48,3.45,.35) and terminate initially around (±3.05,1.6,.8). Legs begin at (±1.2,.65,2.35) and extend toward (±2.05,.36,3.85). These are authoring seeds, not guaranteed final settled particle positions.

Cord radius is .14 in the factory, overriding the solver's .085 default. Hands use contact tip radius .32. Feet use radial contact extent .55 but floor height .36, matching their visibly wider-than-tall scale. Distinguishing tipRadius and tipFloor is essential at the rounded desk edge: a spherical collision assumption would lift a flattened foot too high.

The factory runs up to 600 warm-up updates, stores the settled points as rest, resets, then later settles again at the actual model origin. This makes the visible default depend on desk placement, not merely the original curve. Hand and foot seeds are the reproducible starting values.
Derive Verlet-style movement

For each unpinned point, the solver computes an inertial displacement d=.985*(p-pPrevious), copies the current point into previous, adds d, and subtracts 45*h² from Y, where h=1/120. The gravity displacement per step is .003125 model units. This is a position-based integrator; there is no independently stored velocity vector for each particle.

Root movement updates the pinned first point immediately. If a pointer teleport moves the root farther than twice total rope length, both current and previous free points receive the excess translation. Moving both avoids inventing velocity from the correction. Even when less than one fixed step has accumulated, a moved root invokes constraint solving, preventing a rapid pointer event from leaving the rope stretched until the next tick. Update and integration (src/pear-rope.js:48) implement these safeguards.
Figure MD22.1. Solver time and visible tube updates are separate stages; root movement can constrain attachment even before a full physics step.
Length constraints and convergence limits

For neighboring points A and B, let current separation be d, length l, and rest length L. The correction vector is d*(l-L)/(l*(wA+wB)). A moves by wA times that vector; B moves oppositely by wB times it. The attachment has weight zero, ordinary particles weight one, and the last particle weight .3. Thus the terminal particle receives less positional correction than an ordinary point; it behaves as a relatively heavy tip in this constraint distribution.

The solver performs at most 120 iterations, interleaving segment corrections and collision corrections. It exits early when every segment differs from its rest length by less than .002. A near-zero segment length is skipped to avoid division by zero. This is bounded iterative convergence, not an exact algebraic guarantee for every impossible configuration.

Sleep requires every free point's squared movement to remain below 2e-6 for 24 consecutive integration steps. On sleep, previous positions are copied to current and the accumulator clears. Those operations eliminate residual momentum instead of merely suppressing drawing.
Finite tabletop contact and the hanging foot

The rope's desk model has front Z 10, bottom Y -2.4, and a separate lower safety floor near Y -35. Points over the tabletop use their cord or tip floor. Beyond the front edge, the solver permits hanging below the table instead of applying an infinite horizontal plane.

At the upper front corner, contact uses an ellipse: ((z-10)/radius)²+(y/floor)²=1. Points inside that rounded corner are projected outward. Below the top, the front fascia can push a particle to 10+radius. Supported points receive tangential damping by changing previous X and Z. This is why a foot partly over the edge can slide down instead of resting on an invisible square-expanded ledge. Contact branches show the actual finite geometry.

Body collision is radial around the translated root, using radiusAt at the particle's local height plus cord or tip radius. Arbitrary props, rotating supports, and other ropes are not included. Do not extend the desk result into a claim of general scene collision.
MD22-W01 Reproduce edge-to-table settling

Start with the exact leg seed and options from the unit test, including .14 cord radius, .55 tip radius, and .36 tip floor. Settle at origin (18,0,7.3). The terminal point should hang below -.5 and report tipSupported=false. For each point, check either top support, front clearance, or the elliptical corner condition. Also check the first particle equals rest attachment plus origin.

Move the origin back to (18,0,1) and update for sufficient fixed steps. The terminal point should return to top support, rather than preserve its previous hanging offset. Then return to the edge and allow settling again. This tests the same rope under changed support topology without swapping meshes or resetting its identity.

The executable finite-edge tests also include a foot centered only partly beyond the edge. That negative control is valuable because an over-expanded rectangular tabletop can pass a simple “never below floor” test while producing the wrong hanging pose.
Paint a stable tube without rebuilding topology

Each rope mesh starts with 24 longitudinal and six radial divisions. Painting samples the simulated curve at 25 longitudinal positions, producing seven radial vertices per ring including the seam: 175 positions. The first normal is derived from tangent crossed with either up or a fallback Z vector when the tangent is nearly vertical. Subsequent rings remove the normal's tangent component and renormalize; binormal is tangent cross normal.

For radial angle a, the outward direction is -cos(a)*normal+sin(a)*binormal. It supplies the normal attribute; multiplying by cord radius and adding the curve point supplies position. Both attributes are marked dirty, and bounding box and sphere are recomputed. The tip follows the last local curve point. Supported tips use identity orientation; hanging tips align their up axis toward the preceding segment. Dynamic tube painting is explicit about these ownership conversions.
MD22-R01 Retry with a multi-second callback

Replace regular 1/120 updates with a three-second callback for the same total elapsed time. The solver accepts at most five seconds per update and integrates fixed steps; it does not turn gravity into one giant unstable Euler jump. The unit trajectory test compares sub-Hz, 2 Hz, 30 Hz, and 120 Hz results. Then try a .001-second root movement to exercise the separate inter-step constraint path.

If attachment is correct numerically but the rendered cord detaches, inspect world-to-local conversion in painting. Simulated points are world coordinates; curve points subtract root.position. Subtracting twice or also rotating through the animated face root introduces a visible error unrelated to constraint convergence.

Researched guidance. Current BufferGeometry documentation explains why changed vertex data needs updated bounds for culling and ray queries. Omitting that maintenance can make a correct rope disappear at a camera boundary. It is not evidence that the physics slept.
Figure MD22.2. The visible rope is reconstructed from world simulation into root-local rings, with explicit normals and refreshed spatial bounds.
Integration and limits

Reduced motion settles each changed rope rather than preserving oscillation. Body movement itself belongs to DeskMotion (src/pear-motion.js:59); it is not driven by rope tip forces. Scene rendering invalidates its clearance signature when limbs move (src/scene.js:1367), because the

envelope can change without root translation. The horizontal placement solver then evaluates geometry-derived obstacles (src/desk-clearance.js:3). These three supporting files establish why an idle root does not necessarily mean a settled layout.

The braided cord appearance is a repeating canvas texture with crossing diagonal strokes, not modeled individual fibers. The shared canvas helper uses sRGB color space (src/handheld.js:68). This texture supplies tactile suggestion cheaply; the six-sided tube still determines silhouette and collision radius.
Distinguish solver particles from visible curvature

Seven particles do not mean the viewer sees six straight cord segments. The factory interpolates a Catmull–Rom curve through those points and samples that curve for the dynamic tube. Conversely, collision checks act on the particles, not every interpolated point of the visible curve. A highly curved new limb could therefore look closer to a surface between particles than the particle contacts suggest. This is a meaningful limit of the implemented representation, not evidence that the present authored limbs fail.

Proposed extension. If longer or more tightly bent cords are needed, compare increasing particle count against adding collision samples along the interpolant. More particles increase constraint work and change the dynamic system; more paint rings improve visible smoothness without necessarily improving contact. State which problem is being solved before increasing either resolution. The source separates getSpacedPoints(6) from the 24-division tube precisely enough to make this comparison reproducible (src/pear-boy.js:112).

Another useful negative control is a root teleport exceeding twice total rope length. Check that the solver shifts both current and previous free points by the excess and that no enormous throw appears afterward. Then check an ordinary short move still produces lag. Suppressing all lag would make the teleport test pass trivially while breaking the intended soft motion. The existing attachment-and-inertia unit case provides the positive counterpart. Together those tests explain why the teleport correction is bounded rather than a blanket reset on every pointer event.
MD22-Q01 Identify the unsupported extension

A new swinging hand passes through a cartridge while still clearing the pear and tabletop. Does that contradict the existing solver contract? Propose the minimum additional responsibility required for a real repair.
MD22-A01 Add collision authority, not a cosmetic offset

It does not contradict the current contract: arbitrary props are absent from PearRope.constrain. A genuine extension must provide obstacle geometry in a consistent coordinate frame and reconcile those contacts with pinned length constraints. Merely moving the hand mesh leaves the simulated
endpoint and painted tube behind.

The failure boundary is convergence under competing contacts. Add a negative test where the cartridge blocks the old trajectory, verify finite coordinates and bounded length errors, and define what happens if no feasible rope shape exists. Without that policy, increasing iteration count can hide an impossible configuration rather than solve it.

MD23 / AXOLOTL: THE SILICONE BODY
Axolotl: the silicone body
Reconstruct the actual primitive assembly

Implemented behavior. createAxolotlLamp creates a compact cream-and-pink companion from shared spheres, extruded outlines, a smile tube, and an interior point light. There is no imported organic mesh, sculpting session, skeletal rig, or silicone deformation simulation in this factory. Its returned handles are root, head, silicone, pink, and light. The smaller feature count and lack of face animation distinguish it from Pear Boy, despite their shared movement controller. Complete body setup (src/axolotl-lamp.js:3) is the reconstruction starting point.

Design interpretation. A large rounded head and low elongated body can read as a small friendly night-light. “Silicone” is the implementation's material name and intended visual category, not proof of subsurface scattering, material measurement, or a physical fabrication process. Build the actual geometry and then evaluate the visual interpretation separately.
Establish axes and the two principal ellipsoids

A single unit SphereGeometry(1,32,24) is shared among the oval helper's meshes. The body center is (0,1.12,-1.35) and its scale is (1.22,.97,1.98). The head center is (0,1.45,.2) with scale (1.65,1.3,1.32). Thus the body extends mainly toward negative Z, while the face is authored on the positive-Z hemisphere of the head.

Derive approximate principal extents before adding details. The body spans X ±1.22, Y .15 to 2.09, and Z -3.33 to .63. The head spans X ±1.65, Y .15 to 2.75, and Z -1.12 to 1.52. These are ellipsoid extrema from scale and translation, not the final whole-model box: gills, feet, toes, and tail extend it.

The two meshes overlap. There is no Boolean union or watertight remeshing step. Their common material and rounded overlap create continuity in appearance, but a future export or physical manufacturing workflow would need an explicit solid-union policy. Do not infer one from a smooth-looking render.
Figure MD23.1. Two transformed copies of one sphere geometry form the visible body assembly without a Boolean union.
Geometry sharing and transform ownership

The oval helper adds a mesh under the root and changes object scale, not the shared sphere's positions. That distinction makes sharing safe: changing one eye's object scale does not resize the head. Editing the shared geometry's vertices, however, would affect every oval using it. A proposed shape-specific deformation must clone the geometry or introduce a separate primitive.

Each mesh is named with the axolotl prefix, tagged userData.axolotlLamp=true, and marked to receive shadows. The entire root owns placement and scene yaw. Eyes and cheeks receive their own quaternions for surface orientation, while the head remains an independently returned mesh. The factory does not animate these transforms after creation.

Researched guidance. Current BufferGeometry documentation describes geometry attributes, normals, and disposal. That reference explains the general distinction between modifying a geometry and transforming an object; the actual sharing policy here is established by the one sphere allocation and the helper calls in pinned source.
Project features onto the head

For head-relative coordinates, the ellipsoid equation is (x/1.65)²+((y-1.45)/1.3)²+((z-.2)/1.32)²=1. Solving the positive-Z branch gives z=.2+1.32*sqrt(1-(x/1.65)²-((y-1.45)/1.3)²)+offset. The default offset is .035. Unlike Pear's projection, this function does not clamp the radicand. A proposed feature outside the ellipse produces nonfinite coordinates and must be rejected or handled explicitly.

Eyes are placed at x=±.79, y=1.55, while cheeks use x=±1.05, y=1.24. Their small depth scales make them surface-attached ovals rather than large protruding spheres. The factory aligns their positive-Z axes to an ellipsoid-gradient direction. That supports the sideward tilt needed near the cheeks without requiring a separate facial parent rig. Projection and orientation (src/axolotl-lamp.js:29) supplies both operations.
Material identity is not optical simulation

Cream uses color #fff0dd, roughness .72, emissive #ffdcab, and factory intensity 45. Pink also uses roughness .72, with its own base and emissive colors and intensity 24. The factory's black ink and blush use basic materials with tone mapping disabled. No transmission, thickness, subsurface scattering, or custom skin shader is configured here.

Current MeshStandardMaterial guidance, consulted 2026-11-07, explains roughness and emissive modulation. It does not justify describing a high-emission surface as physically measured silicone. In particular, visible emission and light arriving on the desk are separate: the factory also creates a point emitter. Scene controls later adjust both.

Pear supplies a useful implemented contrast: its shell is lathed and its emission has a canvas gradient, whereas this lamp uses constant standard materials and shared spheres (src/pear-boy.js:8). The difference is an intentional procedural assembly distinction, not evidence that either model went through Blender.
Figure MD23.2. Actual original-factory neutral-studio diagnostic showing head/body overlap; it does not establish native-room brightness or falling motion.

Choose the positive eye center x=.79, y=1.55. First compute u=.79/1.65≈.4788 and v=.1/1.3≈.0769. The radicand is about .7648, safely positive. Its square root is about .8745; multiplying by 1.32 and adding .2+.035 yields a front depth near 1.389. These rounded calculations are explanatory; use actual double precision values for a reproduction comparison.

Next form the gradient-like vector (x/1.65²,(y-1.45)/1.3²,(z-.2)/1.32²) and normalize it. The code uses the already offset feature Z, so this is not exactly the gradient evaluated on the unoffset ellipsoid. Reproduce that detail rather than quietly replacing it with a mathematically cleaner variant. Set a quaternion from local positive Z to the normalized direction.

Finally apply the eye scale (.115,.145,.07). In a browser inspection, read the named eye's position, scale, and transformed local positive-Z vector. Compare the mirrored eye: X position and outward X direction should change sign while the Y and Z magnitudes remain symmetric. This is observable without claiming a new screenshot or a full rendering qualification.

Proposed extension. Increase head X scale from 1.65 to 1.9 while retaining its center and Y/Z radii. If the projection formula and gradient denominators remain 1.65, the features no longer follow the visible shell. The changed condition is not repaired by scaling the eye meshes alone. Update the authoring parameters consistently, then recompute front positions and surface orientation.

Measure the new whole-model box after all features are assembled and after the scene's .3-radian Y rotation. The scene captures axolotl motion bounds from the actually rotated root, translates that world AABB back by its root position, and derives root-workspace limits from its offsets. See scene construction and bounds (src/scene.js:130).

If the shape widens but its stored motion bounds do not, side collisions can accept visible overlap. Recreate or recompute those bounds deliberately in the experiment. A dynamic shape editor would need an invalidation policy; the pinned factory builds a fixed shape.
Movement uses the assembly, not anatomical joints

The axolotl's root moves through DeskMotion. Its gills, head, body, toes, tail, and light follow as children. The controller does not independently articulate feet or change the smile during impact. It stores one velocity and keeps orientation fixed during dragging and falling (src/pear-motion.js:5).

Scene clearance can temporarily displace the lamp during console focus and restore its remembered table XZ coordinates afterward. It treats the model as a spatial participant, not as a special-case painted decoration. The nearest-position helper expands obstacle rectangles by local envelope offsets and a default .25 gap (src/desk-clearance.js:3). Thus topology choices can affect layout even when the body center stays unchanged.
Figure MD23.3. Scene orientation is applied before the movement envelope is measured, preserving the assembled model's actual horizontal reach.
Historical constraint versus current behavior

Documented history. TODO/110_SMALL_AXOLOTL_LAMP.todo records the initial fixed-lamp scope, including the internal-emitter correction and independent brightness levels. TODO/111_MOVABLE_AXOLOTL.todo explicitly supersedes its fixed-position constraint with shared companion movement. The scoped f10fab1752c4d15167baeaaace4623820f0c2bee source history contains the assembled lamp. These records explain chronology, not recovered internal reasoning or fresh user approval. The supersession is recorded at (TODO/111_MOVABLE_AXOLOTL.todo:40), while the earlier optical correction remains historical evidence (TODO/110_SMALL_AXOLOTL_LAMP.todo:52).

A reconstruction agent must therefore implement the pinned movable behavior, not revive the older fixed-position rule because it appears in an acceptance record. Conversely, movement does not authorize inventing face animation, rope gills, or persistent saved lamp locations. Those are absent from this factory and would be separately labeled extensions.
Build an inspection checklist from the representation

Begin a new reconstruction with root identity transforms and verify the head/body centers before applying scene placement. This isolates an assembly error from a camera or layout error. Then check the single shared sphere geometry is used through object transforms, and that the two principal materials remain distinct handles. Their later brightness updates depend on shared material identity: accidentally cloning a cream material for one part can leave that part glowing after the scene switches the original silicone handle off.

That observation follows directly from the factory returning material handles and the scene mutating them, rather than traversing every mesh to find colors (src/axolotl-lamp.js:90; src/scene.js:586). A proposed material override needs an explicit control policy. Either include the new material in the power mapping or document it as deliberately nonemissive. Visual similarity at startup is insufficient if later state changes diverge.

Next inspect front, back, and three-quarter geometry under a neutral diagnostic setup, without treating those views as native-room evidence. A front view checks bilateral arrangement; a back view reveals the elongated body and tail overlap; a three-quarter view exposes attachment depth. Their value is complementary rather than redundant. A beautiful front image cannot prove that a tail layer is centered through its thickness.

Finally compare the complete rotated envelope with the scene workspace and test one rejected occupied placement. This connects the local assembly to its interactive role. The current model is smaller than Pear, but “smaller” alone cannot guarantee clearance when gills spread laterally or a tail extends behind the root.

The head/body junction looks smooth under warm emission. Can another agent claim the model is one watertight silicone mesh? What evidence would be required before exporting it for physical manufacture?

No. The implemented model contains overlapping sphere-based meshes with shared material, not a Boolean-unified shell. A manufacturing export would require explicit union, internal-face cleanup, manifold validation, wall-thickness decisions, and scale units. None follows from the visible overlap.

The useful failure boundary is that scene rendering tolerates intersecting parts inside a deliberately assembled character, while inter-object desk clearance forbids overlap between prioritized models. These are different contracts. Do not “repair” the intentional head/body overlap with the desk placement solver or describe the latter as an anatomical solid-model validator.

MD24 / GILLS, TAIL AND CUTE FEATURES
Gills, tail and cute features
Detail as silhouette, not unverified anatomy

Implemented behavior. The axolotl factory adds six pink gill petals, four feet, twelve toes, two eyes, two cheeks, one smile tube, and layered tail geometry around the head/body assembly. These are procedural shapes, not scanned anatomy or imported reference-image meshes. Their names describe a stylized lamp. Biological realism is outside the demonstrated contract. Feature construction (src/axolotl-lamp.js:33) makes the inventory auditable.

Design interpretation. Large side petals, short feet, small bead eyes, and an upturned tail can make the silhouette readable at desk scale. Calling that arrangement cute is interpretation, not a test result. The engineering question is whether each detail survives projection, lighting, mirroring, and collision-envelope measurement without becoming visually or numerically unstable.
Author one gill petal, then mirror instances

The petal starts at (0,0) and uses two cubic Bézier curves. The first reaches (1.02,.19) through (.28,.34) and (.86,.53); the second returns to origin through (1.14,-.19) and (.45,-.34). The geometry is extruded .12, with bevel size and thickness .09, three bevel segments, and one depth step.

The factory shares that geometry among all gills. For each side, three meshes are placed at (side*1.43,1.48,.24) and rotated around Z using angles side*[-.8,0,.8]. Their X scale is side, so the negative side reflects the local petal. Negative scale is not a request to reverse the authored control points manually; doing both would double-reflect the shape.

The attachment point is the petal's local origin. Rotation therefore fans the tip around its base, not around the center of the whole extruded shape. This pivot ownership is what allows one shared shape to form three distinct silhouette directions. Centering the geometry automatically would change the fan even if all rotations remained identical.
Figure MD24.1. Shared petal topology becomes a bilateral fan through base-pivot rotations and one X reflection per side.
Derive a petal's transformed reach

For a local planar point (u,v), X reflection produces (s*u,v), where s is the side sign. A Z rotation by s*a then mixes the horizontal and vertical coordinates. Add the mesh translation only after applying those local operations. This derivation explains why a petal's maximum world X is not simply 1.43+1.14: its rotation changes which point is extremal, and bevel geometry adds reach beyond the original planar outline.

The actual Three.js object matrix also includes the scene root's .3-radian yaw. A desk-facing screenshot cannot by itself recover the unrotated gill dimensions. For reproduction, inspect local geometry and mesh transforms separately, then compute the assembled world box. Avoid reporting a single hand-estimated width as a verified final envelope.

Researched guidance. Current BufferGeometry documentation explains that geometry bounds must reflect changed positions. Here geometry is fixed after construction, but a proposed deforming petal would need both normal and bounds maintenance. Merely changing the object's rotation uses a different transform responsibility.
Bead eyes and cheeks follow a curved normal

Eyes use the shared unit sphere at x=±.79, y=1.55 with scale (.115,.145,.07). Cheeks use x=±1.05, y=1.24 and scale (.19,.085,.045). Their centers come from the positive-Z ellipsoid function, and their quaternions align local positive Z to a normalized ellipsoid-gradient vector. See facial feature attachment (src/axolotl-lamp.js:46).

The interpretation is a thin colored oval riding the head, not an eye embedded in a flat plane. Near the side, orientation matters as much as depth: an unrotated flat cheek would increasingly cut across the head curvature. The code's formula uses the offset center when computing its gradient-like direction; reproduce that detail before proposing a more exact normal-offset construction.

Pear offers a contrasting strategy: broad expression patches are subdivided and projected vertex by vertex, whereas these axolotl features remain transformed solids (src/pear-boy.js:90). The distinction matters when adapting a large flat marking to this smaller head. Enlarging an oval without revisiting curvature can reveal intersections absent at the original scale.
Feet and toes communicate support

For each side, feet are placed at Z -.65 and -2.45, giving four feet. Their centers are (side*1.08,.3,z) with scale (.34,.3,.46), and their Y rotation is side*-.2. Each foot receives three separate toe meshes at X offsets -.17, 0, .17, center Y .12, and forward offset Z .37. Each toe scale is (.105,.12,.17).

The foot's Y minimum is zero, and so is the toe's, from center minus vertical radius. Those authored support heights help explain why a root Y of zero places the lamp on the tabletop. They do not prove all extruded tail and gill vertices remain above it; inspect the complete assembled bounds for that.

Toes are direct root children, not foot children. Rotating a foot therefore does not rotate its toes. This is an important ownership fact for a proposed walking animation: the pinned model is static, and anatomical-looking naming does not create a joint hierarchy automatically.
MD24-W01 Construct the raised tail in the correct plane

Begin with the cream fin outline. It starts at the origin, curves toward (1.55,1.65), and returns through a second contour to close. Extrude it .12, with .09 bevel size and thickness and three bevel segments. Place the mesh at (0,.55,-2.72) and rotate around Y by pi/2. The original XY outline now reads as a vertical tail extending along the body's depth direction rather than as a side-facing sign.

Next build the separate pink tip outline using its own Bézier coordinates. Its extrusion depth is .4, bevel size and thickness .035, again with three bevel segments. Apply the same position and Y rotation, then call translateZ(-.14). That last operation is local-axis translation after rotation, not a subtraction from world Z. It aligns the thicker pink layer across the cream fin's thickness direction.

For an observable reproduction, compare the two tail meshes' world matrices, not only their .position.z values. Transform the local unit Z direction through each quaternion to see where the offset acts. The exact sequence is visible in tail construction (src/axolotl-lamp.js:69).
The smile is a sampled tube

The smile uses six XY control points, projected to the head with offset .045. Their heights undulate from 1.31 through 1.2, 1.23, 1.2, 1.23, and 1.34. A Catmull–Rom curve connects them, and TubeGeometry uses 32 longitudinal divisions, radius .024, six radial divisions, and an open path. It is neither a filled mouth patch nor a texture.

The small radius keeps the line modest relative to the head, but it creates a sampling tradeoff at distant camera scales: a physically present line can project to less than a pixel. Increasing emission will not necessarily restore black-line readability. A proposed thicker smile should be evaluated for both projected size and shell clearance, not just assigned a larger radius. Current Raycaster documentation helps distinguish a geometrically hittable tube from perceptually legible pixels; neither property automatically proves the other.
MD24-R01 Retry with longer gills and a closer camera

Proposed extension. Scale each gill's local X magnitude by 1.2 while preserving side sign and base pivot. The changed condition increases silhouette reach and may crowd nearby consoles. Recompute the full rotated model envelope; do not retain motion bounds measured before the edit.

Then move to a closer, three-quarter diagnostic camera. Inspect both front and back faces, because the extruded thickness and mirrored transforms can look acceptable from the front while exposing an awkward seam behind. The parent-produced atlas views are appropriate for this diagnostic comparison, but they are neutral-studio views, not proof of room light or animation. No new screenshots are implied by this recipe.

If enlarged gills collide with another desk model during drag, compare the scene's stored axolotlMotion.bounds with the newly measured assembly. The controller integrates one rigid upright root (src/pear-motion.js:5); it does not fold the gills away. The placement helper uses the provided envelope and cannot discover omitted geometry by itself (src/desk-clearance.js:3).
Figure MD24.2. A decorative silhouette edit becomes a movement-envelope edit once the feature extends beyond the old assembly.
Integration, history, and material tradeoffs

The scene tags and picks the actual companion meshes, applies yaw before measuring bounds, and keeps the emitter under the same root (src/scene.js:130). Thus details are not merely display ornaments: their geometry contributes to the measured footprint. The cream and pink materials share roughness but not emission color or strength. Current MeshStandardMaterial guidance describes that distinction; the chosen values remain pinned source facts.

Documented history. The axolotl task record describes a contact-sheet review that found overly dark wine-colored gills and a correction to pink material/emission. That is evidence of a recorded visual iteration, not permission to claim all future lighting conditions look correct. The same record explicitly separates local technical qualification from owner acceptance. The later movable-lamp record supersedes fixed placement without adding gill animation or a facial state machine. See the recorded color correction (TODO/110_SMALL_AXOLOTL_LAMP.todo:54) and movement supersession (TODO/111_MOVABLE_AXOLOTL.todo:40).
Count details without confusing count and quality

The browser geometry fixture checks six gill petals, four feet, and an axolotl-to-Pear height ratio below .4, alongside initial nonoverlap and a real mesh pick. These are useful assembly assertions: a missing mirrored loop or an accidentally doubled root scale becomes detectable without relying on subjective description. They do not prove twelve toes have ideal spacing or that the smile remains readable at every camera distance (tests/browser/dock.spec.mjs:662).

For a proposed feature revision, retain those inventory checks and add a specific observation for the changed condition. Lengthening gills calls for an envelope check; thickening a smile calls for surface clearance and visible line-width comparison; reparenting toes calls for transform tests. A generic “model exists” assertion is too weak to distinguish these failure modes.

The contrast with Pear is instructive. Pear's six freckles are checked as foremost ray hits across expression and gaze states, because animated facial neighbors can occlude them. Axolotl has no corresponding expression state machine, so copying that entire test grid would not automatically add value. Instead, choose observations that match its actual static geometry and shared-root movement. This avoids documenting imaginary animation simply to make two companions appear symmetrical in the handbook.
MD24-Q01 Find a misleading pivot assumption

A developer rotates the front foot and expects its three toes to rotate with it. Nothing happens to the toes, although the foot mesh visibly turns. Should the repair change toe geometry, the light intensity, or transform ownership?
MD24-A01 Build the hierarchy the animation actually needs

Change ownership if articulation is the goal. The implemented toes are root children, so foot rotation cannot affect them. A proposed animated foot would need a group with an explicit pivot, reparented foot and toe meshes, and coordinates converted to that group's local space without changing the neutral appearance.

The failure boundary is not only the joint transform. Reparenting changes how bounds and picking traverse the assembly, and animated toes can change the silhouette without root motion. Add envelope invalidation and tests for the new hierarchy. Until that work exists, document the pinned model honestly as a static stylized assembly moved as one companion.
