MD25 / COMPANION LIGHT EMISSION AND MATERIAL TUNING
Companion light emission and material tuning
Two different meanings of luminous

Implemented behavior. Both companions combine emissive mesh materials with point lights. Emission makes their surfaces appear luminous; point emitters illuminate surrounding geometry. The factories do not configure a physically transmitting silicone volume. Treating the emissive material as if it alone casts the warm desk pool would misdescribe the actual rendering architecture. Pear's setup appears in material creation (src/pear-boy.js:8), and axolotl's in two material families (src/axolotl-lamp.js:6).

Researched guidance. Current MeshStandardMaterial documentation, consulted on 2026-11-07, describes emissive color, intensity, and maps as separate factors. It also distinguishes roughness from emission. These general definitions help reason about the model, but pinned source remains the authority for its actual values and controls.
Reconstruct Pear's surface emission

Pear's diffusion map is a 16×256 procedural canvas. A vertical gradient uses #b8b8b8 at zero, white at .65, and #d6d6d6 at one. The standard material uses cream #fff3d4, roughness .65, emissive #ffe4a0, the gradient map, and factory intensity 77. That gradient modulates a generated lathe surface; it is not a photographed silicone texture.

The shared canvasTexture helper creates the canvas, throws if no 2D context exists, paints it, sets SRGBColorSpace, and assigns anisotropy four. Texture helper (src/handheld.js:68) therefore belongs to the material evidence chain. An offscreen numerical factory recreation that bypasses this helper may reconstruct shape but not the same color pipeline.

Four point lights form a rectangular distribution at X ±1.1, Y 4.4, and Z ±1. Each factory light has warm color #ffd9a8, intensity 560, distance 70, and decay 2. The shell does not cast shadows, explicitly avoiding self-blocking by the opaque shell representation (src/pear-boy.js:325). This is an appearance approximation, not simulated light transport through silicone.
Figure MD25.1. Surface glow and received illumination are independently generated, then jointly affected by scene exposure.
Factory values versus scene-controlled values

The scene starts Pear on at brightness .7. updatePearLight assigns each emitter 800*b and shell emission 110*b when on. At .7 these reproduce the factory values 560 and 77. Power off hides the point lights and sets shell emission to zero. Brightness accepts finite values from .1 through one and does not inherently enable power.

Axolotl starts on at .5. The scene assigns point intensity 260*b, cream emission 90*b, and pink emission 48*b. At .5 these become 130, 45, and 24, again matching factory defaults. Its brightness setter accepts only .5 or one, not an arbitrary continuous slider. Power off sets all three intensities to zero; its light need not be hidden to stop contributing. Control mapping (src/scene.js:563) is more precise than saying both lamps share identical brightness behavior.
Axolotl's internal emitter and readable face

The axolotl emitter is at (0,.65,-.5) beneath the head region inside the assembled body, with color #ffd29e, factory intensity 130, distance 24, and decay 2. Its cream and pink materials have roughness .72 but different base and emissive colors. Black eyes and smile remain basic-material markings rather than luminous parts. Emitter placement is a critical geometric parameter, not merely a lighting metadata detail.

Documented history. TODO/110_SMALL_AXOLOTL_LAMP.todo records that an initial exposed emitter near the face saturated both brightness levels. Moving it inside the body allowed the unchanged stronger rendered-pixel assertion to distinguish them. The record also describes correcting overly dark gill colors. Those are reported iteration outcomes, not recovered internal reasoning or evidence of fresh aesthetic approval. The source record preserves both the failed probe and the stronger unchanged pixel assertion (TODO/110_SMALL_AXOLOTL_LAMP.todo:50).

The lesson is not to memorize one magical intensity. A point light very close to a visible surface can dominate the local result. Moving it can improve readability while retaining an actual desk pool. Merely lowering emission would change a different contribution.
MD25-W01 Derive the two axolotl brightness states

At Sleep .5, compute emitter 260*.5=130, cream 90*.5=45, and pink 48*.5=24. At Bright one, these become 260, 90, and 48. All three double, but the final displayed RGB values need not double: lighting, material response, exposure, and tone mapping intervene. This distinction explains why a property-value assertion is insufficient for visible brightness.

For an observable reproduction, follow the browser fixture: turn off tripod, room, and Pear; select each axolotl level through controls; wait for its state, settled exposure near .018, and completed pending paint work. Sample the same 12×12 patch around the projected head target and compare mean RGB. The existing assertion requires Bright to exceed Sleep by more than five mean channel units. See actual shell photometry.

Keep the sample camera and location fixed. A changed sample that lands on a black eye or background is not a valid brightness comparison. Read the bitmap into the canvas before closing it, and normalize by retained canvas dimensions. The historical record notes that premature dimension handling first produced an invalid probe before the real saturation problem was found.
Exposure makes all-off a separate condition

The scene targets exposure .018 if any tripod, room, Pear, or axolotl light is on; otherwise it targets .45. Damping uses rate four and current delta, with an explicit convergence threshold. See exposure adaptation (src/scene.js:1222).

Consequently toggling the last companion off changes more than its own emission. A before/after image taken during exposure adaptation can make the dark state unexpectedly bright elsewhere. Tests must wait for the intended condition rather than treating an immediate screenshot as a settled optical measurement.

Pear's light test samples near and farther desk locations, requires a red increase greater than blue increase, and checks meaningful illumination beyond the lamp's feet. That is evidence for warm received light, distinct from the axolotl shell-brightness test (tests/browser/pear-boy.spec.mjs:65). Neither test establishes a calibrated lux value or physical bulb efficiency.
MD25-R01 Retry after moving the lamp

Change conditions by relocating Pear while keeping its brightness constant. The lights are children of its root, so their world positions change with it. A desk sample that was bright can become dim even though all intensity properties are unchanged. First record emitter world positions and confirm the sample still hits the intended desk surface.

Then isolate two questions. To test production movement, let body and lights move together. To reproduce a historical fixed-light material comparison, explicitly hold the historical emitter positions while keeping legal body clearance. Label the latter as a controlled diagnostic, not native behavior. The verification ledger records exactly this distinction when clearance moved Pear and altered a DS deck color measurement (docs/VERIFICATION.md:462).

Do not “fix” that comparison by weakening RGB thresholds or pretending the lamp's local coordinates determine received light independently of layout. Root motion comes from the motion controller (src/pear-motion.js:36), and layout can also move it before painting (src/desk-clearance.js:3). These geometric sources belong in a lighting diagnosis because they change emitter-to-surface relationships.
Figure MD25.2. Diagnose geometry, exposure, and state before modifying materials; a lighting mismatch can originate in layout rather than color.
Material and performance tradeoffs

Proposed extension. A transmissive material might produce a different silicone impression, but it would introduce thickness, environment, sorting, and performance questions not answered by the present setup. It must not be documented as an already implemented quality upgrade. Similarly, replacing four Pear point lights with one would alter the spatial distribution even if total nominal intensity stayed similar.

Current MeshStandardMaterial documentation clarifies that a displacement map or edited vertices affect shape differently from normal or roughness adjustments. Here no displacement-driven silicone surface is authored. The useful diagnostic sequence is silhouette first, material response second, actual received light third, and exposure last as an explicitly controlled presentation variable.

Design interpretation. High roughness and broad warm output may suggest soft diffusion. That remains an appearance interpretation. It does not justify using “physically accurate silicone” as a factual claim, especially when self-shadow suppression and multiple interior emitters are deliberate approximations.
Design a bounded optical comparison

Use paired measurements rather than a single impressive image. For Pear, hold camera, desk sample, exposure condition, and root pose fixed while switching its power. Compare the red-channel change with the blue-channel change to test warm contribution, and retain a farther sample to avoid qualifying only a tiny bright hotspot. The existing near/far test explicitly requires both effects rather than reading a light's color property (tests/browser/pear-boy.spec.mjs:65).

For axolotl, compare the same head patch at Sleep and Bright with other lights disabled. Then switch power off and check all three numeric contributions become zero. Selecting Sleep while off must leave power off. Finally wait for all-off exposure to approach .45. These observations test different layers: control semantics, surface response, and adaptation. Combining them into one broad screenshot assertion would make a failure harder to diagnose.

The scene marks reflections dirty when companion lighting changes. That does not mean a reflection capture happens immediately during every held movement. The render path waits for suitable settled conditions before updating DS reflections (src/scene.js:1375). A stale reflection during a drag is therefore a different question from whether the moved lamp's direct light follows its root. Keep those claims separate in both tests and captions.
Avoid misleading brightness units

The point-light constructor includes intensity, distance, and decay parameters, but this chapter does not infer a real bulb wattage from them. The displayed result includes exposure values far from a generic default and intentionally strong mesh emission. Without a calibrated scene, physical camera model, and measurement convention, reporting a consumer-lamp lumen equivalence would be invented precision.

A proposed tuning session should record model pose, camera pose, enabled lights, brightness state, exposure convergence, and the sampled surface. Those are reproducibility inputs, not private conversation memory. Another agent can repeat the comparison from those conditions even if it does not share the original author's aesthetic judgment. The interpretation “soft warm silicone” should remain clearly labeled as a visual aim, while exact colors, offsets, roughness, and intensity mappings remain source-backed facts.

When an edit improves the face but weakens the desk pool, do not report unqualified improvement. State which observation improved and which changed adversely. Emission, internal emitter location, and brightness mapping are independent controls with coupled appearance; a responsible tradeoff preserves that causal structure instead of collapsing it into one saturation slider.
MD25-Q01 Explain indistinguishable brightness screenshots

Both brightness buttons correctly double the three axolotl intensities, yet the sampled face is nearly identical. What should be checked before declaring the control broken? Why is a metadata-only test inadequate?
MD25-A01 Test the displayed response and its causes

Check saturation, emitter proximity to the face, sample location, other enabled lights, and exposure convergence. If the face is already clipped, doubling linear contributions can leave displayed pixels almost unchanged. Metadata proves that a setter executed, not that the intended appearance survived the render pipeline.

The existing stronger boundary is an actual shell-pixel difference with other lights isolated and settled exposure. Preserve that assertion while changing one causal parameter at a time. Conversely, if only a neutral-studio atlas is available, report its geometry diagnostic value and leave native-room photometry unverified. No atlas caption should imply the movement or brightness sequence was captured.

MD26 / DRAGGING, GRAVITY AND DROPPING
Dragging, gravity and dropping
One root controller, two companion assemblies

Implemented behavior. Pear uses PearMotion, a configured subclass of DeskMotion; axolotl uses DeskMotion with bounds measured from its rotated assembly. Both share companion gesture handling in the scene. The controller stores a reference to the root position, velocity, previous position, fixed-step accumulator, held/sleep state, and optional presentation state. It does not simulate angular momentum or soft-body deformation. Controller state (src/pear-motion.js:5) is the authoritative model.

This separation is reusable: model factories build geometry and local parts; the scene interprets input; the controller advances upright translation. Pear's rope and face systems respond to body movement afterward. Axolotl's static feet, gills, and emitter simply follow its root (src/axolotl-lamp.js:3). Similar interaction does not imply identical anatomy or animation.
Construct a camera-plane drag

beginCompanionMove switches toward table mode, saves the pickup origin, and creates a plane whose normal is the camera's world direction. The plane passes through the actual hit point, or a bounds-center fallback. Intersecting the pointer ray with that plane gives a 3D drag point. The saved offset from that point to the root prevents the object center from snapping under the pointer.

Pointer movement must exceed four screen pixels before the gesture counts as moved. A short click can therefore remain a power toggle; a drag releases into physics without toggling. Pointer capture keeps ownership when the pointer leaves the canvas. Cancellation, lost capture, blur, and related reset paths restore the saved pickup origin rather than inventing a new home. Gesture setup (src/scene.js:611) and completion show these responsibilities.

Wheel input adds camera-direction depth using clamped deltaY*.015, bounded to [-2,2] model units per event. The drag plane is translated by the accepted root displacement, preserving subsequent pointer continuity. Keyboard arrows and Page Up/Down use .65-unit world-axis steps, and clear velocity after each deliberate placement.
Figure MD26.1. Input owns a bounded translation transaction; release and cancellation intentionally take different state paths.
Derive release velocity without unbounded throws

moveTo estimates seconds from the previous movement timestamp, clamped between .008 and .1. After the first sample, velocity is displacement divided by that duration, then clamped to total length 22. The clamp limits three-dimensional speed, not each component independently. The first movement has no previous finite timestamp and does not create an arbitrary throw.

drop clears held state, impact report, and accumulator. If more than 100 milliseconds passed since the last movement, velocity becomes zero. This makes holding still before release produce a fall rather than preserve a stale throw. pickUp and reset also remove old velocity and pending presentation. These details explain why keyboard placement explicitly zeroes velocity rather than depending on the user's key-repeat timing. Move and drop are the reproducible rules.
Fixed-step gravity and contact response

Each physics step is 1/120 second. Velocity Y decreases by 45*h; horizontal velocities multiply by .998; position advances by velocity*h. The method accepts at most five seconds from one callback and processes at most 600 steps in one update. It does not integrate an arbitrarily large unbounded suspension.

At the workspace floor, root Y clamps to its minimum. Incoming downward speed is reported as impact speed. If its magnitude exceeds 1.2, vertical velocity rebounds at .23 of that magnitude; otherwise it becomes zero. Supported horizontal motion is additionally damped by .85. Total speed squared below .0025 allows sleep and clears accumulated time.

Obstacle collision expands each box horizontally by the moving model's offset bounds. Previous vertical position distinguishes landing from hitting an underside. If neither applies, the controller chooses the nearest horizontal side. These are box-based contacts, not continuous triangle collision or a general guarantee against tunneling at arbitrary speeds and obstacle thicknesses. The implemented bounded speed and step size define the useful regime.
MD26-W01 Derive the first drop and rebound

Start Pear at height ten with zero release velocity and no obstacles. After one step, vy=-45/120=-.375, and the height decreases by .375/120=.003125. This immediate change is small but physical; a snap straight to zero would violate the implementation.

Ignoring discrete-step error and damping of horizontal components, the continuous reference gives impact speed sqrt(2*45*10)=30. The .23 rebound suggests initial upward speed near 6.9 and a free rebound height near 6.9²/(2*45)=.529. These are explanatory estimates, not exact expected floating-point values: collision is detected at fixed steps and the controller may clamp to supports.

For observable reproduction, use the unit test's raised position, call pickUp, move to height ten, and drop after the stale-velocity threshold. Assert that an early update remains between nine and ten, later updates contain positive vertical velocity, height never goes negative, and the final velocity is zero. See fall and contact tests. This establishes trajectory, not yet visible presentation.
Physical integration is not a painted fall

Documented history. Commit 120d9bd5a3e785d24a9bdc5e96d6e9b332613510 added paint-aware presentation. The verification ledger records an earlier failure where 48 physics steps covered fall and rebound without a main-room render. Correct final position and animation-callback samples did not prove the user saw the fall (docs/VERIFICATION.md:443).

With requirePaint=true, the controller first holds an actual descending pose at or below halfway between release height and relevant support. It preserves the remaining accumulator and refuses further integration while presentation is pending. Main-room rendering acknowledges that pose, allowing the controller to continue toward contact and a first upward pose.

During rebound, it chooses a rising threshold contactHeight+vy²/(4*45), halfway toward the ideal ballistic apex height. The next pending pose is still an integrated rising state, not a fabricated animation key. A second acknowledgment releases the remaining catch-up. Presentation logic explains why queued time and visible state must be managed together.
Figure MD26.2. Sparse updates retain actual descending and ascending poses until main-room submission acknowledges them.
MD26-R01 Retry with a three-second callback

Change the callback interval from 1/120 to three seconds. First run without paint requirements: the unit trajectory test expects equivalent integrated contacts over the same bounded elapsed time. Then enable requirePaint. The first long update should stop mid-fall; a further update should leave position unchanged while adding queued time. Acknowledge paint, update with zero new time, and observe a rising pose. Acknowledge again and allow sleep.

If the body remains frozen, inspect whether the main room render actually occurred. Scene code acknowledges Pear, axolotl, and console motion only after renderer.render(scene,camera) (src/scene.js:1378). A reflection capture or dirty flag is not an equivalent acknowledgment. If it snaps directly to rest, inspect whether release requested paint-aware behavior or bypassed the normal finish path.

Researched guidance. MDN's requestAnimationFrame reference documents variable refresh rates and paused background callbacks. It supports the need for elapsed-time handling, but an animation callback is not evidence of a completed GPU frame. Keep physics, render submission, and observed pixels as separate evidence layers.
Couple reactions and ropes without mixing authorities

Pear receives frightened=true while held or not sleeping. Downward support impact speed can trigger anger at ten or above, followed by pout recovery. Rope updates then follow the changed root. The shell's root remains upright; there is no impact-driven body pitch. The actual hierarchy and face state are in createPearBoy (src/pear-boy.js:235), and rope origin changes are handled independently (src/pear-rope.js:48).

Scene clearance can still adjust horizontal placement before a paint. That is why a sleeping controller is not enough to assert final saved console coordinates. The browser console test explicitly waits for a settled table paint before recording the moved position (tests/browser/console-movement.spec.mjs:159). Geometry reconciliation belongs to the placement solver (src/desk-clearance.js:3), not to a hidden movement animation.

Actual axolotl drop assertions wrap the room renderer, requiring descending and rising positive-height samples and no negative heights (tests/browser/dock.spec.mjs:791). Pear's corresponding fixture additionally checks the painted expression sequence. These are test definitions read for this chapter, not fresh execution claims.
Raised supports and offset origins

A root's floor is not necessarily the mesh's visible bottom. The generic controller uses local bounds offsets to land on an obstacle: support root height is obstacle.max.y-bounds.min.y. The unit fixture with local minimum Y -.5 lands at 8.5 on an eight-unit support, not at eight. The workspace minimum is separately configured to .5 for the table in that fixture. This is why reusing a controller with a new model requires measuring origin offsets rather than copying Pear's zero floor (tests/unit/pear-motion.test.mjs:102).

For an underside hit, the correction uses obstacle minimum minus the moving model's maximum bound. Side contact uses horizontally expanded intervals and reflects the affected velocity component. A proposed nonupright companion would need current-orientation or conservative rotational bounds; the existing translational controller does not update a spinning collision shape for you (src/pear-motion.js:91).

The paint-aware fall threshold also considers raised supports below release height. Otherwise a halfway-to-table hold could lie inside a tall obstacle. The raised-support unit case checks that the held descending pose remains above the support, then verifies catching clears presentation and ordinary integration can settle correctly. This is a concrete changed-condition test, not a blanket claim that all stacked furniture is supported.
Select instrumentation that cannot miss the event

Arm a release observer before dispatching pointerup. Starting a recorder only after a later automation evaluation can miss a genuine short fall and falsely blame physics. Conversely, sampling every animation callback can record positions that were never submitted to the main room renderer. The Pear fixture therefore records both progression and actual room-render samples, and the axolotl fixture wraps the renderer for its descending/rising assertions (tests/browser/pear-boy.spec.mjs:448; tests/browser/dock.spec.mjs:791).

These are complementary controls. An event-time recorder avoids an observation race, while the render wrapper proves presentation was attempted. Neither alone establishes physical monitor scanout, and neither authorizes relaxing the existing no-penetration or expression-order assertions. If a test fails under sparse software rendering, retain the failure evidence and inspect whether time was discarded, presentation was bypassed, or the observer started late.

The historical paint-aware correction changed the controller's presentation contract while preserving gravity and rebound values. That is a more precise lesson than “slow down the animation.” Another agent can reconstruct the mechanism from fixed steps, pending poses, acknowledgments, and tests, without claiming literal continuity with any prior agent's memory.
MD26-Q01 Distinguish cancellation from resetting home

A companion is moved from a nondefault table location, lifted, then canceled. Should it return to the original factory home, the last accepted held point, or the position captured at pickup? What would reveal stale momentum?
MD26-A01 Restore the transaction's origin

Cancellation restores the pickup origin. Factory reset is a separate operation with occupancy checks; normal release drops from the last accepted point. After cancellation, velocity and pending presentation must be cleared. A subsequent update moving the canceled lamp would expose stale controller state rather than a valid continuing throw.

The failure boundary is occupied or externally changed scene geometry. Restoring an origin is not permission to hide overlapping objects; normal pre-paint clearance still applies. Tests should separate cancellation identity, collision reconciliation, and actual painted result instead of conflating all three with a single “position changed” assertion.

MD27 / CLEARANCE, COLLISION ENVELOPES AND HOME POSES
Clearance, collision envelopes and home poses
Why sleeping physics cannot resolve every overlap

Implemented behavior. resolveDeskClearance runs in the main paint path after motion and geometry updates. It reconciles objects according to current interaction mode before rendering. A stationary Pear can otherwise be intersected by an incoming rotated console even though Pear's own physics is asleep. Moving the objects apart is the actual repair; visibility tricks, render-order changes, and disabled depth tests are not substitutes. Pre-paint integration (src/scene.js:1367) establishes this sequencing.

The system has several kinds of remembered position: authored seed coordinates, current root positions, saved console table poses, first legal console homes, temporary focus parking, and companion table snapshots. Their names are not interchangeable. This chapter treats layout as an explicit transaction with geometric evidence rather than a collection of convenient coordinate constants.
Choose envelopes for their actual responsibility

Pear's motion controller uses a simplified body box from (-3,0,-3) to (3,8.1,3). The factory also computes broader bounds and expands horizontal reach to at least ±4.5. For clearance, the scene starts with that broader envelope and unions current child bounds, excluding the contact shadow. The envelope therefore covers more than the instantaneous shell while still accounting for current limbs.

The contact shadow is a 6.6×6.6 plane with transparent material and a clipping plane. It is not a solid support object. Including it in an envelope would make a presentation aid displace real models. The source explicitly excludes it during Pear envelope assembly here (src/scene.js:806).

Axolotl bounds are measured after its scene Y rotation .3, so the offset AABB reflects the actual assembled orientation. Focused consoles can rotate and hinge; current world bounds are therefore needed instead of a historical unrotated width. A current AABB is still not an all-future rotational envelope. Re-evaluation and invalidation make it useful at each eligible paint.
Derive forbidden root rectangles

nearestDeskPosition receives local offset bounds, desired root position, root workspace, obstacle boxes, and a default gap .25. It first rejects desired heights outside workspace limits. Only obstacles with strict vertical overlap contribute forbidden horizontal rectangles.

For obstacle X interval [oMin,oMax] and local moving bounds [bMin,bMax], the forbidden root interval is (oMin-bMax-gap,oMax-bMin+gap). The same expansion applies in Z. This is a Minkowski-style reduction: instead of translating an entire box through every candidate, test one root point against expanded rectangles. The actual implementation is the complete solver (src/desk-clearance.js:3).

Candidate X values are the clamped desired X and every clamped rectangle edge; candidate Z values follow the same rule. Their Cartesian product includes mixed corners formed by different obstacles. Testing only “left, right, front, back” of one obstacle would miss the nearest legal corner in a crowded layout.
Figure MD27.1. Expanded forbidden rectangles reduce box placement to a finite search over desired coordinates and obstacle edges.
MD27-W01 Derive a two-obstacle corner

Use local bounds [-.5,0,-.5] to [.5,1,.5], desired root (0,7,0), and workspace X/Z [-2,2]. The first obstacle extends X -2.25 to .25 and Z -4.25 to 4.25; its right expanded edge is .25-(-.5)+.25=1. The second obstacle extends X -4.25 to 4.25 and Z -2.25 to .75; its forward expanded edge is .75-(-.5)+.25=1.5.

The nearest legal combination is therefore (1,7,1.5), with horizontal distance sqrt(1²+1.5²)=sqrt(3.25). Neither isolated single-axis correction is sufficient because the other obstacle still blocks it. The unit test also reverses obstacle order for this fixture and expects the same answer. See corner regression.

For reproduction, clone inputs before calling the solver and compare them afterward. The result is a new vector; desired position, workspace, bounds, and obstacle boxes must remain unchanged. Mutation would make later retry results depend on whether a previous diagnostic had already run.
Stable ranking and two different tolerances

Distance ranking uses squared horizontal distance. A candidate is rejected when squared>=bestDistance-1e-9; thus numerically equivalent candidates retain the earlier accepted choice. This 1e-9 is a ranking tolerance, not a collision gap and not the vertical overlap tolerance.

Obstacle-interior classification uses 8*Number.EPSILON*max(1,coordinate magnitudes). It accepts legal edges that move a few representable values during world/local bounds reconstruction. It does not replace the .25 geometric gap with a broad collision allowance. The negative test verifies that genuine .01 penetration still moves clear.

Documented history. Commit 6b5d2c552e6b3206bfb3ae36d845896773147a1c added the scale-relative interior allowance. The ledger records an inactive DS return changing X by one ULP, from 11.314174109565958 to 11.31417410956596 (docs/VERIFICATION.md:410). A strict edge classifier rejected the formerly legal point after reconstruction. That evidence supports the bounded numerical fix, not loosening exact-pose tests or claiming all software latency was solved.
Mode priority and transactional placement

In focus, the active console is inserted as an immovable obstacle. The inactive console is placed next, then Pear, then axolotl, then loose props. The active camera-facing pose and hinge are not moved to accommodate lower-priority objects. On the table, companion positions become obstacles first, loose props attempt their anchors, and consoles yield afterward.

The resolver collects placements without immediately mutating roots. A failed placement reports the blocked model and returns false. For equal-priority table consoles, it first tries GBA then DS; if that ordering fails, it restores the candidate arrays and tries DS then GBA. This is a bounded order retry, not a global optimization over every permutation of every object. Priority and retry (src/scene.js:820) provides the exact ordering.

On commit, moved roots update motion's previous position and clear horizontal velocity. Elevated unheld objects can wake to fall. Pear limbs are reset against the new origin. This prevents a layout correction from leaving stale inertial state or detached rope geometry.
Capture legal homes, not overlapping seeds

The scene initially copies console seed positions into home slots, but after the first successful nonfocused clearance it replaces those homes with the collision-free console table poses. This is guarded by initialDeskLayoutStored. Resetting consoles later therefore targets a legal initial layout rather than the old seeds that predated companion clearance. Home capture (src/scene.js:868) is the important implementation point.

The wording “settled home” needs care: the guard records first successful table reconciliation; it does not explicitly wait for a new independent all-physics-sleep predicate. Preserve the exact contract instead of implying a stronger settling algorithm. Companion reset homes remain authored constants, with occupancy checks and explicit errors if another lamp blocks them. They are not automatically replaced by this console-home mechanism.
MD27-R01 Retry after focus parking and explicit movement

First choose a nondefault Pear table position and resolve table clearance. Enter Play or Inspect so consoles take priority. Save the original table snapshot once on entering focus; temporary parking must not overwrite it. Return to table and verify the remembered XZ values are restored while lower-priority models yield.

Now change conditions: reset Pear or explicitly move it while a table snapshot exists. Those operations update the remembered table position so an older focus snapshot cannot undo the user's newer choice. Canceling a move restores its pickup origin and updates the remembered snapshot accordingly. The browser focus fixture exercises both reset and explicit movement overrides (tests/browser/desk-clearance.spec.mjs:163).

If the lamp jumps back after a valid move, inspect snapshot ownership before changing geometry. If it oscillates between sides on successive paints, inspect tie ranking and reconstructed bounds before rounding all positions. Rounding would destroy exact pose identity and can introduce genuine overlap.
Figure MD27.2. Focus parking is temporary geometry reconciliation, not a new authored table pose.
Invalidate a layout when its evidence changes

The clearance signature includes focus state, DS lid rotation, cartridge motion presence, and relevant roots' positions and quaternions. Moving limbs or insertion activity explicitly clears the signature, because geometry can change without root movement. A future animated axolotl tail would require similar invalidation; its current static construction does not supply that automatically.

Rope simulation updates world points and tube bounds (src/pear-rope.js:48; src/pear-boy.js:330). Axolotl geometry contributes its actual extruded feature reach (src/axolotl-lamp.js:33). Body physics separately uses support and side contact boxes (src/pear-motion.js:91). These supporting sources explain why neither a current AABB alone nor a broad static envelope alone is a complete future-motion guarantee.

Researched guidance. Current BufferGeometry documentation notes that edited vertices may need recomputed bounding boxes and spheres. The repository does this for moving ropes. That general advice supports invalidation discipline, but does not prove a new model's envelope is sufficient without measured geometry and tests.
Order dependence has a bounded meaning

The two-obstacle worked example is insensitive to reversing its obstacle array because its nearest corner is unique. Do not generalize that result into universal permutation invariance. Candidate coordinates are stored in sets with insertion order, and equal-distance ranking deliberately retains the first accepted candidate within tolerance. A truly symmetric arrangement can therefore expose deterministic ordering choices. The source's guarantee is stable evaluation under its ordered inputs, not an abstract canonical answer independent of every permutation.

The console-order retry addresses a different problem. Two equal-priority models have different widths, so placing the narrower one first can leave no legal region for the wider one. Retrying the reverse order is a bounded search improvement. It does not remove all layout path dependence, and it does not promote a lower-priority model above the active focus console. Keep rank policy, candidate tie policy, and retry order as separate concepts when extending the solver.
Verify geometry at the paint boundary

The browser clearance fixture deliberately creates overlap without calling the resolver, then requests an actual paint. It records nonintersection and unchanged active pose from the renderer wrapper. This checks integration, not merely the helper in isolation. It additionally verifies that sleeping Pear yields in focus, returning to table restores remembered placement, and console rotations and tripod pose remain unchanged (tests/browser/desk-clearance.spec.mjs:75).

That test does not prove arbitrary triangle-level separation for every future model. It demonstrates the current envelope-based contract at the point the room is submitted. A proposed articulated companion must supply both an adequate envelope and invalidation when articulation changes. Without those responsibilities, a cached signature can certify stale geometry even though the helper's rectangle math remains perfectly correct.
MD27-Q01 Distinguish no solution from unstable choice
One crowded scene returns null; another alternates equally distant sides after bounds reconstruction. Should both be repaired by reducing the gap? What evidence distinguishes them?
MD27-A01 Preserve geometry and diagnose the actual failure

No. Null can mean no legal root candidate exists in the fixed-height workspace. The correct response is an explicit blocked result or a changed layout, not quiet penetration. Alternating sides can instead indicate unstable tie ranking or edge classification. Compare exact desired coordinates, candidate distances, and before/after reconstructed bounds.

The solver's failure boundary is fixed-height horizontal placement with provided envelopes and priorities. It does not search arbitrary heights, rotate models, prove mesh-level clearance, or guarantee a globally optimal layout. The existing occupied-workspace, exact-edge, negative-overlap, and paint-path tests establish useful bounded contracts. Retain their assertions when extending the scene; a visually plausible screenshot cannot replace those geometric and state-identity checks.

MD28 / THE DESK, ROOM AND TRIPOD LAMP
The desk, room and tripod lamp
A room is a coordinate contract

The shared desk is not an imported interior. It is a small, deliberately constructed Three.js world whose furniture establishes where other models can rest, move and receive light. Begin reconstruction with its support surfaces, not with decorative detail. Otherwise every later contact, camera and lighting decision inherits an uncertain origin. The application uses Three.js 0.186.1, exactly, rather than a Blender scene, CAD assembly, model importer or general physics engine (package.json:7–9).

In the constructor of HandheldScene, the tabletop is a box measuring 1000 by 2.4 by 26 world units. Its center is (0,-1.2,-3), so its upper face is exactly world Y zero, its front edge is Z ten, and its rear edge is Z minus sixteen. Its enormous width is a framing expedient: it prevents a side edge from entering ordinary views. It is not evidence that the depicted physical desk is seventeen meters wide. Keep authored scene dimensions separate from claims about real furniture (src/scene.js:73–97).
Figure MD28.1. Construct support and illumination before arranging movable objects; clearance is a consequence of real geometry, not a cosmetic final pass.
Constructing the support surfaces

Create two independently repeated wood textures. The tabletop repeats 1000/16 horizontally and 26/11.5 along the other texture coordinate; the fascia repeats 1000/16 and 2.4/11.5. Separate repetition prevents the narrow edge from inheriting the top's stretched grain. The material array assigns the lighter, roughness .83 material to the positive-Y box face; the remaining faces use the darker .88 edge material. Do not assign a single UV scale to the whole box merely because it has one geometry.

The shared createWood helper makes a 1024-square canvas with a deterministic integer generator seeded at 41. It paints eight 128-pixel planks, each with a slight wash, 110 sinusoidally meandering grain strokes and paired seam lines. Repeat wrapping is enabled before the scene overrides its default repetition. Consequently, rebuilding the texture does not randomly change the grain on every reload. This determinism is useful for visual comparison: a material adjustment should not also move every grain line. The lamp has its own smaller ash-grain generator; do not replace both with one texture just because both are wood (src/handheld.js:657–685).

The wall is a 1000-square plane at (0,464.5,-16), with warm plaster color and roughness one. Its lower edge is Y minus 35.5, close to the floor at minus 35. The floor is a 180-square plane rotated minus ninety degrees about X. Both receive shadows. These broad planes provide a continuous room background without introducing a window, ceiling mesh, chair, skirting board or extra prop that does not exist in this construction. The scene background itself starts black and changes separately with the room-light switch.

Build the physical world and the interaction workspace as different objects. The floor is not the drop destination for tabletop movement. DeskMotion uses a root-coordinate workspace whose minimum Y determines support. The visible table is much wider than that workspace. This intentional restriction keeps interactions near the camera and other models rather than turning the whole oversized support mesh into a draggable territory (src/pear-motion.js:59–89).
Building the tripod in metric-local space

createDeskLamp creates a root and a body group. The body is positioned at (-13.5,0,2) in world units and scaled by 1/.017. Its children are authored in meter-like local dimensions. This is the essential ownership rule: parent translation remains a world-space placement, while child lengths are converted by parent scale. Do not divide the parent position by .017 a second time (src/lighting.js:5–49).

Draw one leg as a closed four-point shape, beginning at (.076,0), then (.094,0), (.027,.174) and (.009,.174). Extrude .013 without bevels, then translate the extrusion by minus .0065 along Z. Centering its thickness before rotating avoids a small systematic twist in the footprint. Reuse this geometry three times. Each leg rotates around Y by .35 + index * 2π/3. Thus the tripod is a radial construction of flat sloping members, not three cylinders leaning toward a guessed center.

The wood material uses a 128-by-512 generated grain canvas and roughness .72. Its strokes vary mildly with X and meander with Y. A short cylinder at Y .162, radius .022, height .018, supplies the shade support. There is no separately authored tall central pole in this factory: record the short support cylinder as the pole/support component rather than inventing a hidden stem. The cream trim is a standard material with roughness .8.

The shade is an open cylinder, radius .09, height .15, with 96 radial segments, centered at Y .225. Its open ends are important: a closed cylinder would introduce opaque caps absent from the model. The double-sided fabric material shows the interior and exterior of this thin surface. Two torus rims sit at Y .15 and .30, each rotated around X to lie horizontally. A sphere at Y .215, radius .018, acts as a warm diffuser. The source explicitly disables shadow casting on shade, rims and bulb; copying the mesh helper's default casting flag without those overrides would change the result (src/lighting.js:51–81).
Figure MD28.2. The supplied neutral-studio front render is for checking leg silhouette, open shade and support proportions, not proof of actual room illumination.
Constructing a lamp that also illuminates

The visible glowing fabric does not replace scene lights. The factory adds a downward spotlight, transmitted-shade area light, open-bottom area light and separate tabletop-bounce area light. The first three belong to the scaled body; bounce belongs directly to the root. This hierarchy makes the finite bounce patch a world-sized approximation rather than a meter-local rectangle accidentally enlarged fifty-nine times (src/lighting.js:82–110).

There is no modeled toggle lever or cord switch. The mesh helper marks the lamp surfaces with userData.lampToggle, and scene picking invokes the lamp callback. This is an interaction model, not an omitted anatomical detail to fabricate. Switching sets light intensities to zero or restores their remembered values and changes shade/bulb emission. It keeps the light objects present to avoid changing shader light counts (src/scene.js:1053–1075).
Figure MD28.3. The bounce patch has a different space owner from the lamp's metric-local parts; preserving that distinction prevents silent size errors.
Reconstructing the weave rather than painting a flat white drum

The fabric canvas is 1024 by 256. At each pixel, the factory combines two period-four cosine signals for warp and weft, their product, and a smaller sinusoidal fiber variation. The base value is 237; both main signals contribute six levels and their product contributes two. The same generated texture feeds ordinary color and emission, which keeps the weave visible when the shade glows. This is actual procedural texture synthesis, not a downloaded fabric photograph or a normal map (src/lighting.js:53–72).

For a material diagnostic, retain geometry, light and exposure while temporarily comparing the generated map with a constant near-white map in an isolated harness. The comparison asks whether texture contrast survives emission, not whether the whole room looks brighter. Restore the original map afterward and dispose only resources the harness created.
MD28-W01 Convert the shade and tabletop by hand

Work through three dimensions before writing geometry. With one world unit representing .017 meters for this factory, shade diameter is .18/.017 = 10.5882 world units; shade height is .15/.017 = 8.8235; top height is .30/.017 = 17.6471. The shade center becomes world (-13.5,13.2353,2). The support cylinder center becomes Y 9.5294. These are derived construction values, not measurements taken from a rendered frame.

The tabletop's upper face is -1.2 + 2.4/2 = 0, which matches the legs' local starting Y. That is why the factory can sit directly on the shared support plane without a compensating root lift. Check this equation before adjusting any contact shadow.

This original browser-module recipe assumes the project's import map, decoded brand assets and served source are already available. It constructs only the lamp; it does not start a renderer or modify the application. Expected output is three leg names and the derived top height.
MD28-R01 Retry after changing the shade diameter

Suppose a proposed extension changes radius from .09 to .11 while retaining height. This is not a request to scale the whole body. Rebuild the shade and both rims with corresponding radii, preserve the support height, and reconsider whether the transmitted area emitter still lies outside the fabric. The current .11 emitter X offset was chosen to avoid an intersecting plane and a hard lighting seam. A wider shade can invalidate that relationship even though every mesh remains legal.

Next recompute the lamp's actual world bounds and rerun desk clearance. The lamp is a fixed obstacle, not a lower-priority object the resolver may quietly move aside. A radius increase expands the occupied territory and can displace companions, cartridges and consoles. A visual improvement therefore has an interaction cost. The clearance browser test explicitly checks that the lamp's pose remains unchanged (tests/browser/desk-clearance.spec.mjs:59–72).
Figure MD28.4. The supplied diagnostic three-quarter view helps distinguish the three radial legs; it cannot establish the spotlight target or bounce strength.
MD28-Q01 Exercise: add a floor without moving the desk

A reconstruction sets the floor at Y zero because that is the usual ground convention in its previous project. Explain which contract breaks, how to diagnose the apparent intersection, and why moving every handheld upward is the wrong repair. Also explain why the wall's huge height is not a furniture dimension to copy into a product specification.
MD28-A01 Explained answer

Here Y zero already belongs to the tabletop. A second horizontal room surface at the same height overlaps the support and can alter depth, lighting and visible grain. Restore the authored floor at minus 35 and leave table and object homes unchanged. Raising every model would require changing workspace floors, saved poses, light targets and camera fits to compensate for one mistaken surface. The wall is oversized scenery with its lower edge near the floor; its dimensions ensure coverage, not architectural fidelity.

Finally separate geometry from acceptance. A leg count assertion verifies factory structure; a clearance assertion verifies placement; a neutral studio image helps judge silhouette. None says the owner likes the lamp in the integrated room. That distinction is explicit project practice (docs/VERIFICATION.md:1–8).

MD29 / LIGHT UNITS, EXPOSURE AND COLOR
Light units, exposure and color
Begin with the source of each brightness

Three distinct mechanisms make this room appear bright: surface emission, actual light objects and renderer exposure. They are not interchangeable. A bright shade material makes the shade visible; a spotlight illuminates surfaces; exposure maps scene radiance into display values. Replacing a misplaced light with global brightness can make a screenshot legible while destroying the all-lights-off behavior. The renderer explicitly uses sRGB output, ACES filmic tone mapping and initial exposure .018 (src/scene.js:39–47).

The checked current Three.js color-management guidance explains why lighting should be computed in Linear-sRGB and output converted for an sRGB display. This is contemporary guidance consulted on 2026-11-07, not proof of which library revision the application runs. That proof is the exact dependency in package.json:7–9. Never substitute a current documentation default for an explicit source assignment.
Figure MD29.1. Input encoding, physical-light arithmetic and display encoding are separate stages; changing light intensity cannot repair a missing conversion.
The authored hierarchy and its units

The tripod factory uses .017 meters per world unit. Its spotlight intensity is 12/.017², approximately 41522.49. This scaling preserves an inverse-square relationship when meter-authored geometry becomes world-sized geometry: at corresponding distances, intensity and squared distance acquire the same factor. It does not certify the modeled lamp against a photometer or establish a real bulb wattage.

The spotlight has decay two, unlimited distance, cone angle π/3 and penumbra .65. Its local target includes the inverse placement needed to aim toward the desk. The transmitted-shade rectangle has intensity 300 and explicit dimensions .18/.017 by .15/.017; the open-bottom rectangle uses 90 and .16/.017 square. Dimensions are explicit because the source warns that rectangle-light dimensions do not inherit parent scale. Its bounce rectangle is six by six with intensity 50, rooted outside the metric-scaled body (src/lighting.js:82–110).

Room lighting is a separate switchable group: a 14-by-12 ceiling area light at (0,10,5), intensity 132, looks toward the origin; a hemisphere light with intensity 22 represents warm reflected room illumination. The ceiling is a light, not a visible ceiling mesh. The hemisphere and tabletop patch
are authored approximations, not a traced global- illumination solution (src/lighting.js:113–123).

Companion lamps are part of the same exposure problem. At defaults, Pear brightness .7 produces intensity 800*.7 = 560 on each of its lights and body emission 110*.7 = 77. Axolotl brightness .5 produces point-light intensity 130, silicone emission 45 and pink emission 24. These numbers describe source coefficients, not equivalent radiometric units across material and light properties. Turning off only the tripod and room therefore does not establish an LCD-only room (src/scene.js:563–603).
Sampling screen light in linear space

ScreenIllumination samples a 24-by-16 canvas, so each sample visits 384 pixels. A 256-entry floating-point lookup table converts byte channels from sRGB to linear values. The code sums converted values, divides by 384, and interpolates its current color toward that target. Averaging encoded bytes first would not conserve average light energy: half black plus half white averages to linear .5, not the linear equivalent of encoded middle gray (src/lighting.js:5–7, src/lighting.js:163–187).

Sampling a live source happens at most once per 125 milliseconds unless the source changes. Interpolation can still advance on eligible room paints. Its coefficient is 1-exp(-18*delta), making the response depend on elapsed seconds instead of a fixed fraction per callback. A maximum channel error below .00001 snaps to the target, allowing eventual idle rendering rather than an asymptote that stays dirty forever.

The maximum current channel, called peak, determines area-light intensity as peak*12. Normalizing color by peak separates hue from overall strength. Experimental control spill uses peak^.25*.1; it makes dim content contribute a small amount near coplanar controls without inventing global ambient light. At peak zero, intensity is zero. The code avoids dividing by zero, and clear() explicitly zeros both emitters when a source goes away.
Exposure is stateful, not a one-off correction

During rendering, exposure targets .018 if any tripod, room, Pear or axolotl lamp is on, and .45 only when all are off. It damps toward the target with rate four. That is a factor of 25 between endpoints, not a sudden multiplication applied to LCD pixels. The GBA indicator's emission compensates by multiplying 80*.018/currentExposure, preventing dark adaptation from bleaching its green appearance (src/scene.js:1222–1236).

The DS accent fill also follows this branch. Its emission is copied from material color only in the brighter-room target state and cleared for the dark-room target. It is an explicit stylization, not evidence that metallic paint generates light. Document this approximation rather than hiding it behind the word realistic. Active LCD materials avoid tone mapping entirely, so their picture and the room's adaptation have different ownership.
Figure MD29.2. All four switch families participate in adaptation; forgetting one changes both illumination and exposure.
Diagnose color by changing one stage

Use an ordered diagnostic rather than tuning several coefficients. First establish which object a sample actually hits. A ray landing on the glossy screen instead of blue paint invalidates a shell-color conclusion. Next identify material state: active basic LCD, inactive physical glass, ordinary painted shell or emissive accent. Then record every lamp switch and exposure target. Only after those conditions are explicit should a light coefficient be changed.

A color texture and a data texture also have different meanings. The checked current color-management guide recommends sRGB annotation for color imagery, while roughness, normal and other noncolor data must not receive a display-color conversion. The lamp's generated fabric is color imagery; calling every generated canvas “data” would therefore be an incorrect shortcut. Conversely, a proposed numeric roughness texture should not inherit the color helper's annotation without review. This is researched extension guidance, not a claim that a new roughness canvas exists in the lamp.

Finally compare settled states. A frame taken during exposure damping mixes old and new adaptation even if the light switch changed instantly. Record current exposure or deliberately wait for convergence. Do not demand an arbitrary fixed wait universally: eligible GPU paints and interpolation time determine progress. For exact LCD invariance, material type plus unchanged samples is stronger than a loosely described screenshot. For shell appearance, acknowledge that chosen probes cover only their local surfaces and views. A passing blue-channel threshold does not establish calibrated color across all monitors, camera angles or tone-mapping alternatives.
MD29-W01 Work a half-white screen through the sampler

Assume the downsampled canvas contains 192 white pixels and 192 black pixels, with equal channels and no resampling ambiguity. Converted linear white is one and black zero, so target RGB is (.5,.5,.5). Starting from black, after .1 seconds the interpolation coefficient is 1-exp(-1.8), approximately .83470. Current RGB becomes approximately (.41735,.41735,.41735). Peak is .41735, the primary area intensity becomes about 5.0082, and normalized light color is white. Control spill is approximately .0804. These are calculated expectations under stated assumptions, not recorded browser samples.

The following standalone Node recipe uses no browser or model assets. It reproduces that arithmetic and should log a primary intensity close to five. It intentionally does not approximate the renderer's ACES curve, which would add a different stage to the experiment.

For comparison, taking an encoded average .5 and then linearizing it yields about .214, less than half the desired average energy. This explains why a lookup table is a correctness mechanism rather than merely a micro-optimization.
MD29-R01 Retry a dark upright DS without global ambient

Change the condition from a console lying on the table to the straight, camera-facing DS play pose. The historical repair moved its target from (5,5.1,8) to (-2,5.1,-8). It did not raise exposure, recolor paint or add a camera light. The causal diff explains that the face must remain behind the existing emitter instead of being backlit (commit 9be851e).

Reproduce the diagnosis with the checked desktop and phone fixture: disable both companions, use real static status LCDs, verify the root is straight, ray-check eight shell probes, and compare tripod-only, all-off and room-only pixels. The test requires blue above 75 under the tripod and

maximum channel below three in darkness; it also requires the LCD RGB values to remain identical across states. These are assertions read in source, not a new successful run (tests/browser/ds.spec.mjs:1412–1486).
MD29-Q01 Exercise: why is “all off” still bright?

An agent switches off the tripod and ceiling controls, sees bright table pixels, and reduces LCD spill until they darken. Identify two uncontrolled inputs and explain why the apparent repair would damage a valid dark-room experiment.
MD29-A01 Explained answer

Pear and axolotl remain independent illumination sources and also keep the low-exposure target selected. Disable both using their scene methods, then wait for adaptation and a real eligible paint. Otherwise the experiment mixes changed light energy with changed exposure. Reducing LCD spill would compensate for an incorrect fixture and remove legitimate screen-driven lighting from the actual all-lamps-off state.

The public verification record explicitly separates fixture isolation from production changes and reports parked lighting coverage as debt, not fixed behavior (docs/VERIFICATION.md:21–37). Use that same discipline when deciding whether a color mismatch belongs to encoding, material, geometry, exposure or evidence.

MD30 / SHADOWS, REFLECTIONS AND SHADERS
Shadows, reflections and shaders
Three effects that must not share a diagnosis

A dark patch beneath an object, a bright moving patch on lacquer and a discolored LCD may all look like lighting defects, yet they arise from different pipelines. Shadows estimate blocked direct light. Environment reflection samples surrounding radiance. Screen shaders or canvas effects transform image content. Start by naming the pipeline before changing a parameter. This scene does not contain a universal reflection or global-illumination engine: it combines a spotlight shadow map, authored fill, selected physical materials and a cached room cubemap (src/scene.js:39–47, src/lighting.js:82–110).

The current official shadow guide, checked 2026-11-07, explains the basic cost: shadow-casting lights render casters from their own viewpoint before the main view. Its examples are recommendations, not measurements of this application. In particular, adding shadow-casting point lights to every glowing companion would introduce extra scene views rather than simply making their existing glow more accurate.
Figure MD30.1. A surface combines different evidence paths; a cubemap highlight is not a shadow and neither is a screen filter.
Constructing the shadow path

The renderer enables shadows, selects PCFShadowMap and disables automatic shadow updates. The tripod spotlight casts the mapped shadow. Its map is 1024 square, near plane .7, far plane 120, bias -.00012, normal bias .008 and radius 16. These are authored settings, not guarantees of a particular penumbra width on every GPU. Preserve them as a baseline before testing an alternative shadow technique (src/lighting.js:82–92).

The lamp mesh helper initially makes objects both casters and receivers, but shade, rims and diffuser override casting to false. The tabletop casts and receives; wall and floor receive. This asymmetry is purposeful. An opaque shadow-casting thin drum could block the very light used to suggest transmitted fabric. It would also make an illumination approximation look like a modeling hole. Shadow flags therefore belong to the material-and-light contract, not merely to a mesh-construction convenience.

The main render path marks shadows dirty when scene change, active pose change or button motion requires it. Reflection capture also requests shadow updates before and after its temporary renderer state change. Disabling automatic updates is safe only while these invalidation paths remain complete. A new animated prop that never sets changed can leave a stale shadow even if its own transform is correct (src/scene.js:1367–1386).

Pear additionally has a stylized contact plane. The scene keeps it at world Y .012 by subtracting body height from its local Y, fades opacity no lower than .12, and enlarges its scale with height. Picking explicitly ignores it. Treat this as a visual attachment, not a physical obstacle or an accurate soft-shadow solution. The room's mapped shadow and the character's contact cue serve different jobs (src/scene.js:547–553, src/scene.js:894–899).
Building the reflected environment

The constructor allocates a 128-square half-float cube render target, a cube camera with near .1 and far 1500, and a PMREMGenerator. It traverses the DS and stores its physical materials in a Set. That Set avoids duplicate assignment when meshes share a material; it does not mean every glossy object in the room receives this environment map (src/scene.js:161–167).

updateDsReflections records console visibility and renderer tone mapping, hides both consoles, moves the capture camera to the DS root, and captures with NoToneMapping. It then filters the cube texture, assigns the filtered texture to collected physical materials, disposes the previous filtered target, and clears the dirty flag. A finally block restores visibility and tone mapping even if capture or filtering throws (src/scene.js:1077–1100).

Hiding both consoles prevents self-capture and the other console from appearing in this approximation. It also limits fidelity: this is not a full mutually reflective scene. A single capture point cannot reproduce parallax-correct nearby reflections across the whole clamshell. Describe

the result as an actual-room sampled environment with explicit omissions, not as perfect mirror physics. Physical material roughness can blur that environment but cannot supply missing spatial information.

The current official MeshPhysicalMaterial reference supports understanding clearcoat and roughness as distinct surface layers and parameters. It now contains properties and deprecations newer than the pinned runtime. Consult it for concepts only; do not silently add a current property to a reconstruction of revision 1e4ef518.
Cache policy is part of appearance

Room capture waits until there is no transition, inspection drag, pinch, companion move or console move, both companions are sleeping, and consoles are not moving. Light switching paints direct illumination first, then permits reflection refresh on a later settled paint. This is a latency tradeoff: a temporarily stale reflection is preferable to making every direct-light switch wait for six extra views and filtering.

Switching tripod lights changes intensity instead of removing light objects. Keeping shader light counts stable reduces compilation churn. This is a concrete implementation choice, not a blanket promise that material changes never compile shaders. The browser fixture compares program counts and requires a direct-light paint while reflections are still pending; it is explicitly CI-parked in the pinned source (tests/browser/scene.spec.mjs:150–199).
Figure MD30.2. Reflection quality is scheduled behind responsiveness; the first switched frame intentionally uses the previous environment.
Shader selection is not the canvas CRT pipeline

The word shader is particularly easy to overextend here. Renderer materials compile GPU programs; preferences expose validated native CRT choices; generated status pictures receive a canvas overlay. drawLcdCrt uses ordinary 2D composite operations and a cached pattern. It is not a custom imported GLSL file secretly responsible for the DS clearcoat or room shadow map (src/lcd-crt.js:1–39).

When diagnosing a dark edge, first reproduce it with a static status image and fixed camera. If it remains painted into that image independent of room state, inspect the vignette and picture generation path. If it moves with viewing direction on inactive glass, inspect physical material and environment. If another object changes it by blocking the lamp, inspect the shadow path. These experiments isolate causes without rewriting three pipelines at once.

For a proposed higher-quality reflection mode, state the budget before implementation. Doubling cube-face side length quadruples texel count per face, and there are six faces before filtering. A 128-square cube contains 98,304 base face texels; 256-square contains 393,216. Those counts exclude mip levels, attachment formats, filtering intermediates and implementation overhead. They are arithmetic, not measured VRAM consumption. Any claim of actual memory use or

timing needs profiling on the target renderer. Preserve current responsiveness and settled-refresh behavior while evaluating the new quality mode, and make any changed resolution contract explicit rather than silently altering the baseline.
MD30-W01 Trace a light switch through two eligible paints

Assume the scene has settled with no outstanding fence and the tripod is on. The user switches it off. First, setLamp(false) stores/restores known intensities, sets all four to zero, disables shade and bulb emission, and sets changed, lightingChanged and dsReflectionsDirty.

On the next eligible render, lightingChanged allows recovery bypass but not outstanding-fence bypass. Reflection capture is excluded because lightingChanged is true. The main view paints the switched direct lighting, resets that flag and inserts a GPU fence. Once the fence and any severe-load recovery permit another frame, a settled scene may capture and filter the new room environment. No numeric duration follows from these steps: eligibility depends on actual GPU completion.
This explicit pseudocode is a teaching reduction, not replacement application code. It assumes capture succeeds and retains the ordering needed for a responsive switch.

on switch:
  directDirty = true
  environmentDirty = true
on eligible paint:
  if environmentDirty and not directDirty and settled:
    capture and replace environment
  render main view
  directDirty = false
  insert completion fence
Expected outcome is a direct-light frame before environment replacement. Record frame order, flags and actual sampled pixels; a checkbox changing alone does not demonstrate the effect.
MD30-R01 Retry after a moving companion changes reflections

Change the condition: the axolotl is dragged while its light is on. Do not capture a fresh environment on every pointer event. Let movement dirty the main view and retain deferred reflection refresh until the object sleeps. If the DS seems to reflect the old position during movement, that can be the intentional cache policy rather than failed light propagation.

After landing, verify that dirty state eventually clears and that the previous filtered target is disposed. If it never clears, inspect held/moving flags and pending presentation acknowledgments before increasing capture frequency. If memory grows across repeated replacements, inspect

target ownership rather than deleting arbitrary scene textures. The checked official cleanup guide reinforces that render resources require explicit release; material disappearance from a scene is not disposal.
MD30-Q01 Exercise: can clearcoat fix missing shadows?

A proposed change increases clearcoat until the DS has a brighter edge, claiming it restored lamp shadow detail. Explain the category error and propose independent observations for reflection, direct occlusion and cached-state correctness.
MD30-A01 Explained answer

Clearcoat changes the reflective response of a material; it cannot create a missing caster or update an old shadow map. Check caster, receiver, light and renderer flags for the shadow path. Then move a known light or object and inspect whether shadow invalidation occurs. For reflection, inspect the assigned environment texture, capture origin and settled refresh conditions separately. For cached state, compare dirty flags before and after an eligible paint, not after an arbitrary animation callback.

Keep the evidence limitation visible. CI parking retains the original switch assertions but does not prove they currently pass; the verification record calls such exclusions coverage debt (docs/VERIFICATION.md:93–107). An appealing reflection and a passed structural assertion still require separate human aesthetic review.
