MD31 / SCREEN MATERIALS AND PIXEL PRESERVATION
Screen materials and pixel preservation
A screen has several independent representations

The physical LCD is geometry, its picture is a texture, its powered-off appearance is a reflective material, and its contribution to room light is a separate emitter. Combining those into one vaguely emissive glass material would make room exposure alter game colors and would confuse touch mapping with a decorative overlay. Reconstruction begins by preserving these responsibilities rather than choosing a shader that looks screen-like (src/scene.js:1106–1142).

The library is exactly Three.js 0.186.1 (package.json:7–9). The checked current color-management manual supports the distinction between color textures, linear lighting and sRGB output, but does not establish historical runtime defaults. Keep the source's explicit color-space annotations even if a newer example appears to work without them.
Figure MD31.1. Picture display and room illumination share an image source but not a material or exposure path.
Active display versus inactive glass

When the GBA powers off, the scene clears its source and screen illumination, then installs MeshPhysicalMaterial with color #101713, roughness .24, clearcoat one and clearcoat roughness .22. That is deliberately reflective dark glass. When a live canvas is attached, setScreen creates an sRGB CanvasTexture, sets both filters to LinearFilter, disables mipmaps and uses MeshBasicMaterial with toneMapped:false. These assignments mean the active picture does not acquire the room's tone mapping or direct-light response.

The DS follows the same active/inactive distinction but not the same live-texture filtering. Its powered-off path uses reflective physical material. Status screens use basic non-tone-mapped materials. When the retained native framebuffer starts, the controller creates two 256-by-192 canvas textures with both filters set to NearestFilter, no mipmaps, and non-tone-mapped basic materials (src/ds-controller.js:266–294, src/ds-controller.js:415–435).

This difference matters. “All active LCDs use nearest” would be false for the pinned GBA path. Nearest is the exact DS native pixel-preservation contract; linear filtering is an explicit GBA choice for a supplied canvas that can already contain filtered content. Neither implies a one-to-one mapping between source pixels and final device pixels at every camera angle. Perspective projection, canvas density and screen footprint remain involved.

The controller verifies the native canvas layout and requires a retained drawing buffer before accepting it. paintScreens copies each region into its output canvas with imageSmoothingEnabled=false, then marks the corresponding texture dirty. These copies occur even when the room-render budget defers another 3D paint (src/ds-controller.js:662–675). Do not describe texture dirtiness as proof that the main view has already presented the new picture.
Curved outlines without a second framebuffer warp

createLcdGeometries gives the GBA viewport width 4.05 and height width*2/3 = 2.7. The curved option builds a shape outline; the flat option builds a plane. For curved geometry, UVs are explicitly set from XY position divided by viewport dimensions plus one half. This preserves a direct image mapping inside a curved boundary instead of warping an already-filtered framebuffer again (src/handheld.js:49–65).

The recess is regenerated with the screen, and old geometries are disposed during a curve change. Geometry owns silhouette; the emulator or built-in drawing path owns the picture. Moving the outline vertices and then adding another barrel distortion to UVs would create two unrelated distortions. That might be a proposed artistic experiment, but it is not the implemented reconstruction.

Pixel preservation also requires preserving the original source. Changing world exposure to rescue dark shell paint should leave active LCD RGB unchanged. A fixture that samples powered-off glass cannot assert that rule because the powered-off material is intentionally light-responsive. The
upright DS lighting test therefore installs real status LCDs before comparing light states, and checks material type as well as RGB (tests/browser/ds.spec.mjs:1421–1484).
Built-in CRT is a canvas effect, not an imported model

drawLcdCrt uses a WeakMap keyed by the destination canvas. It caches a three-column mask tile, a repeated pattern and a radial vignette. Cache identity includes canvas width, height and row count. It saves context state, resets the transform, multiplies the mask over the picture, overlays the vignette and restores state. The effect belongs to generated startup/status pictures, not to a new modeled CRT tube or a universal postprocessor (src/lcd-crt.js:1–39).

Each tile column has a slightly different near-white tint. The last row gets a translucent black scanline. The radial gradient stays transparent until its outer region and darkens the edge. These are restrained overlays; no random noise or frame-time-dependent mask is generated. A WeakMap avoids keeping an otherwise unreachable canvas alive solely because its cached pattern exists, although GPU textures still require their separate disposal.

Preferences list supported native CRT presets and allow disabled; validation rejects unrecognized values. That list does not mean all presets run through drawLcdCrt. Distinguish native preset selection from the built-in canvas treatment (src/preferences.js:1–13, src/preferences.js:67–90).
Figure MD31.2. The built-in treatment overlays a generated canvas and returns its drawing state to the caller.
A practical pixel-preservation audit

Follow the image through its boundaries. At the native boundary, record canvas dimensions, retained-buffer eligibility and region layout. At the 2D boundary, record source rectangle, destination rectangle and smoothing state. At the texture boundary, inspect color space, filters and mipmap generation. At the material boundary, inspect basic versus physical and tone-mapping state. At the final view boundary, record camera, projected viewport size and renderer pixel ratio. Each stage can be correct while another introduces blur or color change.

Use a chart with alternating single-source-pixel columns to expose resampling. At exact integer enlargement, nearest should retain hard repeated blocks; linear should interpolate transitions. At arbitrary perspective tilt, the chart may alias under nearest or blur under linear. That is a sampling tradeoff, not evidence that the native framebuffer was corrupted. Keep a direct native or canvas sample beside the projected-view observation when isolating the cause.

Do not assume disabling mipmaps is universally best for every scene texture. It is the explicit LCD choice here. The wood and fabric maps have different visual frequencies, screen footprints and lifecycle. Copying an LCD texture policy to all room materials could worsen distant texture aliasing. Likewise, anisotropy on the general canvas helper does not supersede the explicitly assigned DS nearest filters.

For memory ownership, each newly attached screen map replaces an older one through setDisplay, which disposes the prior map and material. A debugging chart that is injected outside that path needs its own cleanup. Removing its DOM canvas does not release a corresponding GPU texture automatically. Keep that distinction in a reconstruction checklist rather than treating debug-only resources as cost-free.

A useful negative control is a solid black active picture. Its basic material should remain black rather than acquiring a reflected lamp highlight, while the separate sampler should converge toward zero emission. Powered-off glass can still show the room. Comparing these two superficially similar dark screens exposes accidental material reuse. A second control, a constant white chart, separates exposure invariance from source animation. Neither requires private gameplay content. Use public generated charts first, then qualify native behavior separately where execution is authorized. This keeps a failed picture pipeline from being misdiagnosed through a moving, uncontrolled emulator scene.
MD31-W01 Work out the cached scanline tile

Use the GBA status size 720 by 480 and default 160 rows. round(480/160) is three, so the mask tile is three by three. At DS status size 512 by 384 with 192 rows, the tile height is two. Its three columns repeat across width regardless of whether the width divides evenly by three; the pattern is clipped by the destination fill rectangle.

The following original browser-console recipe assumes same-origin served modules. It draws a generated chart, not emulator content, and deliberately applies the effect only once. Expected outcome is a chart with a fine repeating mask and darker outer corners. The assertion checks caller state, not aesthetic quality.

Do not call this repeatedly on the same unchanged image without redrawing its base. Multiplication accumulates darkness. The cache saves pattern construction; it does not make the overlay idempotent. That is an important distinction between caching an effect's resources and caching an effect's final output.
MD31-R01 Retry after doubling the destination height

Change the chart height to 960 while keeping 160 rows. The cached tile must be rebuilt because its height becomes six and the vignette radius changes. If an extension caches only by canvas identity, it will retain the old scale and produce denser-looking lines after resize. Preserve the width/height/rows key, not just the WeakMap container.

If DS native pixels look softened, inspect both stages before raising texture resolution: the 2D copy must disable smoothing, and texture minification/magnification must remain nearest. Then inspect actual projected footprint. A subpixel-wide source feature cannot be universally preserved after arbitrary perspective minification. No renderer flag establishes that impossible guarantee.
MD31-Q01 Exercise: fix a false LCD-light regression

A test powers off the DS, toggles room light, and fails because LCD center RGB changes. It proposes disabling tone mapping on every material in the scene. Explain the wrong premise and design two narrower tests.
MD31-A01 Explained answer

Powered-off glass is physical and reflective, so its appearance should respond to surroundings. Test that state for reflective material properties and sensible room dependence. Separately install an active status or native display and require a basic non-tone-mapped material plus unchanged picture samples across lighting states. Disable both companions when claiming LCD-only illumination; otherwise their light and exposure branch remain uncontrolled.

Keep any native-input test independent from this static color fixture. A generated status chart can prove material isolation but cannot prove that the emulator advanced or received touch. The public verification document explicitly distinguishes technical evidence from human acceptance and from deployment (docs/VERIFICATION.md:1–8).

MD32 / PICKING, OCCLUSION AND INPUT OWNERSHIP
Picking, occlusion and input ownership
Visibility does not automatically grant input

An interactive procedural model needs more than triangles under the cursor. It needs a rule for which surface owns a gesture, when that ownership ends, and how an action reaches its intended subsystem. The same canvas supports table movement, inspection, lamp switching and DS stylus interactions. Those actions cannot all respond to the same pointerdown. HandheldScene therefore dispatches by mode, transition state, hit metadata and current movement ownership (src/scene.js:180–231).

Begin with a state table rather than adding event handlers until the desired click works. In table mode a console click can become movement or play selection; in inspection it rotates the active body or edits a hinge; in DS play a lower-screen touch can become native touch. A modal dialog, transition or held stylus changes what is available. These are behavioral ownership boundaries, not incidental UI details.
Figure MD32.1. A successful pick is only the middle of an interaction; gates and cleanup make ownership reliable.
Converting browser coordinates into a world ray

pick gets the scene canvas's CSS bounding rectangle. It converts client coordinates into normalized device coordinates by subtracting the rectangle origin, dividing by its CSS size, mapping X into minus one through one, and flipping Y. Raycaster.setFromCamera then produces the world ray. It intersects GBA, DS, tripod, Pear and axolotl roots recursively and uses the first permitted hit (src/scene.js:547–561).

Do not divide client coordinates by the drawing buffer dimensions. A device-pixel ratio of two doubles the buffer but does not double CSS pointer coordinates. Conversely, framebuffer reads need buffer coordinates. Many apparently small picking offsets come from mixing these spaces, especially after moving a canvas away from the viewport origin.

Two exceptions refine nearest-hit selection. Pear's contact plane is ignored because it is a visual cue rather than a selectable object. A docked stylus marked dsStylus is ignored while the stylus is held, preventing its inactive original geometry from stealing input. These exclusions should remain specific. A general rule that ignores all transparent meshes could break legitimate screen or decorative-surface interactions.

DS native touch has a stricter ray test. It intersects the complete DS model and accepts only when the first permitted hit is the lower screen itself. It does not raycast directly against the LCD and accept a point through an intervening lid. The resulting UV is converted by dsTouchFromUv, then sent with a pressed or cancelled state to the retained iframe (src/ds-controller.js:490–508).
Dragging owns a plane, offset and pointer identity

A console movement record stores system, original position, pointer ID, initial CSS coordinates, a camera-facing plane and grab offset. The plane passes through the picked point, so dragging follows a constant-depth surface initially. Subtracting the ray-plane point from root position preserves where the user grabbed the object; without it, picking a corner snaps the root under the cursor (src/scene.js:635–654).

Movement becomes a drag only after more than four CSS pixels of pointer travel. Wheel depth is separately treated as movement. Its displacement follows camera forward, clamped to two world units per event. When a move is accepted, the interaction plane is translated by the actual accepted displacement, not the requested displacement. This matters at workspace edges: using the unclamped request would leave the next pointer event intersecting a plane the object never reached (src/scene.js:233–246, src/scene.js:295–323).

Pointer capture keeps the original owner receiving subsequent events outside the element. Release, cancellation and lost capture have different meanings. A normal release after motion drops with bounded inertia; cancellation restores the original position; a stationary console release activates play. Blur, resize, view change and console selection also cancel owned movements. A robust extension must cover these exits before claiming a new drag interaction is complete.

Keyboard movement uses .65-unit steps along X, Y and Z. It clears velocity after each accepted step because deliberate keyboard placement should not imitate a fast pointer throw. Enter drops and Escape cancels. Inspection has different arrow-key semantics, so movement ownership is checked first. The project architecture documents that positions are session state, not reload-persisted placements (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:43–68).
Projected controls need their own occlusion contract

DS control DOM elements project from physical anchors. The controller first rejects wrong mode, transitions, back-facing normals and offscreen positions. It then raycasts the lid and hides a control if the lid is nearer than the anchor distance minus .08. Only visible targets receive projected CSS position and scaled size, with a minimum 44-pixel power target and 14-pixel ordinary target (src/ds-controller.js:677–700).

The stylus button uses a separate obstruction check and margin .16. Do not copy one tolerance blindly into the other: their anchors and target geometry differ. Likewise, these DOM checks are not a universal scene-wide occlusion solver. They implement the specific DS lid and stylus ownership requirements of the current application.

Projection cannot wait for the next eligible GPU paint. updateViewMatrices updates camera and active-model matrices and projects controls immediately after pose/camera changes. Otherwise a deferred room frame could leave current DOM targets paired with stale touch rays (src/scene.js:484–500).
Figure MD32.2. Input geometry becomes current before GPU scheduling decides whether another room image can be submitted.
Native messaging has session ownership too

touch requires both a frame and a running controller. Its message includes the touch payload and current session and is posted to location.origin. A visually correct stylus therefore does not prove a native touch was accepted: the controller must still have a valid retained target. Keep session identity in any diagnostic log, without publishing unrelated private user data (src/ds-controller.js:498–508).

A complete regression observes at least three stages. First, the ray produces a legal lower-LCD UV under current geometry. Second, the controller sends press and release for the current session. Third, a native response demonstrates effect where the fixture supports it. A moving physical button cap proves neither the second nor the third stage. Conversely, an iframe accepting input does not establish that its hit target matches the visible handheld.

For accessibility, preserve the distinction between target size and physical size. The power control's minimum 44 CSS pixels is an input affordance; it does not enlarge the modeled button cap or change native geometry. A projected target can be larger than its visible cap while still belonging to the same anchor and occlusion rule. Test pointer hit area and physical travel independently. If the target remains active through a closed lid, a generous size is not an excuse: visibility gating must hide it before sizing. This is a practical reason to keep projection checks in their current order.

This distinction also guides cancellation tests. Hold a pointer, change view or open tools, and inspect whether all owned sources release. Repeat with keyboard and touch ownership separately; one synthetic release cannot stand in for every source. Then resume the retained session and confirm no old hold remains. These are proposed diagnostic steps derived from the controller's cleanup contract, not claims of newly executed browser results. They make the boundary reusable for a future model without assuming that another console shares the DS's exact message schema or stylus availability rules.
MD32-W01 Convert a pointer and preserve its grab

Assume the canvas CSS rectangle is left 100, top 50, width 800, height 600. A pointer at (500,200) produces X (400/800)*2-1 = 0 and Y -(150/600)*2+1 = .5. Those coordinates stay the same at pixel ratio one or two. If the ray intersects the movement plane at world (3,4,2) while the object's root is (5,4,1), the stored offset is (2,0,-1). A later intersection (4,5,2) requests root (6,5,1), preserving the original grab.
This runnable Node recipe checks the coordinate arithmetic only; ray generation still requires camera matrices and Three.js. It is intentionally small enough to print beside a diagram.

Expected behavior after a rejected placement is different: the model stays in its accepted position, and no fabricated successful displacement is recorded. Keep intent, acceptance and presentation as separate observations.
MD32-R01 Retry with a closed lid and deferred room paint

Change the condition from a flat, unobstructed DS to a lid covering the lower LCD while GPU recovery is active. Update pose matrices immediately. The lower-screen-only raycast shortcut would still return UVs, but the complete-model nearest-hit rule should reject touch through the lid. DOM controls obscured by the lid should likewise disappear.

If the visible image is one frame old, that does not justify sending input through current occluding geometry. Test current projection and ray ownership independently, then verify the next eligible painted pose. Do not remove recovery or fake future timestamps simply to make the test click its old target. The DS browser coverage explicitly includes inaccessible controls and lower-screen rejection in an occluded pose (tests/browser/ds.spec.mjs:250–268).
MD32-Q01 Exercise: explain a stuck native press

A new tool dialog opens during a held DS pointer action. The dialog looks correct, but gameplay continues receiving the old hold. Why is visual correctness insufficient, and which ownership cleanup should the tool reuse?
MD32-A01 Explained answer

Opening a dialog changes who can receive the eventual release. The existing controller's openTools first calls releaseInputs: keyboard release, cancelled touch, stylus return, release of recorded pointer sources, and map clearing. A tool that only changes visibility bypasses that contract (src/ds-controller.js:265–266, src/ds-controller.js:509–514).

Reuse the owner-level cleanup rather than synthesizing one arbitrary keyup. Preferences separately validate unique bindings and reserve browser-sensitive keys; valid bindings do not remove the need for release semantics (src/preferences.js:63–90). A complete interaction test checks press, ownership transfer, release/cancellation and absence of stale state, not just whether a dialog appeared.

MD33 / RENDER LOOPS, GPU BUDGETS AND LIFECYCLE
Render loops, GPU budgets and lifecycle
A callback is not a completed picture

The browser can call JavaScript again before previously submitted graphics work finishes. A modeling application that treats every animation callback as a completed picture can queue expensive room renders faster than the GPU drains them. It can also integrate an entire fall between visible frames. This project separates callback time, render submission, completion fences and presentation-aware motion (src/scene.js:1167–1217).

The main renderer uses antialiasing and caps device-pixel ratio at two. It does not dynamically lower sharpness after a slow frame. Root dependencies pin Three.js 0.186.1 (package.json:7–9). Budgeting here primarily changes when another room image may be submitted, not how many source pixels are discarded.

The checked MDN WebGL best-practices page recommends avoiding blocking calls in production, flushing when awaiting fence results, and budgeting memory conservatively. Those are current recommendations consulted 2026-11-07. They explain the design, but do not constitute a benchmark of this room or proof of universal browser behavior.
Figure MD33.1. The render loop updates more often than it necessarily submits room work; a fence protects the queue rather than creating another animation clock.
Constructing the scheduling state

The constructor checks whether fenceSync, clientWaitSync, deleteSync and flush are available. Following a main room render, fenceRoomPaint inserts a completion fence and flushes. Later callbacks poll it with zero timeout. A timeout retains the outstanding fence and withholds another room submission; failure reports an explicit synchronization error. A signaled fence allows deletion and scheduling of the next eligible paint.

This proves completion of submitted GPU commands before the fence, not that a human saw a frame at a particular display scanout. It is nevertheless stronger evidence than “one rAF elapsed.” Startup uses this distinction: waitForFirstPaint waits for scene changes and reflections to settle, then fences the completed first frame when supported (src/scene.js:413–449).

Recovery depends on observed completion delay. For a fence observed no later than 100 milliseconds after submission, no extra idle interval is added. Beyond that threshold, delay is twice observed elapsed time, capped at 1000 milliseconds for settled playing and 200 otherwise. “Otherwise” includes transitions and cartridge insertion. The no-fence fallback has its own earlier-callback heuristic and is not identical to the fence path.

paintDue also requires no failed synchronization, no native busy operation and no open dialog. A lighting change bypasses the recovery timestamp, but not an outstanding fence or those other gates. This precise exception lets direct switching feel responsive without submitting work on top of an unfinished room frame.
Different loops have different owners

The scene still updates body motion, gaze, limbs and control state before returning at the room gate. DS paintStylus and paintScreens also run before that return. The latter copies retained native framebuffer regions into output canvases; it is not the expensive full 3D room render. Moving the copy behind the gate would couple native LCD freshness to room recovery again (src/scene.js:1303–1342, src/ds-controller.js:662–675).

At an eligible paint, screen illumination samples use elapsed time since the last paint. Clearance resolves before actual rendering. An idle guard then checks sources, dirty flags, active pose, button movement, adaptation and illumination settling. If nothing requires a new picture, it returns without waking a settled room. A new component must dirty the scene when its appearance changes and eventually stop dirtying it when settled.

After rendering, body motion acknowledges its required presentation pose; transition and cartridge elapsed values are committed to that painted step. GPU completion remains tracked by the fence. This is a pipeline with separate submission and completion contracts, not a claim that every physics acknowledgment waited for monitor presentation (src/scene.js:1372–1412).

Fullscreen screen focus suspends the room animation loop. On return it resets lastRender, recovery, rendered-frame state and dirtiness before restarting (src/scene.js:537–545). Context loss reports an error without claiming saves were deleted; restoration clears synchronization failure and requests a fresh paint. Failure of LCD light sampling similarly clears and parks that sampler, reports the error, and retains the game instead of retrying it every frame.
Resource lifecycle is a model contract

setDisplay releases the old screen map and material. setScreenCurve releases replaced geometries. Reflection replacement disposes the previous filtered target. Final scene disposal stops animation, removes registered global handlers, disconnects resize observation, deletes the pending fence, releases reflection resources, traverses geometry/material resources, and disposes the renderer (src/scene.js:1114–1130, src/scene.js:1430–1450).

Do not exaggerate this into a universal resource manager. The traversal handles current material maps and explicitly handled DS bump maps; it does not enumerate every possible texture property a future material might acquire. Shared leg geometry and materials can also be encountered more than once. A proposed extension should track unique owned resources with a Set and define external ownership rather than blindly disposing every referenced texture.

The current official cleanup guide explains explicit geometry, texture and material disposal, including resource tracking. Apply that principle when extending this implementation, but label a new tracker as a proposal until it is actually installed and tested.
Figure MD33.2. Releasing GPU resources starts with ownership and callback shutdown; removing a mesh alone is not cleanup.
Quantify a budget without inventing performance results

Pixel count is a useful first estimate, not a benchmark. For a CSS canvas 800 by 600, pixel ratio one gives 480,000 drawing-buffer pixels; ratio two gives 1,920,000. That fourfold count helps explain why density matters without asserting that total GPU time must also quadruple.
Geometry, shaders, shadows, captures, copies and driver behavior contribute different fixed and variable costs.

Similarly, the screen sampler visits 384 pixels per sample regardless of the native picture's source size. Its readback remains a synchronization-sensitive operation, so reducing sample dimensions does not prove zero stall. The source catches readback failures and quarantines the failed emitter. A proposed optimization should measure actual sample cost and retain error visibility rather than merely removing the catch because the canvas is small.

For a trustworthy experiment, record CSS size, buffer size, device ratio, browser/GPU environment, active lights, moving objects and whether an environment capture occurred. Separate CPU callback duration from observed fence delay. The latter includes queued completion observed by a later callback; it is not automatically an isolated GPU timer query for one mesh. Also distinguish initial shader compilation from settled switching, since their costs and remedies differ.

The checked current MDN guidance suggests batching, smaller buffers when appropriate and avoiding needless synchronous queries. Here, smaller buffers would alter an explicit product constraint. Investigate redundant submission, repeated environment refresh or perpetual dirty state first. If a new quality mode later changes density, name it as a new authorized feature with its own visual acceptance and regression criteria, not as a transparent repair of the existing full-resolution path.

For lifecycle testing, repeat an owned operation rather than reading one final memory number. Replace status screens several times, toggle curve geometry, refresh reflections and dispose the scene. Track which resources should be created and released at each step. A stable memory reading alone can hide a retained object if driver allocation is pooled; a rising reading alone can include intentional caches. Pair ownership counts with renderer diagnostics and actual disposal paths. This is a recommended future harness, not a claim that a repeated-resource profile was run here. Keep the current cleanup limitations visible until such coverage exists.
MD33-W01 Work through three fence observations

Assume settled play, no transition, no insertion and a room frame submitted at time 1000 milliseconds. If its fence is observed complete at 1100, elapsed is exactly 100: the strict >100 check is false, so nextPaint=1100. If observed at 1101, elapsed 101 gives recovery 202 and nextPaint=1303. If observed at 2000, twice elapsed would be 2000, but the settled-play cap gives 1000, so nextPaint=3000.

Now change only mode to a moving transition. At observation 2000, recovery caps at 200 and next paint is 2200. These are source-derived scheduling examples, not measured frame rates. The following runnable Node calculation reproduces the threshold and cap.
MD33-R01 Retry after a long real GPU wait

Change the test condition: callbacks have been manually paused while real time advances during GPU recovery. Starting the next rest sample from stale lastRender can submit a synthetic timestamp earlier than the real operation's creation time. The sparse-paint regression therefore retires the prior fence, waits recovery, resets the old render baseline and starts from performance.now(), not from a guessed old timestamp (tests/browser/scene.spec.mjs:338–363).

The reusable fixture waits real recovery separately and rejects a caller timestamp earlier than nextPaint. It does not fabricate later time merely because waiting took longer. Preserve both clocks in a retry; otherwise a passing fixture can conceal a scheduling defect (tests/browser/pixel-lab.mjs:8–41).
MD33-Q01 Exercise: make a slow scene faster responsibly

An extension proposes lowering pixel ratio after every 100-millisecond frame and calling gl.finish() before each readback. Explain why neither matches the existing budget contract, and identify a safer first experiment.
MD33-A01 Explained answer

Automatic ratio reduction violates the retained full- resolution sharpness contract. A blocking completion call can stall the main thread and native work rather than solve queue pressure. First measure which work is being submitted, whether reflections are recaptured unnecessarily, whether idle invalidation ever settles and whether real fences are respected. Change one scheduling cause while retaining resolution and assertion bounds.

The original GPU recovery browser scenario is explicitly CI-parked, so its retained assertions are a specification, not a fresh success claim (tests/browser/scene.spec.mjs:437–445). Record both performance observations and missing coverage when handing off the experiment.

MD34 / ALGORITHMS AND DATA STRUCTURES
Algorithms and data structures
Simplification is useful only when its domain is explicit

This desk uses custom clearance and motion algorithms, not a general collision engine. Their strength comes from a limited problem: upright or orientation-locked objects, axis-aligned bounds, a bounded workspace and a small set of obstacles. Understanding those assumptions is more reusable than copying a function name. A nearest legal translation is not the same problem as continuous collision detection during arbitrary rotation (src/desk-clearance.js:3–35, docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:43–101).

The important data structures are modest. Relative Box3 bounds describe an object around its root. A Vector3 stores a proposed root position. Arrays hold obstacles and staged placements. Sets deduplicate candidate coordinates and reflection materials. Small state objects preserve pointer ownership, motion velocity and pending presentation. There is no spatial tree to imply a large-world scalability claim.
Figure MD34.1. Clearance converts geometry bounds into a finite root-position search before mutating any scene object.
Deriving forbidden root rectangles

Let a moving object's local X bounds be bmin and bmax. At root X p, its interval is [p+bmin,p+bmax]. For obstacle interval [omin,omax] and gap g, horizontal overlap occurs when p > omin-bmax-g and p < omax-bmin+g. These two limits form the forbidden root interval. Repeat for Z, after filtering out obstacles that do not overlap at the proposed fixed Y.

The asymmetric formula is essential. A console root can be off-center after rotation, so replacing its bounds with one radius would either miss a corner or unnecessarily move it. The function refuses proposed Y outside workspace limits; it does not search for an alternative height. Its
returned vector preserves Y and is independent of the input vector.

For each axis, the algorithm collects the clamped desired coordinate and both clamped edges of every forbidden rectangle in a Set. It tests their Cartesian product, rejects points in a strict forbidden interior, and minimizes squared distance to the original desired root. For this fixed-height rectangle problem, a nearest free point occurs at a desired coordinate or a boundary coordinate. Squared distance avoids a square root without changing ordering.

With n vertically relevant obstacles there are at most 2n+1 coordinates per axis, thus at most (2n+1)² candidate pairs. Each may test n rectangles: worst-case time is cubic, coordinate and rectangle storage linear. This bound excludes the scene traversal that first computes boxes. It is acceptable for a small authored desk, not a reason to apply the same search to thousands of actors.
Numerical stability and deterministic choice

The strict-interior test allows boundary contact, with a tolerance of eight machine epsilons multiplied by coordinate magnitude. This repairs tiny world/local round-trip errors without forgiving a visible overlap. The unit test separately accepts a one-ULP boundary reconstruction and rejects a real .01 overlap. These are complementary obligations (tests/unit/desk-clearance.test.mjs:90–123).

A different tolerance, 1e-9 in squared-distance comparison, preserves the first candidate when distances are effectively tied. Candidate enumeration follows Set insertion order. Do not advertise complete order independence for every conceivable symmetric layout. The test proves the stated multi-blocker example is invariant under reversed obstacles, while stable ties prevent one-ULP noise from switching sides in repeated scene reconstruction.

The scene's multi-object resolver stages placement arrays before committing transforms. In table mode, companions retain priority, then loose props, then equal-ranked consoles. It tries GBA followed by DS; if that fails, it restores the staged arrays and tries DS followed by GBA. This is two bounded orderings, not all permutations and not global optimal packing (src/scene.js:796–890).
Orientation bounds are a separate algorithm

Current-orientation AABBs work for locked translation but cannot guarantee clearance across the DS transition from table pose to upright play. dsPoseBounds evaluates each mesh bounding box under hypothetical root and lid transforms and unions the results without changing the live pose. That supports camera framing and candidate-space reasoning for an intended endpoint (src/scene.js:502–519).

Even endpoint hypothetical boxes do not prove continuous rotational clearance. An extension promising an unobstructed whole rotation needs swept bounds or sampled intermediate poses with a justified margin. Label that as proposed work. Do not infer it from a successful upright endpoint or from the current desk translation solver.
Fixed-step motion and visible state

DeskMotion integrates at 1/120 second. Update elapsed is capped at five seconds, so at most 600 substeps are processed. Gravity is 45; horizontal damping per step is .998; support restitution is .23 for sufficiently large incoming speed and zero for small contacts. Motion remains upright with no angular momentum, impulse exchange or articulated rigid-body solver (src/pear-motion.js:1–58, src/pear-motion.js:59–89, src/pear-motion.js:91–157).

Pointer velocity is based on a bounded .008–.1 second sample and capped in magnitude at 22. Releasing after more than 100 milliseconds of stale input clears inertia. These limits prevent timing noise or a stationary hold from becoming a huge throw.

Sparse painting needs additional state. A drop can require an intermediate falling pose, an impact and a rising pose. While a required pose awaits paint acknowledgment, motion queues elapsed time instead of racing through the entire event unseen. Unit coverage checks sparse .5- and three-second updates, support speed, orientation locking and presentation transitions (tests/unit/pear-motion.test.mjs:1–180).
Figure MD34.2. Presentation state constrains when simulation may consume queued time; fixed steps alone cannot guarantee a visible fall.
Separate caches from authoritative state

The scene holds authoritative transforms in object roots and motion state. Its clearance signature is only a shortcut for detecting unchanged inputs, not an alternative source of truth. It is saved only after successful placement. If an extension updates the signature before attempting a layout, a failed attempt could look clean on the next callback and suppress the required retry. This is a general transaction lesson derived from the resolver's actual commit boundary.

The array of staged positions is likewise temporary. Successful commit may zero lateral velocity of displaced objects while preserving vertical velocity and waking an elevated sleeper. That detail prevents clearance repair from cancelling a real fall or leaving an unsupported object asleep. A data structure that stores only positions is therefore insufficient to describe the whole commit's behavior.

Three other small structures solve different problems. The screen sampler's lookup array trades a fixed 256-entry allocation for repeated color conversion. The CRT WeakMap allows per-canvas caches without a permanent global strong reference. The reflection material Set deduplicates shared physical materials. Choosing among Array, Set and WeakMap follows access and lifetime requirements; it is not a generic preference for one fashionable container.

When extending the scene, write down expected cardinality. For ten relevant blockers the candidate upper bound is 441 pairs, each checking at most ten rectangles. For one hundred it is 40,401 pairs and potentially over four million interior checks before geometry traversal. These are worst-case arithmetic bounds, not measured runtimes. They show where a spatial index or different packing strategy might become worth researching. Do not introduce that complexity into the small desk without evidence, and do not promise large-world scalability from the current limited test fixtures.
MD34-W01 Solve one asymmetric placement

Assume bounds X [-1,2], Z [-.5,.5], obstacle X [4,6], Z [0,2], overlapping height, and gap .25. Forbidden root X is [1.75,7.25]; forbidden root Z is [-.75,2.75]. Desired root (3,1) in XZ lies inside. Moving left to (1.75,1) costs squared distance 1.5625. Moving to the nearer Z boundary (3,-.75) costs 3.0625. Therefore the left edge wins if the workspace admits it and no second obstacle blocks it.

The following runnable Node recipe imports the actual solver and makes these assumptions explicit. Expected root X is 1.75, Y stays one and inputs remain unchanged. Save it as clearance-example.mjs at the repository root and run node clearance-example.mjs in an authorized scratch checkout with dependencies installed.
MD34-R01 Retry with a second blocker and swapped order

Add a blocker covering the previous left-edge candidate. Rebuild forbidden rectangles and search all candidate pairs; do not merely push right by a fixed distance. The closest free point may combine one rectangle's X edge with another's Z edge. That is why the Cartesian product exists.

For multiple objects, a different failure occurs when the first console consumes the only legal position for the second. The scene retries the opposite console ordering before declaring failure. Keep the lamp fixed, preserve companion priority, and roll back the temporary placement arrays. Mutating the first root before success would make the retry operate on a different starting problem and could visibly jump even when both orders fail.
MD34-Q01 Exercise: add free console rotation

An agent keeps the current relative box and adds arbitrary rotation during dragging, claiming clearance remains exact. Identify which assumptions cease to hold and what evidence would be needed before making that claim.
MD34-A01 Explained answer

Relative bounds now change with orientation, so a box computed before rotation no longer describes the object. Recompute transformed geometry bounds for each candidate orientation, then consider swept motion between old and new poses. A fixed endpoint AABB can be conservative there yet miss an intermediate sweep. Full free rotation also changes support, pivot and inertia assumptions in DeskMotion.

The existing transition helper freezes elapsed when paint is unavailable and preserves an intermediate DS desk step; it is not a continuous collision detector (src/transition-motion.js:1–8). Build explicit rotation and swept-clearance tests before expanding the solver's advertised domain.

MD35 / DESIGN PRINCIPLES AND FAILURE BOUNDARIES
Design principles and failure boundaries
Principles must explain a concrete choice

A useful modeling principle predicts what to do when a condition changes. “Keep it modular” is too weak unless it identifies ownership, dependencies and failure behavior. This application provides stronger examples: a model factory owns procedural parts; scene integration owns world placement; native controllers own emulator input; clearance stages movement before committing; and publication tools copy an explicit allowlist. These are different boundaries with different reasons to exist (src/lighting.js:9–16, src/scene.js:796–890, scripts/site-files.mjs:4–25).

Do not infer an elaborate design-pattern framework from ordinary functions. The code is direct JavaScript with Three.js objects and explicit state. Its reuse value lies in contracts, not in invented class hierarchies. A correct reconstruction can explain where a dimension is authored, who converts its space and who must invalidate a cached result when it changes.
Figure MD35.1. Reusable responsibility boundaries follow actual space, input and rendering ownership, not a decorative architecture taxonomy.
Preserve invariants rather than apparent screenshots

The tabletop's upper face at world Y zero is an invariant. The lamp's body converts metric-local child lengths exactly once. Active LCD pixels use a basic non-tone-mapped material. Locked console translation preserves its orientation. Each statement is stronger than “the screenshot looks similar,” because it explains what must survive a new camera, device size or light state.

Invariants should also say what is deliberately approximate. The tabletop bounce is a finite authored rectangle, not computed global illumination. Screen spill averages a 24-by-16 image, not per-pixel indirect lighting. DeskMotion is an upright bounded integrator, not a general rigid-body solver. The reflection cube omits both consoles. These limitations are useful design choices when their costs and consequences remain visible (src/lighting.js:103–110, src/lighting.js:126–188, src/pear-motion.js:91–157).

The current official physical-material reference describes capabilities such as clearcoat and transmission. That does not obligate every modeled surface to use every capability. More physically elaborate materials increase cost and demand better illumination data. The correct question is which additional behavior solves a demonstrated problem, not which property makes a material sound advanced.
Make illegal transitions explicit

Clearance is transactional. The scene computes staged positions under fixed priorities, tries the two permitted console orders, and only then commits roots. If no complete layout exists, it reports an error and withholds the next paint rather than knowingly displaying an overlapping repair. This is a failure boundary: an impossible scene is not silently reclassified as acceptable.

Reset is similarly conditional. A companion may have occupied a saved console home, or another object may occupy a companion home. The application refuses that reset with an explicit reason rather than moving the fixed tripod or teleporting an unrelated object (src/scene.js:698–712, src/scene.js:768–794).

An interaction failure should preserve unrelated state. The context-loss message says the game and saves were retained and offers recovery tools. Screen-light sampling failure clears the failed source and quarantines it instead of retrying the same readback every animation callback. Neither strategy declares success; it narrows the failed subsystem while retaining a usable path forward (src/scene.js:383–391, src/scene.js:1343–1364).
Boundaries for identity and assets

Website identity is not interchangeable with hardware decoration. Architecture documentation distinguishes the site chrome, purple GBA identity and DS styling. Replacing every surface with the website logo would flatten those roles and make the modeled objects less legible (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:11–31).

src/brand.js decodes four approved images and exposes cached assets only after successful decoding. Site file mapping explicitly names vendor modules and eligible top-level source/assets files; it is not a recursive copy of the repository. This matters when adding a procedural model with reference material: a private reference directory does not become public merely because the project has an assets directory (src/brand.js:6–15).

The build script clears distribution, copies that mapping, generates the two original demo artifacts and writes the Pages marker. It is a publishing preparation action, not a harmless manuscript validator. This writing task does not run it (scripts/build.mjs:7–16). Keep permission to document separate from permission to build, synchronize, commit or deploy.
Invalidating caches at the owner boundary

A cache is correct only when all changes to its inputs are represented. drawLcdCrt keys by canvas plus dimensions and row count. The scene's clearance signature includes relevant poses, hinge and cartridge state. Reflections have their own dirty flag because direct lighting can paint before environment capture. These caches have different lifetimes and must not be collapsed into one global “needs update” boolean.

When adding an extension, list its inputs beside the cache. A shade radius affects geometry, lamp bounds, possible emitter seams and reflections. A brightness change affects lighting and exposure but not necessarily leg geometry. A texture replacement affects resource disposal as well as appearance. This dependency exercise is more valuable than adding updates everywhere until the visible bug disappears (src/lcd-crt.js:1–27).
Figure MD35.2. Clear dirty state only after the dependent update succeeds; a failed refresh must remain distinguishable from a valid cache.
Prefer narrow adapters over cross-system shortcuts

The scene asks the DS controller to copy screens and project controls through explicit methods. It does not reach into native gameplay and reinterpret emulator state as room lighting state. Likewise, a screen picture becomes illumination through a sampler rather than by changing every shell material to emissive. These narrow adapters allow one subsystem to fail or run at a different cadence without silently redefining another.

The same principle applies to new models. A proposed desk clock might return a root, a display source and an interaction callback. Its scene adapter would own placement, light sampling and invalidation. It should not directly mutate the active console's camera target or private native
session. This is a hypothetical extension example, not an assertion that a clock exists in the current room.

Prefer explicit state transitions to “helpful” global repair. If a lamp switch needs fresh reflections, mark that dependency. Do not rebuild all model factories. If a new movement cannot fit, report it. Do not move the fixed environment. If a display source is invalid, surface that failure and retain unrelated native state. Such narrow responses make causal debugging possible because one user's action has a bounded set of effects.

Finally design rollback at the same abstraction level as the change. A material experiment restores material properties; a staged layout restores staged arrays before trying another order; a capture restores renderer tone mapping and object visibility in finally. Mixing those levels produces partial recovery: for example, restoring only the camera after a failed capture leaves both consoles invisible. The concrete restoration in updateDsReflections is a better teaching model than a generic instruction to “handle errors gracefully.”

Use names as diagnostic interfaces, not as magical selectors for broad behavior. The factory gives legs, shade and emitters useful names, while interaction uses explicit metadata or returned references. An extension should preserve both roles: names make ray-probe failures understandable, and references keep application logic independent of display wording. If a test deliberately depends on a name to establish which shell surface was sampled, a rename changes that evidence contract and deserves a coordinated test update. Do not silently drop the surface check because a friendlier label was introduced. Naming is a lightweight but real part of observability.
MD35-W01 Design a reversible lamp-material experiment

Propose changing shade roughness from .95 to .8. First identify the owner: shade and both rims share the same material. One assignment changes all three. Record the old value, perform the proposed assignment, dirty the scene and reflection cache, and compare the same camera and light state. Do not separately mutate each rim with a cloned material unless a different finish is the explicit goal.

Expected effects are surface-response differences, not new emitted power: retain emissive intensity 60, diffuser intensity 80 and all four light coefficients. If the room becomes broadly brighter, inspect accidental light or exposure changes before attributing the result to roughness.
The following pseudocode is a proposed transaction for an isolated harness, not a new application API. It assumes a lamp factory result and a scene invalidator.

remember shade.material.roughness
try:
  set shared roughness to 0.8
  invalidate main view and reflected environment
  capture matching diagnostic observations
finally:
  restore remembered roughness
  invalidate the same dependents

A reversible harness protects the baseline and makes the changed condition explicit. The comparison still requires human review; no roughness value alone proves that the cloth reads more convincingly.
MD35-R01 Retry when the experiment changes geometry

Now change the shade diameter instead. The previous material-only invalidation list is insufficient. Rebuild the cylinder and rims, dispose replaced owned geometry, recompute lamp bounds and test nearby placement. Inspect the transmitted rectangle's position relative to fabric. Then request reflection refresh.

This retry illustrates why a generic “visual tweak” work item is poorly specified. State precisely which inputs change, which invariants remain fixed and which old tests cease to cover the new domain. Do not weaken the fixed-lamp assertion because a larger lamp makes a layout inconvenient. The test checks a product behavior, not an arbitrary obstacle to editing (tests/browser/desk-clearance.spec.mjs:59–72).
MD35-Q01 Exercise: can automation approve the redesign?

An agent reports valid geometry, no detected overlaps, passing color thresholds and a green deployment. It concludes that the redesigned desk has owner approval. Explain which inference fails and how to word a truthful handoff.
MD35-A01 Explained answer

Each observation covers a separate technical layer. Geometry tests do not establish aesthetic preference; color thresholds cover chosen probes; deployment shows a revision became available. None supplies the owner's visual acceptance. Report exactly those observations and mark aesthetic approval pending.

The verification document makes this distinction explicit and treats previously parked scenarios as coverage debt, not silently passing cases (docs/VERIFICATION.md:1–8). Likewise, the GIF-first root README introduces the project while standalone books carry deep detail; new documentation should extend that navigation instead of replacing the public identity with a wall of engineering receipts (README.md:1–30).

MD36 / VALIDATION AND BOUNDED RECOVERY
Validation and bounded recovery
Evidence is a ladder, not one green checkbox

A procedural model can have valid geometry and still fail when touched, lit, moved or published. Validation should therefore identify the layer being observed. Source inspection establishes construction intent; unit tests establish mathematical contracts; browser tests establish integrated behavior under particular fixtures; screenshots support visual review; deployment records identify a published artifact. Human aesthetic acceptance remains separate. The public verification record explicitly warns against collapsing those layers (docs/VERIFICATION.md:1–8).

This chapter gives reproducible validation instructions, not a claim that tests ran while this handbook was written. The pinned assertions are evidence of what the project checks and where gaps remain. A recipe without an execution receipt is a planned experiment, not a result.
Figure MD36.1. Later evidence adds information rather than replacing earlier contracts; publication still does not imply owner approval.
Validate construction before appearance

Begin with counts, dimensions, transforms and ownership. For the tripod, verify three shared-geometry legs, an open drum, two rims, support cylinder, diffuser and the four actual light objects. Confirm that body scale is 1/.017 and root placement is not scaled twice. Those checks detect a malformed reconstruction before a pleasing light setup can conceal it (src/lighting.js:9–110).

Next validate bounds under the intended orientation. The desk solver's tests cover multi-blocker nearest placement, independent returned vectors, vertical separation, asymmetric extents, numeric gaps and one-ULP boundary stability. They do not prove free rotational collision

behavior (tests/unit/desk-clearance.test.mjs:1–123). For a DS endpoint, use hypothetical geometry bounds; for a proposed full rotation, add explicit swept coverage rather than rebranding endpoint tests.

Motion validation checks trajectories and state transitions separately. The unit test with sparse three-second updates requires falling and rising presentation states to survive until acknowledgment. It also verifies that resetting clears pending presentation and inertia (tests/unit/pear-motion.test.mjs:75–154). A final resting position alone cannot reveal an entire skipped bounce.
Browser fixtures must establish their own conditions

The upright DS lighting fixture is unusually instructive. It uses both desktop and narrow-phone dimensions, turns off Pear and axolotl, establishes a straight root, installs genuine status LCD materials and ray-checks shell probes before sampling pixels. This avoids accidentally measuring a background, reflection or occluding lid instead of paint (tests/browser/ds.spec.mjs:1412–1486).

The fixture's tripod-only blue threshold above 75 and all-off maximum below three express a bounded product expectation. They are not universal color calibration. If another renderer produces different pixels, inspect probe ownership, fixture state, exposure convergence and actual geometry first. Do not lower the threshold until the intended condition disappears.

Room-paint fixtures must honor GPU readiness. installRoomPaintFixture retires the real fence, waits bounded recovery, rejects timestamps before nextPaint and requires renderedLastFrame. It does not equate any callback with a picture (tests/browser/pixel-lab.mjs:8–41). Use it to distinguish state mutation from actual render submission. A later GPU fence gives stronger completion evidence, though not proof of display scanout or human observation.
One bounded repair, then explicit parking

The project has documented repeated headless application failures rather than pretending every scenario is green. Its policy permits one bounded repair, then parks a repeating scenario while retaining its assertions, deadlines and resolution contract. Coverage debt remains linked to an actual issue. Parking is neither a code fix nor permission to call the scenario passed (docs/VERIFICATION.md:93–107).

A bounded repair changes one evidenced cause: for example, disabling both companions when a fixture claims LCD-only lighting, or starting a rest experiment from current performance.now() after real GPU waiting. Removing native framebuffer assertions, reducing density, inventing synthetic future time or extending every deadline is not equivalent. Those actions can change the product contract merely to satisfy the harness.

If failure repeats, preserve its original assertion body, report the exact exclusion and open or update the corresponding issue and Project status through the authorized owner. Do not retry indefinitely until environmental luck produces a receipt. The ledger records this distinction and rejects receipt-only deployment loops (TODO/04_DEVELOPMENT_LEDGER.todo:1–106).
Figure MD36.2. Bounded recovery preserves assertions and records unresolved coverage instead of manufacturing a green result.
The actual workstream record

Numbered TODO workstreams carry eight core fields: Status, Milestone, Dependencies, Purpose, Tasks, Acceptance criteria, Completion evidence and Completion log. TODO/116_DS_UPRIGHT_LIGHTING.todo shows this structure and links actual GitHub issue 115. A workstream number is therefore not an issue-number formula (TODO/116_DS_UPRIGHT_LIGHTING.todo:1–38).

Tracking documentation describes local TODO text as the managed source, preview-first synchronization, refusal to overwrite divergent remote changes, persisted backlinks and final readback of issue body, state, Project membership and status. Index and perpetual ledger are not ordinary numbered workstreams to mirror blindly. This is a real workflow, not authorization for every documentation agent to synchronize or publish (docs/GITHUB-TRACKING.md:1–63).

Write completion evidence in past tense only for actions that actually occurred. Planned checks belong in Tasks or Acceptance criteria. A chapter describing a test cannot reuse a historical success as its own execution receipt.
Keep the experiment's stopping rule explicit

Before a browser run, state the expected terminal outcomes: pass with retained assertions, fail with diagnostic evidence, or explicit exclusion after the bounded repair policy. Also state which exact command, revision and shard inventory will be monitored. Without that stopping rule, an agent can accidentally substitute an endless series of partial runs for one complete verification attempt.

A useful failure packet contains the scenario name, fixture setup, actual assertion text, relevant console or application error, timing/fence state and any captured diagnostic image. It also distinguishes a harness timeout from a product assertion failure. Both matter, but they suggest different next actions. A timeout before startup ownership is established does not prove an LCD shader defect. A native source assertion after valid startup should not be dismissed as cosmetic rendering noise.

Preserve negative controls. The upright-light fixture's all-off state protects against adding global ambient as a shortcut. Its LCD equality protects against rescuing shell brightness by changing picture output. Its ray probes protect against sampling the wrong surface. Removing any one can allow a different wrong implementation to satisfy the remaining checks. This is why a good regression contains several orthogonal observations rather than one elaborate screenshot threshold.

For documentation validation, use a different scope. Check chapter names, required markers, balanced fences, Mermaid parsing, source-path existence, verified line bounds and prose depth. Those checks can establish manuscript integrity without building the application or exercising native gameplay. Report them as documentation checks only. A successful Markdown validator must not be added to the runtime test-pass total, just as a runtime deployment must not be presented as an aesthetic review. This separation keeps future handoffs honest even when several agents produce different evidence at the same time.

Also record what a diagnostic image cannot establish. A still image can show a shell silhouette and local brightness, but not a press/release sequence or a deferred native update. A short animation can show motion, but may omit the exact moment that a held source should cancel. A GPU fence can establish command completion, but not who reviewed the picture. Choose evidence to match each claim and preserve the missing dimensions explicitly. This avoids requesting ever more screenshots for a state-ownership defect that needs event traces, or replacing visual review with a numeric bound that covers only one small region.
MD36-W01 Reconstruct a truthful result summary

The public record identifies historical exact-source run 387537b602f44a5bc85d10ee0196d0ccb099e968. Its declared browser inventory is 119: 98 passed, 21 explicitly skipped, zero failed and zero unrun. The arithmetic 98+21=119 reconciles declared coverage, but “119 passed” would be false. The record
also identifies all nineteen shards and build/deploy evidence. Those receipts belong to that source revision and run (docs/VERIFICATION.md:9–37).
This runnable Node recipe checks only reconciliation. Expected output keeps passed and excluded separate.

The same record says 48 public runtime files matched, while a stricter 49-entry checker still exited one because the Pages marker returned 404. Report both facts. Do not convert an explained checker failure into a forty-ninth successful response, and do not imply this chapter repeated the published-byte checks.
MD36-R01 Retry when the fixture, not the model, is wrong

Suppose the first upright LCD test used powered-off glass and observed changed pixels after switching lights. The changed condition is reflective material, not corrupted active LCD output. The bounded repair is to install status LCDs, verify their basic non-tone-mapped material and retain the original RGB equality requirement.

Rerun the affected desktop and phone scenarios under the exact same geometric and lighting assertions. If application failures repeat, park them explicitly and preserve coverage debt. Do not replace an active-LCD assertion with a weaker “image exists” assertion. The historical lighting TODO records this correction and its limited reason; it does not justify generalized fixture weakening.
MD36-Q01 Exercise: identify the unsupported conclusion
A report says “Pages deployed successfully, so the shader, native input and owner-approved appearance are verified.” Which additional receipts would make each narrower claim defensible?
MD36-A01 Explained answer

Deployment proves availability of a particular artifact only after revision identity is checked. Shader behavior needs material/state observations and appropriate pixel or visual evidence. Native input needs a real transition or native framebuffer response, not merely button animation. Owner approval needs the owner's explicit review.

For each claim, record revision, command or fixture, environment, exact outcome and remaining exclusions. Monitor the exact run to a terminal state and reconcile all shards rather than substituting a later unrelated green run. This separation turns a report into reusable engineering evidence rather than persuasive but untraceable optimism.

MD37 / THE CAUSAL MODELING HISTORY
The causal modeling history
History teaches causality, not just chronology

A useful modeling history explains why the present implementation has its shape. Listing commits is insufficient: each change should connect a symptom, a tested mechanism, a bounded repair and an evidence limit. This chapter distinguishes checked diffs from documented historical observations. It does not recreate private conversation, claim perfect memory or treat an old screenshot as proof that today's source was tested.

The current manuscript's baseline is 1e4ef518d6943ab1af39cef3b4d558f209a17891. When an earlier diff has a different constant, teach the earlier value only as history. The current runtime's exposure, GPU thresholds and placements come from the pinned source, not a commit message (src/scene.js:14–25, src/scene.js:1182–1236).
Figure MD37.1. Causal history preserves rejected explanations and evidence limits instead of converting every commit into an unqualified success story.
The upright DS: a spatial repair, not brighter paint

Commit 9be851e96098e0dfd4beedffd911185cf33a11a6 changes the DS play position from (5,5.1,8) to (-2,5.1,-8). The checked application diff does not alter shell materials, light intensities or exposure. That is the causal point: a straight camera-facing shell had been behind the wrong side of the existing lamp, so the repair moved the shell into the authored illumination.

The workstream records old blue-channel values around nine or ten, and final documented shell blue ranges 108–113 on the lid and 117–157 on the deck. These are historical observations reported in the TODO, not values newly measured for this handbook. It also records an

intermediate candidate (-2,5.1,-2) that improved lighting but had a rotation-clearance gap of -1.047. Brightness alone therefore could not select the final placement (TODO/116_DS_UPRIGHT_LIGHTING.todo:1–56).

The final regression is geometrically specific: eight probe rays must hit named deck/lid shell surfaces inside the frame; all lamps off must be nearly black; tripod and room conditions must produce the expected blue shell. Status LCD RGB must not change. Those controls rule out a fake repair that simply increases global ambient or recolors the paint (tests/browser/ds.spec.mjs:1412–1486).
GPU fences changed the meaning of readiness

Commit 34484498de6be19a48c5191c4d717035bf84a320 introduced real room-paint fences and separated DS LCD copying from room-paint-only controller work. This addressed two coupled problems: JavaScript could outpace graphics completion, and budgeting the room could accidentally freeze native LCD copying.

The earlier diff used a 50-millisecond slow-frame threshold. The pinned implementation uses 100 milliseconds. Do not copy the historical threshold into a current recipe simply because the commit explains the mechanism well. The key lasting design is zero-timeout polling, explicit flush, bounded recovery and independent native picture updates.

Later commit 836fc093bc4e72b06898e983cdf524c8fe772047 retained severe-load recovery while avoiding an added wait for moderate completed frames. Its checked tests distinguish the exact 100-millisecond boundary from 101 milliseconds. This is not a claim that all devices now reach a particular frame rate. It is an algorithmic policy improvement under stated observations.

Another subtle repair concerns the test clock. After a real GPU wait, starting a rest sample from stale lastRender can place synthetic time before actual work creation. The current test resets the baseline and starts at real performance.now() (tests/browser/scene.spec.mjs:338–363). History therefore teaches a testing lesson as well as a renderer lesson: clocks are part of a fixture's causal model.
Why fixed steps needed presentation state

Commit 120d9bd5a3e785d24a9bdc5e96d6e9b332613510 added fall/bounce/rise presentation behavior. Ordinary fixed stepping can compute a correct final rest position after a long gap while never showing the fall. The repair preserves meaningful intermediate poses until the room acknowledges them, while bounding integration to 600 substeps.

This is deliberately not a replacement for accurate rigid-body physics. Motion remains upright, support and side contact are simplified, and queued elapsed time serves the visible interaction. The unit tests prove the intended sparse-update sequence and eventual behavior, not angular momentum or arbitrary contact manifolds (src/pear-motion.js:91–157, tests/unit/pear-motion.test.mjs:75–154).
Tiny numeric errors, large visible layout changes

Commit 6b5d2c552e6b3206bfb3ae36d845896773147a1c adds a magnitude-scaled eight-epsilon tolerance to forbidden-rectangle interior checks. A legal edge can move a few ULPs when world bounds are translated to local bounds and reconstructed. Without tolerance, the candidate can be misclassified as inside and jump to a different side of the desk.

The repair does not replace the .25 physical clearance gap with a broad collision fudge. The separate squared-distance tie tolerance remains, and the tests retain rejection of an actual .01 overlap. Historical context explains why both numerical and product-scale tests are necessary (src/desk-clearance.js:18–31, tests/unit/desk-clearance.test.mjs:90–123).
Built-in CRT became explicit reusable drawing

Commit 06e9c8240b6f3a8c5e2c91a408db0be61ccdfef2 introduced the cached built-in CRT treatment. The present helper caches mask and vignette by canvas dimensions and row count, then restores drawing state. This history supports a bounded claim about generated status images, not a claim that all native CRT presets use this canvas implementation (src/lcd-crt.js:1–39, src/preferences.js:1–13).
Figure MD37.2. A historical mechanism becomes a current teaching claim only after comparison with the pinned implementation and its exclusions.
Read a history entry in both directions

Forward reading asks what changed after a symptom. Backward reading asks which present invariant would break if the change were removed. Removing the ULP tolerance can destabilize a legal edge. Removing presentation acknowledgment can hide a fall under sparse painting. Putting DS copies behind the room gate can stale native pictures. These counterfactuals make the history useful for future regression design.

Counterfactual reasoning is not a new experiment. Unless the removal was actually tested, label it as an explanation derived from source and tests. The distinction is especially important when historical entries include numerical observations: those values depend on their fixture and environment, and cannot be reproduced merely by repeating them in prose.

Look for unchanged files as well as edited ones. The upright repair's lack of material or light edits rules out several claimed mechanisms. Conversely, a commit that touches renderer, tests and verification prose does not automatically prove all three are correct. Read its actual changes and compare to the final baseline, where later edits may alter thresholds, exclusions or fixture preparation.

The development ledger is a causal index, not the complete evidence itself. Its newest entries distinguish exact-source deployment, book artifacts outside the runtime allowlist and preservation of nine unrelated dirty historical images (TODO/04_DEVELOPMENT_LEDGER.todo:1–36). Those distinctions explain why documentation work must not casually rebuild or commit the whole worktree. A model change, a book change and a published runtime receipt can coexist while having different owners. Record which one a history claim concerns, and avoid promoting a navigation or receipt update into an application-behavior change.

For each historical measurement, preserve its subject as carefully as its number. The lighting TODO's final ranges refer to lid and deck samples, not two universal device classes. Its rendered desktop inspection is explicitly not owner approval. Its focused browser run is not an all-suite result. These qualifiers may look small beside the headline repair, but losing them changes the claim. A causal history should make later engineering decisions safer, not accumulate impressive numbers stripped of their conditions. When a receipt lacks a needed condition, mark the gap rather than manufacturing a more convenient interpretation.
MD37-W01 Build a causal receipt for the DS repair

Write four rows: symptom, changed source, controlled variables and evidence limit. Symptom is an upright blue shell reading too dark under the tripod. Changed source is the play-position constant. Controlled variables include material, light intensity, exposure, straight root and both disabled companions. Evidence includes eight verified shell rays and separate LCD invariance; the limit is that documented historical samples are not a new execution.

Then compute the displacement: new minus old is (-7,0,-16), whose horizontal length is sqrt(49+256), about 17.464 world units. That large relocation explains why framing and rotational clearance also needed attention. It does not explain brightness by distance alone: surface orientation relative to the lamp and cone also matters.
This runnable Node recipe checks displacement only. Expected output is the stated vector and length, not a predicted pixel value.
MD37-R01 Retry when a historical test becomes unreliable

Change the condition from a successful local fixture to repeated headless application failure. Commit 19f499643c9d02a0be219713ae0059d9fd531309 records loader-aware restoration and explicit parking. The public account retains the failed broad SwiftShader attempt—52 passed, 55 failed, two unrun—and says that broad change was reverted. It does not prove SwiftShader was the sole cause (docs/VERIFICATION.md:79–107).

Apply one bounded evidenced repair, then park repeating scenarios with assertions intact and coverage debt visible. History is most useful when it preserves this uncomfortable outcome rather than smoothing it into “CI fixed.”
MD37-Q01 Exercise: which constant should a reconstruction use?

An agent reads the fence-introduction commit, copies its 50-millisecond threshold and claims it reproduced the pinned application exactly. What should its correction include beyond changing one number?
MD37-A01 Explained answer

Use the pinned 100-millisecond threshold and its strict boundary, recovery caps and lighting exception. Explain that 50 belongs to an earlier iteration. Reconcile tests at exactly 100 and 101, inspect the real-time fixture baseline, and report whether the retained browser scenario is excluded in CI. Correcting a constant alone does not establish the whole scheduling contract.

Keep the ledger's causal account and exact-source receipts separate from this documentation's validation. Old successful runs remain valuable history, but they cannot be silently promoted into tests of newly written chapters or a future implementation.
