MD09 / PROCEDURAL TEXTURES AND ASSET BOUNDARIES
Procedural textures and asset boundaries
Procedural does not mean asset-free

The project creates many textures at runtime, but their inputs differ. Wood grain is generated from seeded arithmetic. Cartridge text is rasterized by the browser. The bezel wordmark is derived from supplied artwork. Rear engraving turns supplied alpha into geometry while retaining image color on the cavity floor. Calling all of these “generated textures” hides important reproducibility and provenance boundaries.

The shared canvasTexture(width,height,paint) helper creates a canvas, obtains a 2D context, invokes a painter, and wraps the result in THREE.CanvasTexture. It throws an explicit error if drawing is unavailable. The texture is marked sRGB and assigned anisotropy 4. These are actual implementation settings; they do not prove every consuming material or renderer uses the same sampling behavior. Texture helper (src/handheld.js:68).

The current CanvasTexture documentation, consulted 2026-11-07, describes canvas-backed texture construction and inherited sampling defaults. Use it as explanatory guidance, not a version-pinned historical receipt. This project explicitly overrides color space and anisotropy, so copying generic defaults into a parameter table would be wrong.
Color data and coverage data have different jobs

sRGB marks how encoded color should be interpreted. Alpha describes coverage, not brightness. The bezel derivative uses source RGB to decide which pixels belong to neutral lettering, but ultimately preserves a reconstructed alpha silhouette and fills that silhouette with stylized color. The rear engraving uses alpha to create contours, while its floor samples the color image. A bright RGB pixel with zero alpha contributes no visible mark; a dim but opaque pixel may still be important to geometry.

This distinction explains why debugging should inspect channels separately. If a logo is missing, first determine whether the color is dark, alpha was removed, UVs point elsewhere, or another surface occludes it. Increasing light only addresses one of those possibilities. Disabling depth writing on a transparent label addresses a different problem again: whether the plane's rectangle prevents later geometry from drawing.

Text labels use a canvas height of 128 and width ceil(128*aspect), centered text alignment, middle baseline, and a maximum drawing width eighteen pixels smaller than the canvas. The world plane's width-to-height ratio supplies the aspect. Thus text size, canvas resolution, and world footprint are related but not identical. A font size in canvas pixels is not a world-space letter height. Text and label helpers (src/handheld.js:81).
Figure MD09.1. The same RGBA input can supply visible color or geometric coverage, but those outputs have different contracts.
The bezel wordmark is a derived asset

loadBrand() decodes logo.png, star.png, orbit.png, and glow.png. The handheld module imports brandImage; it does not use all four images directly. The full wordmark texture is drawn at 1024×342 for rear artwork. A separate bezel canvas is 1536×174, cropped from the supplied image and placed into a centered region occupying sixty percent of each canvas dimension. Preserve that distinction: the rear uses full artwork, while the front derives letter-only branding. Input loader (src/brand.js:1); initial derivative (src/handheld.js:475).

The derivative first computes the minimum RGB channel and uses it to attenuate alpha, rejecting saturated orbital accents while retaining neutral lettering and highlights. It then finds solid alpha cores using a seven-by-seven neighborhood. Those seeds flood into connected nonzero-alpha pixels. The seed test selects components; the flood reconstructs their original edge pixels rather than simply eroding the whole mark.

This algorithm has a concrete failure boundary: if no solid cores remain, it throws. A replacement artwork with thin lettering may therefore be unsupported even when it looks valid as a PNG. Broadening the threshold is not automatically safe because detached exterior contours may return. Inspect the retained components before changing the test. Core selection and flood (src/handheld.js:487).

Finally the canvas applies vertical chrome color bands with source-in, adds a horizontal iridescent tint with source-atop, and restores source-over. The resulting material uses roughness .4 and metalness .1. The colored bands are baked stylization, not physically traced reflections or a thin-film simulation. Their appearance can coexist with room lighting, but the gradient itself does not respond to camera movement. Compositing and material (src/handheld.js:529).
MD09-W01 Reproduce the wood generator's controlled variation

createWood() paints a 1024×1024 canvas. It starts from seed 41 and advances a 32-bit linear congruential generator using multiplier 1664525 and increment 1013904223. Eight bands of 128 pixels establish planks. Each receives low-alpha tonal variation, then 110 grain strokes whose paths combine sampled Y positions with sine displacement. Thin dark and light seams separate planks. The texture repeats twice along both axes. Complete wood painter (src/handheld.js:657).

The seed makes the arithmetic sequence repeatable. It does not promise identical raster pixels across every browser implementation, GPU, and operating system. Canvas line rasterization and color handling can differ. The useful invariant is stronger within one environment: two calls follow the same painter and seeded sequence, so their pixel results should agree there.

The following original browser-console recipe assumes the project's import map and a usable 2D canvas. It hashes canvas pixels, not GPU readback, and creates no scene. Expected results are equal hashes in the same execution environment and repeat values [2,2]. It is a diagnostic proposal, not a historical test.

Derive what changing seed versus repeat means. A seed change alters the generated grain arrangement while preserving canvas size and the eight-band structure. A repeat change alters how often the same image tiles over the receiving geometry; it does not repaint new planks. If a desk looks too repetitive, changing only seed cannot remove the fact that the same tile repeats twice. If grain appears stretched, inspect mesh UVs and aspect before repainting.

The function returns a texture, not a desk mesh or material. Its placement and physical scale belong to the consumer outside this part's scope. Recording that boundary prevents “wood model” from becoming an unsupported claim about desk dimensions or UV orientation.
MD09-R01 Retry when a replacement wordmark fails

Suppose a new licensed wordmark decodes correctly but the factory throws that it has no solid lettering. Begin with the derivative canvas, not the mesh. The crop constants refer to the current source artwork layout. A differently arranged image may place its letters outside that crop or make them too thin after resampling. Successful decode proves only that the image loaded.

Retry by inspecting crop coverage, alpha thresholds, and seed neighborhoods separately. First verify that the crop contains intended letters. Then inspect neutral-channel selection. Finally inspect whether any seven-by-seven solid regions survive. Changing all three at once can produce a plausible output while leaving the cause unknown. A replacement should carry its own explicit derivation parameters rather than silently inheriting assumptions about the old image.

The earlier geometry chapter records why threshold-only filtering damaged lettering and why component reconstruction was introduced. That historical explanation supports retaining component identity, but the exact current loop remains authoritative. It also distinguishes the later colored finish from earlier neutral ink; do not describe both as simultaneous source behavior. Recorded derivative evolution (docs/book/chapters/04-handheld-geometry/README.md:95).
Figure MD09.2. Wordmark diagnosis follows each image-processing boundary instead of treating every missing pixel as an asset-loading error.
Asset delivery and legal provenance remain separate

The static allowlist copies top-level JS, SVG, and PNG files from src and assets, maps the inspection logo separately, and vendors selected Three files and license. A runtime-generated texture need not exist as an exported PNG to be reproducible. Conversely, a local asset outside the allowlist is not automatically available at the same browser URL. Public delivery rules (scripts/site-files.mjs:4).

The root manifest's Three dependency establishes the geometry library; it does not establish rights to every supplied image or system font. The historical reference workstream explicitly avoids extracting unavailable model assets. Preserve that discipline when adding references: use authorized inputs, document derivation, and do not infer permission from technical accessibility. This chapter does not perform a new rights audit. Library declaration (package.json:7); historical provenance limit (TODO/07_REFERENCE_SHAPE.todo:19).
Own the lifetime of generated resources

Each helper call creates a new canvas and texture. The text contour routine disposes its temporary texture after reading pixels, and the rear-mask routine similarly disposes the mask. Those calls release texture resources; they do not imply that every scene object is automatically cleaned up when removed from a group. Temporary glyph resource (src/handheld.js:232); temporary rear mask (src/handheld.js:255).

An agent writing a repeated diagnostic should therefore distinguish temporary extraction inputs from textures retained by materials. Disposing a shared retained texture while another material still uses it can invalidate the display. Failing to release unique diagnostic resources can accumulate allocations across many specimens. Track ownership explicitly instead of assuming traversal and removal constitute disposal.

The same principle applies to caches. The brand loader returns early only when all four image exports are present; that is an input cache, not a cache of generated handheld geometries or wordmark textures. Calling the factory twice still constructs two model trees and derived canvases. A proposed factory cache would need rules for material mutation, texture reuse, and disposal, especially because cloned finishes and mutable control state belong to individual instances. Resource reuse is an extension design, not something established by the current loader's early return.
MD09-Q01 Make the book fully reproducible across fonts

An agent wants every A/B contour and cartridge title to match across machines. Is a fixed random seed enough? Propose a bounded extension and explain what existing behavior it would change. Include why matching the bezel bitmap would not solve the action glyph problem.
MD09-A01 Control the actual source of variability

A seed controls wood's arithmetic choices, not browser font rasterization. Action glyph geometry begins with Arial text rendered to a canvas, and cartridge labels use browser text as well. If the selected font differs, contours and line breaks can differ even with identical Three versions. The bezel is derived from a supplied image, so matching its bitmap does not determine the separately rendered A/B letters.

A deterministic extension could supply appropriately licensed font data and await its loading before rasterization, or provide authorized fixed vector contours for the required glyphs. Each changes the input contract and should be labeled as a new design. The first retains rasterization dependence but controls font selection; the second removes raster contour recovery for those glyphs but introduces vector-asset maintenance and provenance responsibilities.

Verification should compare contour topology, footprint, counter preservation, and actual rendered readability, not only a file hash. Keep the existing baseline available so the extension is not misrepresented as recovered historical tooling. The player test's direct-video assertion further reminds us that decorative texture reproducibility must not replace the live framebuffer with a baked image. The model's labels, brand derivations, and game display are three different asset boundaries. Live-video boundary (tests/browser/player.spec.mjs:265).

MD10 / DS ASSEMBLY AND THE PARAMETER MAP
DS assembly and the parameter map
Read the assembly as a set of contracts

The DS is not one sculpted object. It is an assembly whose convincing appearance depends on separate transform spaces, layered solids, readable controls and a stable pixel surface. The reconstruction problem is therefore not “make a blue rectangle.” It is to preserve relationships while parts move: the upper display follows the lid, the lower display stays with the base, and the stylus remains available without stretching the camera envelope toward the pointer.

Implemented evidence. createDsHandheld() imports Three.js and three helpers from handheld.js; it constructs groups, extrusions, cylinders, lathed caps, planes and canvas textures. There is no model-file loader in this factory. The repository and installed package both identify Three.js 0.186.1. This chapter describes JavaScript procedural authoring, not a Blender, CAD or imported-mesh workflow. Read the factory entry and materials (src/ds-handheld.js:1) and dependency declaration (package.json:7).

Numbers below are model-space units, not measured millimetres. A screen width of 4.5 establishes a useful internal scale, but it does not establish a manufactured part's dimensions. Surface names are authoring labels, not a promise of mechanical equivalence to every Nintendo DS revision. Begin a reconstruction by recording those limits; otherwise seemingly precise arithmetic becomes misleading hardware documentation.
Figure MD10.1. Reconstruct in dependency order: silhouette and ownership precede decorative details and interactive targets.
Build a parameter ledger before changing geometry

The lower assembly contains a parting line, rear shell and control deck centered at local Y −2.43. Their common nominal width is 8.5 and height 4.75. The lid's nominal footprint is 8.5 by 4.65, centered at its own Y 2.43. The opposing signs place the joint near the root origin instead of at either shell's center. This origin choice makes articulation simpler: the lid rotates around its parent origin while its geometry is offset away from that origin.

These are nominal constructor inputs, not final beveled bounds. The DS wrapper supplies bevel min(.02, depth/3, radius/3) to the shared rounded-box helper. Extrusion bevels extend the outline and thickness; an 8.5-wide shape can therefore occupy more than 8.5 in its generated bounding box. The shell construction (src/ds-handheld.js:68) must be read with the centered extrusion helper (src/handheld.js:19). That combination explains why center-to-center spacing is insufficient for clearance work.

The lower rear shell uses depth .19 at Z −.135; the control deck uses depth .22 at Z .105. The parting line is much thinner, .025 at Z −.025. These layers establish visible seams without requiring a single watertight enclosure. Do not silently reinterpret them as a production injection-molding cross-section: intersecting layered meshes are acceptable here, but manufacturing wall thickness and internal fasteners are not being solved.
Assign transform ownership before assembly

The root owns the base, lower LCD, controls, card and stylus. The lid owns its shell layers, upper LCD, speaker details, bumpers and hinge leaves. The separate hinge group is root-owned; its barrel does not rotate merely because the lid rotates. This distinction prevents double articulation. Attaching the hinge under the lid and then rotating both would create a plausible-looking but structurally wrong joint.

The return object is the public assembly interface: root, lid, hinge, screens, screen, controls, led, power, cartridge, stylus references, branding and accent materials. screen aliases the second entry of screens, so downstream lower-touch logic can address the intended surface directly. The returned interface (src/ds-handheld.js:273) is more reliable than guessing targets from traversal order.

Research guidance, not pinned implementation evidence. Current Three.js Object3D documentation, consulted 2026-11-07, distinguishes local transforms, world matrices and radian rotations. Use that model to reason about parent-child composition. Do not adopt a newer documented property merely because it appears on the current page; this implementation uses group origins and offsets, not a newly introduced pivot API.

Figure MD10.2. Parent-supplied neutral-studio constructor diagnostic, intended for silhouette and layering inspection; it is not native gameplay, historical development evidence or a claim that every control is unobstructed in every pose.
Separate visual construction from application completion

A factory instance is not the finished application state. Its branding plane starts invisible and without the supplied logo map. DsController.initialize() loads the image, assigns an sRGB texture and reveals the plane. Its screens initially use unlit materials, but the controller constructor subsequently selects reflective powered-off glass. A bare-constructor diagnostic must therefore identify which initialization stages it includes.

The controller initialization (src/ds-controller.js:186) establishes this asset boundary. It is a supplied artwork texture on procedural geometry, not evidence that the whole console was imported. Likewise the scene puts the root into a desk or focused-play transform; a local positive Y coordinate is not automatically “up” in the room.

The scene pose constants (src/scene.js:18) use a rotated table quaternion and an identity default play quaternion. Keeping that distinction in the ledger prevents mistaken descriptions of the card's travel or the lower expansion slot. The modeled front/bottom expansion opening is separate from the rear DS game-card slot near the hinge; the factory names and places both.
MD10-W01 Audit a face-button clearance numerically

Consider the leftmost face button, Y, at X 2.75 with cap radius .195. Its recessed socket has radius .195 + .025 = .220, so the socket's leftmost nominal X is 2.75 − .220 = 2.530. The outer touchscreen bezel starts with width 4.88, giving half-width 2.440, but its .035 depth limits the DS wrapper bevel to .035/3 ≈ .011667. The outer bound is therefore approximately 2.451667. The nominal horizontal gap is about .078333.

That result explains two decisions. First, the socket, not just the smaller cap, is the limiting feature. Second, ignoring the bezel's extrusion bevel would overstate the available gap. The browser test requires greater than .05 between every cap/socket bound and the actual bezel, and greater than .1 toward the deck edge. Read the bound-based assertions (tests/browser/ds.spec.mjs:1309).

Original diagnostic pseudocode follows. Assumptions: a browser has constructed the model, matrices are current, and boundsInBase() transforms all eight geometry-box corners into root space. The expected result is positive margins, not an assertion that this recipe was executed here.

bezel = boundsInBase("Touch fine cyan bezel edge")
deck = boundsInBase("Metallic blue control deck")
for label in X, A, B, Y:
  for part in button, recessed_socket:
    box = boundsInBase(label, part)
    require box.minX - bezel.maxX > .05
    require deck.maxX - box.maxX > .10

For a beveled corner, an axis-aligned box is conservative: it can reject space that is geometrically empty near the rounded edge. That is useful for a readable diagram and predictable safety margin, but it is not exact mesh-to-mesh distance. Record which measurement you use rather than switching between them when a test fails.
MD10-R01 Retry after widening the screen surround

Suppose a proposed surround change increases its width by .12 without changing controls. Its right edge advances .06. The previously calculated .078333 gap becomes about .018333 and violates the .05 criterion. Moving only the Y legend does nothing; moving only its cap leaves the socket overlapping. Shrinking the LCD would change a separate display contract.

The corrected proposal must move the entire diamond or redesign the surround, then recalculate both inner and outer margins. Moving all four controls outward by .04 might recover the inner threshold but consumes .04 of the A button's deck-edge margin. Inspect both limits before choosing a value. Historical commit 89d905f moved the complete cluster outward by .2; that recorded correction supports the method, not permission to move it indefinitely.
Figure MD10.3. A parameter change is accepted only after checking both adjacent constraints; passing one side does not preserve the assembly.
Make parameter changes transactional

Proposed reconstruction practice. Keep a small change ledger with four columns: parameter, dependent geometry, dependent behavior and evidence to regenerate. For example, changing LCD width affects the plane, all three surround layers, illumination viewport metadata, control clearance and camera bounds. Changing only shell roughness affects appearance but should not change those dimensions. This classification keeps an agent from treating every visual complaint as a material problem.

Work from a reversible baseline. Change one relationship, rebuild the affected geometry and capture numerical bounds before interpreting a new image. A plane becoming wider without a matching viewport metadata change is an internal inconsistency even if the image still looks acceptable. A moved cap with an unmoved shell label may be visually inconsistent even though its input anchor follows correctly.

Resource lifetime is another dependency. The existing controller disposes replaced display materials and maps; proposed geometry replacement should similarly account for the old geometry rather than retaining every revision indefinitely. Do not copy that disposal strategy blindly onto shared objects: first determine whether another mesh still references the resource. The factory intentionally shares several materials, including the shell/rim relationship, so mutation has a wider scope than one named mesh.

Finally, save both the intended effect and the invariant that must remain unchanged. “Move the diamond outward while keeping screen size” is testable; “improve the controls” is not. This makes later debugging a comparison of contracts rather than a reconstruction of undocumented taste.
MD10-Q01 Exercise: choose the correct editable object

A diagnostic operator wants the top display to fold while the lower touchscreen, battery cover and branding remain fixed. They propose rotating root, then counter-rotating every lower component. Explain the ownership error, choose the minimal correct transform, and identify one downstream calculation that must be refreshed.
MD10-A01 Explained answer

Rotate lid.rotation.x, not the root. Counter-rotation replaces a clear hierarchy contract with many compensating transforms; every later base detail becomes another opportunity for a missed correction. The upper LCD already belongs to the lid and therefore follows automatically. The battery cover and underside branding remain root-owned. The hinge barrel also remains root-owned while the lid-owned leaves move with the shell.

Refresh articulated bounds and view matrices before trusting projected input. dsPoseBounds() evaluates separate root and lid transforms; a single cached flat rectangle cannot describe both poses. This is a geometric correctness requirement, not merely a camera convenience. The pose/bounds implementation (src/scene.js:502) supplies the actual application mechanism. This chapter read source and assertions; it did not rerun browser tests, render production images or establish owner approval.

MD11 / HINGES, LIDS AND ARTICULATION
Hinges, lids and articulation
A hinge is first a coordinate-system decision

An articulated object fails when its pivot is chosen after its geometry. A lid centered on its own origin spins like a signboard; it does not fold around its lower edge. This factory instead places the lid group's origin at the joint and offsets its visible shell to local Y 2.43. The group receives an initial X rotation of 70 degrees and a Z offset of .07. The upper screen and surrounding details are children, so one transform carries the complete upper assembly.

Implemented evidence. The lid creation (src/ds-handheld.js:71) precedes the separately created barrel group. That ordering makes the visual joint independent of the mathematical articulation. No torque, detent spring, hinge friction or collision-constrained rigid-body joint is implemented by these groups. The physical mechanism is approximated through recognizable geometry and bounded pose editing.
Figure MD11.1. Offset geometry creates the lever arm; rotation belongs to the joint frame rather than the shell center.
Construct the barrel without confusing its axis

Three.js cylinders are initially aligned along their local Y axis. The central barrel uses radius .255, width 6.90 and 48 radial segments, then rotates around Z by π/2 so its length lies along the hinge's X axis. A right lime cap at X 3.80 uses width .72. The left end is assembled from two half-cylinder sections at X −3.80 with angular starts −π/2 and π/2. Their names distinguish front and rear sections, but both use the same lime material at this cutoff.

Two collars sit at X ±3.43 with radius .258 and width .035. The slight radial increase creates a legible seam without making the joint look like disconnected cylinders. Lid-owned leaves at those X positions bridge the upper shell toward the barrel. The microphone, MIC legend and indicator recesses belong to the barrel frame, so they do not unexpectedly orbit the upper LCD. Inspect the complete joint details (src/ds-handheld.js:111).

The barrel is a visual approximation rather than a mechanically interlocking mesh. A continuous cylinder and narrow collars are inexpensive and readable at desk scale; modeling internal axles would add surfaces that the current interaction does not expose. If an extension requires an exploded mechanism, add that as a new documented model contract rather than claiming the existing continuous barrel already contains one.
Opening degrees and stored rotation are different quantities

The scene's getter reports 180 − radToDeg(lid.rotation.x). Its setter clamps an opening angle to 30–180 degrees and stores the complement in radians. Thus an opening of 180 corresponds to zero stored rotation, 145 corresponds to 35 degrees, and the factory's 70-degree rotation corresponds to a 110-degree opening. These conversions are not interchangeable descriptions of one raw number.

Research guidance. Current Object3D documentation, consulted 2026-11-07, describes rotations in radians and local positions relative to parents. MD11-W01 Calculate a useful diagnostic pose

Use the lid center point (0, 2.43, 0) in the lid's local coordinates, ignoring shell thickness for this calculation. After an X rotation θ, the root-space point becomes approximately (0, 2.43 cos θ, .07 + 2.43 sin θ). At a 145-degree opening, θ is 35 degrees, giving Y about 1.9905 and Z about 1.4638. The center rises away from the lower assembly in root space while retaining the joint origin.

This is not yet a room-space prediction. If the root has the tabletop quaternion, multiply the result by that root transform before calling a direction world-up or world-forward. The useful diagnostic outcome is relative: the upper screen changes orientation and the lower screen's local transform does not. A root rotation would move both, exposing a hierarchy error immediately.

The following original browser-module recipe assumes a constructor-capable DOM and imported Three.js. It creates a new diagnostic instance, not a live application mutation. Expected result: a 145-degree opening under the scene convention, with updated world matrices. No production render is requested.

There is no hinge setter returned by the factory. The returned lid is the exact factory API for this operation. In the application, use view.setDsHinge(145) only after entering unlocked DS Inspect and waiting for the transition to finish; that method accepts opening degrees and also reframes the camera. Do not call setDsHinge(35) expecting a 35-degree stored rotation.
Preserve three pose purposes

Desk pose, Inspect pose and optional gameplay lock serve different jobs. The desk has a remembered placement and resting hinge. Inspect allows independent root rotation and hinge edits. Locking records a clone of the root quaternion plus the current lid rotation; it does not rewrite the saved desk arrangement. Unlocked gameplay defaults to the flat, front-facing configuration.

Historical commit e885636 introduced independent hinge controls and locked gameplay poses. The associated construction task (TODO/87_DS_HINGE_GAMEPLAY_POSE.todo:1) explicitly separates the desk's 110-degree resting opening from gameplay. Those records ground the feature's purpose; they are not a fresh execution or a substitute for reading the current setter.

The pose lock is session state, not permanent storage. Cloning the quaternion matters because keeping a mutable reference would allow later root edits to mutate the supposed saved pose. Clearing drag and pinch state at the lock boundary similarly prevents an earlier gesture from continuing through a new ownership rule.
Figure MD11.2. A gameplay lock captures a chosen pose without converting that pose into the console's remembered desk placement.
MD11-R01 Retry with a nearly folded lid

Change the opening from 145 to 30 degrees. The stored rotation becomes 150 degrees, placing much of the upper assembly over the lower half. A previously visible control may now be covered even if the whole console remains inside the camera frustum. The correct retry does not increase exposure, disable depth testing or keep invisible controls clickable.

Recompute articulated bounds and update matrices, then let occlusion decide availability. projectControls() checks facing, clip-space limits and lid intersections before exposing projected HTML buttons. Its projection path (src/ds-controller.js:684) explains why a folded control can disappear correctly. For touch, the first relevant root intersection must be the lower LCD, not simply any intersection farther down the ray.

Also recheck materials at an oblique angle. Shared rounded solids obtain their bevels through ExtrudeGeometry construction (src/handheld.js:19). A highlight vanishing on a grazing face is not automatically a missing normal; first determine whether the face points away from the lamp or is physically hidden.
Precision checks for a convincing joint

Recommended diagnostic procedure. Inspect the joint from front, rear and a grazing side direction while holding the root transform fixed. A front view checks continuity across barrel sections; a rear view checks whether the leaves remain attached to the shell; the side view reveals an offset pivot that a frontal image can conceal. These are complementary questions rather than three decorative views of the same proof.

Measure in the joint's local frame before measuring in world space. A collar radius .258 versus barrel radius .255 creates a radial difference of .003. That is a deliberate small geometric distinction in the source, not a reason to round every number to two decimals. A rounded diagnostic export could erase the distinction even though the original geometry retains it. Conversely, do not report the .003 as a manufacturing clearance: both are visual surfaces and are not an axle-and-bearing tolerance pair.

If a collar appears detached, inspect its width and axial position independently of radius. A larger radius repairs a radial silhouette gap but cannot repair an axial separation. If a leaf penetrates the barrel, first decide whether the overlap is intentional cover geometry or a visible discontinuity. A mechanical mesh requires different checks from an economical visual joint, and the current source promises the latter.

For a proposed alternate shell size, preserve the pivot origin and change the child offset deliberately. Moving the lid center without revisiting its nearest edge can create an exposed gap at the joint. Calculate the edge position from half-height, center offset and bevel extension, then inspect the resulting seam through the allowed opening range. Checking only the 145-degree diagnostic pose can miss a collision or gap near 30 degrees.

Finally distinguish geometry precision from input precision. A correctly rotating lid can still leave stale hit targets if the scene matrix refresh is omitted. Record the opening angle, stored radians, root quaternion and matrix-update stage together. That record turns an intermittent “hinge bug” into a reproducible question about either geometry, state guards or projection.
MD11-Q01 Exercise: diagnose a lid that translates while folding

A reconstruction rotates a shell mesh about its own center and then updates the lid group's position on each frame to make the lower edge “approximately stay put.” The barrel is also parented under that group. Why is the result fragile, and what should a replacement validation measure?
MD11-A01 Explained answer

The implementation has replaced one stable joint frame with two coupled approximations: rotation plus corrective translation. Small changes to shell dimensions invalidate the correction, and the barrel moves with the lid even though it should identify the fixed joint axis. Put the lid origin at the joint, offset shell geometry in the child frame, and keep the barrel root-owned. The replacement needs only one articulation transform.

Measure a joint-adjacent reference point over several openings and confirm it follows the intended hinge neighborhood rather than circling the shell center. Check that the lower LCD, battery cover and branding retain their root-local transforms. Then validate occlusion and actual input in the articulated pose. The browser's independent-hinge scenario (tests/browser/ds.spec.mjs:927) is read evidence for those application expectations, not a test rerun in this authoring task. A stationary hinge point alone cannot prove usable screens or correct projected input.

MD12 / DS SHELLS, RECESSES AND HARDWARE
DS shells, recesses and hardware
Use depth where depth is part of the evidence

Small hardware details communicate how an object is assembled. A seam says two shells meet; a screw recess suggests fastening; an inset floor says a depression has depth. These meanings are not interchangeable. Painting a dark square can suggest a recess from one camera, but it does not create an aperture that a ray can pass through before hitting a lower surface.

Implemented evidence. The DS outer lid actually contains holes in its Shape. Two rounded-square paths are added before extrusion, while separate blue floors sit behind them. By contrast, the speaker openings are small dark cylinder meshes and the rear card slot is a dark rounded box. The construction deliberately mixes true outline topology with economical surface approximations. The lid aperture construction (src/ds-handheld.js:77) is the authority for which technique applies.
Figure MD12.1. A genuine modeled recess needs an open outline and a separately positioned floor, not merely a darker top-facing patch.
Reconstruct the outer lid cross-section

Start with a centered rounded outline 8.5 by 4.65 and corner radius .14. Generate each hole from a .54-by-.54 rounded shape with radius .055, sample its points and shift them by local Y ±.38. The hole X offset is zero. When the complete lid mesh is placed at Y 2.43, the hole centers become Y 2.05 and 2.81 in the lid group.

The outer geometry extrudes .12 with bevel size and thickness .02, three bevel segments and eighteen curve segments, then translates Z by −.06. Its mesh position adds another −.10. Ignoring curvature at the bevel, the main extrusion therefore spans approximately Z −.16 to −.04 before the bevel thickness expands that range to about −.18 through −.02. The inset-floor centers are at Z −.14, with .008 nominal thickness and the DS helper's small depth-limited bevel.

This arrangement is most usefully understood from the rear, looking along positive local Z. A ray through intact outer shell first encounters the rear skin around −.18. At a hole center that skin is absent, allowing the ray to continue to the floor around −.147. The floor is deeper into the lid from that rear viewpoint. Saying “behind” without specifying the viewing side can reverse the explanation.

The shared solid helper (src/handheld.js:19) explains centered extrusion and bevel expansion. Research guidance: the current ExtrudeGeometry documentation, consulted 2026-11-07, distinguishes depth, bevel size, bevel thickness and segment counts. It also notes that modifying the recorded constructor parameters does not rebuild geometry. Treat that documentation as current guidance; the pinned factory's actual values and geometry creation remain the implementation evidence.
MD12-W01 Verify two recesses and the land between them

The diagnostic needs three rear rays, not a screenshot of two dark squares. Cast along positive local Z through (0, 2.05), (0, 2.81) and (0, 2.43). The first two should hit the named inset-floor meshes; the midpoint should hit the metallic outer lid. Transform both origins and directions through the lid's current world matrix so the same test works after articulation.
Original pseudocode, assuming a constructed instance and current matrices:

for y in 2.05, 2.81, 2.43:
  origin = lid.localToWorld(0, y, -1)
  direction = transformDirection(lid.matrixWorld, 0, 0, 1)
  first = raycast(lid, origin, direction)
  record y, first.object.name
expect floor, floor, outer_lid

The expected names correspond to the actual browser surface test (tests/browser/ds.spec.mjs:1324). This chapter read that assertion; it did not execute it. If all three rays hit the outer lid, the hole paths are not cutting the intended outline. If the first two miss everything, inspect floor placement and face orientation before changing ray distances.

A rear-side ray is important because planes and mesh triangles have oriented faces. Blindly making every material double-sided can hide a reversed-normal defect. Diagnose winding, geometry transforms and viewing side first. Double-sided shading is a deliberate rendering choice, not a general repair for uncertain construction.
Lower-shell hardware is its own subsystem

The battery cover is root-owned on the underside: a 2.81-by-3.51 seam at X 2.35, Y −2.43, Z −.27, then a slightly smaller cover at Z −.278. Five screw recesses include one associated with that cover; their head slots sit farther toward negative Z. Four pale-green square pads occupy X ±3.65 and Y −.70/−4.30 at Z −.30.

The underside hardware construction (src/ds-handheld.js:227) uses overlapping shallow solids, not boolean cavities cut into every base layer. Screw slots are boxes, not full threaded fasteners. The pads clone button plastic and raise roughness to .9, separating a matte support surface from the metallic hinge trim. These approximations are appropriate to the existing desk model but should be disclosed in a reusable reconstruction manual.

Figure MD12.2. Parent-supplied neutral-studio underside diagnostic for shell layers, battery-area layout and rear detail placement; constructor-only branding may remain hidden until its supplied texture is initialized.

The lower-base branding plane is centered at X −1.65, Y −2.43, Z −.265, faces outward after a Y rotation of π, and preserves a 2149:732 artwork aspect. It belongs to the lower root, clear of the right-side battery cover, not to the swinging lid. initialize() supplies its image later. See branding geometry (src/ds-handheld.js:138) and texture initialization (src/ds-controller.js:196).
Distinguish the two slots explicitly

The front navy expansion opening is placed at local Y −4.842 and rotated around X by π/2. It represents the lower/front expansion-slot feature, not the original hardware's rear DS-card slot. The separately named rear DS game-card slot is a 1.68-by-.18-by-.24 dark rounded box at X 1.4, Y .1, Z −.02. The insertable DS card is aligned to that rear-side region.

Do not infer insertion direction from the word “bottom” in a caption. Local Y becomes a different room direction after the root's table rotation. Nor should a dark slot-shaped box be described as a fully hollow connector with modeled contacts: the source supplies a visual opening approximation. The scene's root placement constants (src/scene.js:18) establish the transform boundary that makes direction language conditional.
Historical correction: topology and parenting changed together

Commit 6f5083a changed the hole-point offsets and inset-floor X positions from −2.8 to zero. The same diff moved the emblem from the lid to the base underside. This is stronger evidence than a generic statement that the rear “looked better”: both the topology and the floor placements were corrected, while branding changed ownership.

The rear-markings task (TODO/95_DS_REAR_MARKINGS.todo:5) records the requested centerline and battery-clearance requirements. Its historical verification is not a new verification of this manuscript. Preserve that distinction when turning a development ledger into teaching material.
MD12-R01 Retry after increasing the floor thickness

Suppose a proposed floor depth changes from .008 to .08 while its center stays at −.14. Its rear face moves much farther toward the outer skin and may become flush with or protrude beyond the aperture entrance once bevel thickness is included. The source name “inset floor” would no longer guarantee an inset appearance.

Compute the floor's actual geometry bounds after rebuilding, compare the rear-most floor Z against the aperture entrance, and repeat the three rays. If the goal is a deeper recess, moving the floor farther positive Z from the rear viewpoint may be appropriate, but check the inner shell and display layers too. Making a floor thinner or darker cannot compensate for incorrect world-space occlusion.
Figure MD12.3. A depth edit changes both exterior evidence and interior clearance; rebuilding and remeasuring are separate from changing a parameter label.
Debug topology without hiding it under materials

Recommended diagnostic procedure. Temporarily reason about the aperture with a single neutral material and explicit ray origins before comparing metallic highlights. This is a proposed inspection technique, not a change made to the shipped model. A blue floor can visually merge with a blue shell under diffuse illumination even when the recess topology is correct; a sharp reflection can make a shallow overlap look deeper than it is.

The floor is slightly wider than the nominal hole: .56 versus .54. That gives a nominal .01 overlap on each side before bevel details. The overlap helps avoid an uncovered edge when looking obliquely, but its sufficiency should be judged from generated geometry and the intended viewing range. It is not a universal anti-crack constant. If the hole radius or floor corner radius changes independently, the edge relationship changes even when both widths stay the same.

Inspect boundary continuity separately from shading continuity. A hole can exist while its side-wall normals produce an unexpected highlight, and a smoothly shaded decal can look recessed without any hole. The rear rays establish surface ordering; a side view establishes wall visibility; a normal-oriented lighting pass can help isolate shading. No single one of those observations replaces the others.

Also account for layered shell intersections. The rear skin, inset floors, perimeter lip and inner lid are separate meshes. A proposed deeper aperture might expose an unrelated layer rather than create empty interior space. Trace a ray through the entire lid hierarchy and record all relevant hit distances when diagnosing that condition, instead of stopping at a conveniently named first hit.

These practices preserve the distinction between an aesthetic recess and a physically bored opening. The existing paired recesses intentionally terminate at floors. Calling them through-holes into an empty enclosure would be as inaccurate as calling them flat dark decals.
MD12-Q01 Exercise: can a logo be moved onto the battery cover?

A proposed wider emblem still fits inside the total lower-shell rectangle but overlaps the battery-cover region. Its author argues that transparent pixels make the overlap harmless. Identify the missing geometric constraint and the ownership rule that must remain unchanged.
MD12-A01 Explained answer

The constraint is not only the shell boundary. The emblem must remain in the clear area beside the battery cover, with positive measured separation from that cover. Transparent pixels do not change the plane's layout contract or preserve a readable service-panel boundary. Measure the actual plane bounds, not only its opaque artwork, and compare them with the battery cover in the same root space.

Keep the emblem root-owned and outward-facing. Moving it onto the lid to find more area would violate the documented lower-base placement even if the image became easier to see. The regression requires battery gap greater than .25 and meaningful shell margins; these are explicit model checks, not inferred hardware tolerances. The same discipline applies throughout this chapter: preserve named relationships, then improve appearance within them.

MD13 / DS CONTROLS AND READABLE MARKINGS
DS controls and readable markings
A control has more than a visible cap

For this model a control combines geometry, a rest transform, an input identifier and a projection anchor. Those components solve different problems. A cap communicates touchability; its socket communicates mounting; its anchor places an HTML input target; its identifier routes native button state. Editing only one can make a screenshot look corrected while the actual control still overlaps a bezel or receives input in the wrong place.

Implemented evidence. The factory stores controls in a Map. Face buttons use their mesh as anchor, while the D-pad uses four separate child anchors on one shared cross. The cap builder and face layout (src/ds-handheld.js:145) establish that construction. Socket radius is cap radius plus .025; clearing only cap centers cannot prove the whole assembly fits.
Figure MD13.1. Geometry and interaction meet at the anchor: a pressed visual should not leave its input target behind.
Lathe the caps rather than stacking flat discs

The cap profile starts on the axis, moves outward across the underside, climbs a rounded side and returns toward the axis over the top. For radius r, the radial samples include r − .018, r, r − .015 and .65r; axial samples range from −.0425 to .047. LatheGeometry revolves this profile with 32 segments, then the geometry rotates around X by π/2 before placement at Z .29.

That rotation has a useful consequence: the lathe's original axial coordinate becomes local Z. The subsequent press animation can move mesh.position.z inward without changing the cap's orientation. The visible legend is a child plane at Z .052, so it follows the cap instead of floating above the deck. This is a geometric reason to attach a marking to its moving owner, not simply a convenient grouping habit.

The four .195-radius caps form a diamond at X/Y (3.3, −1.32), (3.84, −1.87), (3.3, −2.41) and (2.75, −1.87). START and SELECT use smaller .095-radius blank caps with separate light labels on the shell. Power uses radius .20 plus actual torus-and-stem icon geometry. These differences prevent a one-size-fits-all label helper from dictating the hardware layout.

The text helper paints bold Arial into a canvas, then uses a transparent MeshBasicMaterial with depth writing disabled and tone mapping disabled. It chooses 96 pixels for a single character and 512 for longer labels. See the text and circle helpers (src/ds-handheld.js:54) and the shared texture helper (src/handheld.js:68). These are procedural raster markings on modeled parts, not engraved font outlines.
Build one molded D-pad with four semantic directions

The cross is a twelve-corner Shape, extruded .085 with .018 bevel size and thickness. It is placed in a group at (−3.17, −1.83, .285). Four small rectangular direction marks occupy its arms, and four child anchors sit near the arm tips. All direction entries refer to the same mesh group; they differ in anchor and indicator.

The cross and anchors (src/ds-handheld.js:165) explain why the controller must compute one composite pose. Rotating the cross once per input entry would apply competing updates to one object. Instead, held inputs become a signed two-axis vector, normalized so a diagonal does not exceed the intended .16-radian combined tilt.

The response uses elapsed-time damping, with stronger release response than press response. A .012 compression accompanies any directional hold. Opposing directions cancel the corresponding rotational axis but still count as held and still highlight their individual marks. That combination distinguishes physical pose from semantic input state: zero tilt does not necessarily mean no buttons are held.
MD13-W01 Derive the Up-plus-Right pose

For Up and Right held, the controller computes x = down − up = −1 and y = right − left = 1. Magnitude is √2, so target pitch is approximately −.113137 radians and target yaw approximately .113137 radians. Their Euclidean magnitude is .16, matching the cardinal target rather than exceeding it by √2.

Rest Z .285 becomes .273. For an approximate arm-surface point at local Y .5 and local Z .068, negative pitch lowers the upper arm in root-local Z. A small-angle estimate gives a top-versus-bottom edge difference around sin(−.113137) ≈ −.1129 across unit separation, while the simultaneous yaw tilts the horizontal axis. Exact transformed heights should be measured with the mesh matrix, not inferred from Euler signs alone.
Original runnable arithmetic recipe, requiring only JavaScript:

The expected output has negative pitch and positive yaw. It calculates targets, not damped intermediate frames. The actual feedback implementation (src/ds-controller.js:634) applies damping and exact near-target snapping. The unit assertions (tests/unit/ds-controls.test.mjs:29) check signed edge heights, diagonal bounds, neutral return and a surface remaining above .235.
Shoulder orientation turns local travel into edge travel

L/R housings sit at X ±3.4, Y .08, Z −.255 and rotate around X by −π/2. Their sockets and caps are children of those rotated housings. The existing generic depression moves cap local Z by −.065; under the housing rotation that becomes motion into the top-edge mounting direction rather than through the underside.

The shoulder construction (src/ds-handheld.js:192) is a reusable recipe: orient the control frame once, then retain a consistent local press axis. Do not scatter world-axis exceptions throughout the animator. However, the controller's projected facing normal is derived from the root, so do not claim every shoulder target is a full perspective-correct projection of its rotated cap surface.
Contrast is deliberately split between surfaces

The pale accent is #C5F2B1. Button lettering and the power symbol are dark navy; shell-mounted START, SELECT and POWER labels remain light. Metallic lime hinge trim uses physical paint, while matte pads use rough plastic. Read the material setup (src/ds-handheld.js:35). A single universal text color would lose contrast on either the pale caps or the darker shell.

Documented history. Commit c59de69 replaced repeated flat depression with bounded rocking and held-direction material changes. The D-pad task history (TODO/97_DS_DIRECTIONAL_DPAD.todo:5) records readability as the purpose. It does not justify adding extra lights or changing native input timing merely to improve a screenshot.
MD13-R01 Retry with Up and Down held together

Change the example to Up plus Down. Both signed axes become zero, but held remains true. The correct result is neutral rotation with .012 compression and both direction marks highlighted. An implementation that uses only vector magnitude to decide whether anything is pressed would incorrectly lift the cross and clear the cues.

Now add Right. The vertical axis still cancels; yaw reaches the cardinal .16 target. Release only Up and verify Down continues to contribute. Native state ownership matters here: the controller receives authoritative bba:control messages and uses them for visual feedback, rather than assuming a local keydown is the only source.

Projected controls also need current matrices and occlusion checks. The scene's immediate update path (src/scene.js:494) avoids waiting for another eligible GPU paint before refreshing target alignment. This is essential when the pose changes under sparse rendering.
Figure MD13.2. Opposite directions cancel rotation, not their individual held state or the cross's shared compression.
Diagnose legends, normals and travel independently

Recommended reconstruction practice. Begin a marking check in the unpressed state, with a known camera and deterministic lighting. Confirm that the label is on the intended parent and lies in front of the visible cap surface. Then press the control and compare the relative transform. If the label remains at the old world height, its ownership is wrong; changing font size will not repair that defect.

The cap's lathed profile includes both a side wall and a gently raised top. Its appearance depends on the generated surface normals as well as color. A bright ring at the shoulder of the profile can be a legitimate specular highlight, while a discontinuity repeated at every segment can indicate insufficient tessellation or a shading issue. The current 32-segment lathe is a concrete implementation choice, not proof that more segments always improve the result. Evaluate projected size before increasing geometry.

Travel must be checked in the correct local frame. Face caps start at Z .29 and depress by .065, leaving their group origins at .225. That origin can lie below the deck's front region while the cap's raised surface remains visible. Testing the origin alone would produce a false penetration diagnosis. The D-pad unit test correctly samples a surface point, not just the group center.

Contrast diagnosis likewise needs the right surface. Dark navy text on a pale cap and light text on a blue shell solve different contrast problems. A blanket rule such as “all legends should be white” discards the material context. If a label becomes unreadable only under one light, first separate a low-contrast legend from an overexposed cap, and compare the same geometry point across conditions.

For a proposed alternate theme, keep identifiers, anchor sizes and native mappings unchanged while evaluating new colors. That isolates visual design from behavior. Only after the theme passes geometry and contrast checks should a separate interaction change be considered. A reusable agent manual should make these change boundaries explicit so a typography edit cannot accidentally become an input remap.
MD13-Q01 Exercise: separate a geometry bug from a key-map bug

The Y cap is visually clear of the screen, but pressing A on the keyboard activates a shoulder when the emulator frame has focus. Should the modeler move the Y cap, enlarge its hit target or change the runtime mapping? Explain the evidence needed before editing.
MD13-A01 Explained answer

This symptom depends on keyboard focus, not geometry. Inspect fixed DS mappings and the runtime owner before moving any mesh. DS_CONTROLS assigns KeyA to Y and KeyS to X, while shoulders use Q/W. The mapping declaration (src/ds-cartridge.js:7) establishes the intended routing, and the browser native-key scenario (tests/browser/ds.spec.mjs:271) checks scene and runtime focus separately.

A geometry repair cannot prevent an inherited keyboard preference from shadowing a DS binding. Conversely, correct native button IDs do not prove sockets clear the beveled screen. Keep both classes of evidence, name the failed boundary, and avoid using one successful test as a substitute for the other. The cited tests were read, not rerun here.

MD14 / DUAL LCDS AND CURVED GLASS
Dual LCDs and curved glass
Correct the premise before modeling the glass

The chapter title names a useful topic boundary, not a claim that the DS constructor contains curved display glass. At this cutoff both DS active surfaces are planar PlaneGeometry(4.5, 3.375) meshes. The repository has a separate curved-outline LCD helper, but the scene's curve setter applies it to the GBA this.model, not to this.ds. Applying that helper to the DS by association would invent an authoring step and risk breaking lower-screen UV input.

The DS display loop (src/ds-handheld.js:98) is decisive. Read it alongside the shared curved-outline helper (src/handheld.js:49) and GBA curve setter (src/scene.js:1122). “Curved” there describes a shaped outline with explicitly remapped UVs, not evidence of a bulging DS surface.
Figure MD14.1. The DS display illusion comes from geometry layers and state-specific materials, not an undocumented curved overlay.
Construct a display cross-section from outside inward

Each screen assembly starts with a fine cyan bezel edge, nominally 4.88 by 3.77 and .035 deep. A 4.80-by-3.69 metallic surround follows at Z offset .018, then a 4.60-by-3.475 black recess at offset .048. The active 4.5-by-3.375 plane sits at offset .085. The upper assembly's base Z is .18; the lower assembly's base Z is .265.

Thus the active upper plane is at lid-local Z .265 and the active lower plane at root-local Z .350. Each is forward of its recess. These offsets separate visible layers and reduce coplanar competition. They do not form a physically simulated stack of polarizers, liquid crystal, cover glass and air gaps. Using that manufacturing vocabulary without qualification would overstate what the meshes contain.

The common aspect is 4.5 / 3.375 = 4/3, matching 256 / 192. Both geometry objects expose userData.viewport width and height for illumination. The lower surface also carries a touchscreen flag. The upper parent is lid; the lower parent is root. Parenting is part of the display definition because the upper emission and picking surfaces must fold with their shell.

Short, nonzero layer offsets should be evaluated relative to the camera's depth precision. If flicker appears only at certain distances, first inspect nearly coplanar triangles and material depth settings. Do not solve every flicker by increasing all offsets: that can make the screen look detached from the bezel and alter occlusion near the controls.
Powered-off glass and active LCDs obey different invariants

The bare factory creates dark unlit screen materials. The controller subsequently uses showPowerOff() to replace them with MeshPhysicalMaterial: dark green-black color, roughness .24, clearcoat 1 and clearcoat roughness .22. This is reflective powered-off glass. It is expected to respond to lighting and view angle.

Status and active native screens instead use MeshBasicMaterial with toneMapped: false. Status screens use procedural 512-by-384 canvases; native outputs use 256-by-192 canvases with nearest filtering and mipmaps disabled. The controller disposes replaced materials and maps before assigning new ones. See the power-off and status states (src/ds-controller.js:266) and native material handoff (src/ds-controller.js:426).

The active invariant is narrow and important: scene-light changes should not relight or tone-map the active pixel surface. It does not say powered-off glass must remain unchanged, or that screen pixels are unaffected by texture sampling, browser color management or the selected framebuffer content. The upright-lighting regression (tests/browser/ds.spec.mjs:1425) deliberately selects static status LCDs before comparing pixels across lighting states.
Split the combined framebuffer without resampling twice

dsScreenRegions(width, height) accepts a top/bottom image whose width is an integer multiple of 256 up to 2048 and whose height is 1.5 times its width. It returns equal upper and lower halves. For native width 256 and height 384, the regions are (0,0,256,192) and (0,192,256,192).

The region validator (src/ds-cartridge.js:48) rejects side-by-side layouts and gaps rather than trying to guess. paintScreens() copies each region into its own output canvas with smoothing disabled. The copy path (src/ds-controller.js:665) then marks the textures for update.

This separation matters for debugging: a wrong half-image can be a region-layout failure even when geometry, materials and UVs are correct. Conversely, correct output canvases can still appear wrong if the upper and lower texture references are swapped. Inspect the intermediate canvas before touching the model.
MD14-W01 Calculate pixel scale and a touch location

One horizontal pixel corresponds to 4.5/256 = .017578125 model units. One vertical pixel corresponds to 3.375/192, exactly the same value. This equality is a useful construction check: the planar display has square source pixels in its own coordinate system, independent of perspective foreshortening.

At UV (0.25, 0.75), the touch converter yields X floor(.25 × 256) = 64 and Y floor((1 − .75) × 192) = 48. The vertical reversal maps the plane's upward-increasing UV coordinate to the native screen's downward-increasing row index. At UV 1, clamping prevents the inclusive edge from producing an out-of-range pixel.
Original arithmetic recipe, suitable for Node or a browser:

Assumptions are an accepted lower-LCD ray hit and UVs inside zero through one. This recipe does not perform the raycast or permit clicks through the lid. Preserving those preconditions is as important as preserving the arithmetic.
Emission is modeled separately from displayed color

Two ScreenIllumination instances attach area lights to their respective screens. Each uses the viewport metadata, a small sampled canvas, linear-channel averaging and damped light color. The additional control-spill emitter is explicitly labeled experimental in source; it approximates first-bounce visibility for nearby controls rather than solving global illumination.

The illumination implementation (src/lighting.js:126) samples live sources at intervals of 125 ms and derives intensity from the peak averaged channel. The scene update (src/scene.js:1353) clears and hides DS illumination when no powered source exists. This keeps lighting separate from the active LCD material.

Research guidance. Current Object3D documentation, consulted 2026-11-07, supports the explanation that child emitters inherit their screen transform. That current reference is not a claim that every newer rendering feature is used by Three.js 0.186.1 here. Inspect actual light classes and renderer paths before proposing a different illumination system.
Figure MD14.2. Pixel presentation and illumination share a source image but use different materials and update responsibilities.
MD14-R01 Retry with a proposed curved DS surface

Change the assumption: an extension now requests an actually bulging DS cover. That is a proposal, not the existing workflow. A geometric bulge changes normals, silhouette and ray intersections; an outline-only shape changes the boundary but remains planar. Decide which effect is needed before choosing an algorithm.

For a true bulge, define a height function, preserve a well-understood UV map, recompute appropriate normals and test lower-screen ray-to-pixel correspondence over the full surface. Keep active pixel material behavior separate from any reflective overlay. A transparent overlay can become the first ray hit and block input unless picking ownership explicitly accounts for it. Never add it and then globally ignore every non-LCD hit; that would also allow touches through the folded lid.
A failure tree for apparently damaged pixels

Recommended diagnostic procedure. Start at the output canvas rather than the final camera image. If the canvas already contains the wrong half-frame, investigate layout validation and region copying. If it contains correct pixels but the model shows the other display, investigate screen-array ownership and map assignment. If both are correct but diagonal edges look soft, investigate filtering and projected scale before changing geometry.

Nearest filtering preserves discrete source samples; it cannot guarantee every source pixel occupies an integer number of final screen pixels under perspective. A tilted plane naturally foreshortens, and minification can produce uneven apparent cell widths. The honest invariant is that the application avoids an additional smoothing copy and uses nearest texture sampling for native outputs. “Perfect integer pixels at every angle” would be an unsupported stronger claim.

The status-texture path and native-output path also have different source resolutions. Status is drawn at 512 by 384, while native output canvases are 256 by 192. Both share the same physical viewport aspect, but a text edge in one is not an appropriate one-pixel reference for the other. Choose a deterministic fixture that matches the property being measured.

For a proposed reflective active overlay, write the visibility and input consequences before implementing it. A clearcoat-like sheen on the same material is not equivalent to a separate transparent mesh. A separate mesh can introduce additional depth ordering, reflections and first-hit ownership. If the overlay should not receive native input, that exception must remain narrow enough that shell and lid occlusion still work.

Finally inspect normals and front/back visibility in an oblique pose. The planar LCD has a defined front side; rotating the entire console behind the camera-facing direction does not make the display physically visible through its back. Making the material double-sided may be appropriate for a diagnostic, but it changes the presentation contract and must not silently become the production repair.

These recommendations extend the source-grounded workflow without claiming an unimplemented glass stack. They give a later modeler an ordered experiment: source image, texture, geometry, material, projection and occlusion. Changing all six at once prevents a useful causal diagnosis and makes any apparent improvement difficult to preserve.
MD14-Q01 Exercise: why did the lighting test fail with power off?

A test expects identical LCD RGB values with the lamp on and off, but it never powers the DS or installs status textures. It observes different pixels and proposes making all screens unlit permanently. Identify the mistaken fixture and the functionality that proposal would remove.
MD14-A01 Explained answer

The fixture selected reflective powered-off glass, not an active LCD. Its lighting response is intentional. Install a deterministic active status texture before testing the unlit, non-tone-mapped invariant; qualify reflective glass separately with view-dependent expectations. Making every state permanently unlit would remove the powered-off material distinction rather than repair the test.

The historical upright-lighting task (TODO/116_DS_UPRIGHT_LIGHTING.todo:40) records exactly this fixture correction. Its reported outcomes are historical evidence, not tests rerun for this chapter. The lesson is to state the material state before stating the invariant.

MD15 / STYLUS CONSTRUCTION AND TOUCH GEOMETRY
Stylus construction and touch geometry
Separate the prop, the pointer and the contact

A stylus appears simple until it must work over an articulated screen. Three distinct systems are involved: the docked pen is part of the console silhouette; the held pen is a camera-oriented visual; the native touch contact is a pixel coordinate plus a pressed state. Making the held mesh itself the input sensor couples decoration to gameplay and can cause the pen to intercept its own ray.

Implemented evidence. The constructor creates a docked group at (4.39, −2.43, −.025), while the controller clones that group into a separate scene object, scales it to .8 and disables raycasting on every clone descendant. The original remains in the DS hierarchy and is hidden while held. See the docked construction (src/ds-handheld.js:248) and held-clone setup (src/ds-controller.js:25).
Figure MD15.1. The held mesh illustrates the contact; it does not replace the lower LCD's ray-to-pixel input contract.
Assemble the pen around a known contact point

The shaft is a 3.64-long cylinder with radii .073 and .065, positioned slightly off the group center. A flat pull tab, short retention hook and release groove establish the docking end. The other end uses a .20-long tapered cylinder, followed by a sphere of radius .032 scaled by (1, 1.8, 1) to make a short rounded nib.

The exact contact anchor lies at Y −2.07 − .032 × 1.8 = −2.1276, not at the sphere center. That distinction matters when solving a held pose. Aligning the group origin or nib center to the pointer would leave the visible tip systematically displaced. A named Object3D anchor records the intended extreme without requiring the controller to rediscover mesh topology.

The shaft's cylinder orientation already follows the pen's local Y direction, unlike the button cylinders rotated to face local Z. Keeping those conventions explicit avoids an incorrect held quaternion. The controller aligns local positive Y toward the camera-side “back” direction; the nib lies toward negative Y.

The docking channel is a separate dark rounded box at X 4.27; two shell-owned clips remain on the base. The hover halo is a back-sided transparent cylinder with depth writing disabled, hidden by default. Stylus plastic is cloned from button material so hover emissive changes do not recolor every console cap. These are small ownership choices with large debugging value.
Solve the held pose from the tip backward

paintStylus() converts the pointer into normalized device coordinates and casts through the camera. It takes the first non-stylus intersection with the DS root, falling back to a camera-facing plane through the lower display's world position. That fallback keeps the visual moving outside the screen; it does not create valid native touches outside the LCD.

The target tip is lifted along the pointer ray, by −.06 while hovering or −.008 during contact. A shift along a perspective ray changes depth without moving the projected point. A shift along the LCD normal generally changes screen position in an oblique pose. This is the geometrical reason for the implementation's direction choice.

The controller chooses a camera-relative back vector with X/Y signs adjusted near the top and right edges, rotates local positive Y to it with setFromUnitVectors, then computes the transformed tip offset. The group position becomes targetTip − rotatedScaledLocalTip. The complete placement algorithm (src/ds-controller.js:611) is a tip-constraint solver, not a cursor sprite approximation.
MD15-W01 Calculate the root-to-tip offset

With uniform scale .8, the local tip's Y magnitude becomes 2.1276 × .8 = 1.70208. If a diagnostic orientation maps local positive Y to world positive Z, the nib offset is (0,0,−1.70208). To put the nib at target (1,2,3), place the group root at (1,2,4.70208). The back extends toward the camera while the tip remains at the requested contact.
Original pseudocode, assuming a unit quaternion q, scale s and an already chosen world target:

localTip = (0, -2.1276, 0)
offset = rotate(q, componentMultiply(localTip, s))
rootPosition = targetTip - offset
reconstructedTip = rootPosition + offset
require distance(reconstructedTip, targetTip) < tolerance

The expected reconstruction error is numerical roundoff. This recipe isolates attachment math from raycasting, so it can diagnose a wrong anchor or scale without needing native gameplay. For nonuniform scale, component multiplication must happen before quaternion rotation, matching the source's operation order.

Research guidance. Current Three.js Raycaster documentation, consulted 2026-11-07, describes NDC input, distance-sorted intersections and hit UVs. Its face-orientation warning is relevant when a rotated display unexpectedly stops receiving hits. The recommendation is to inspect facing and ownership first, not to assume the current documentation proves every behavior of the pinned 0.186.1 application.
Native touch belongs to the lower display only

touchAt() casts through the entire model, ignores stylus-tagged hits only while the pen is held, and accepts a contact only if the first remaining object is screens[1]. It does not search arbitrarily deeper for any LCD hit. A folded lid or shell in front of the screen therefore blocks input.

The touch hit gate (src/ds-controller.js:490) feeds UV conversion (src/ds-cartridge.js:55). Finite UVs within zero through one map to X 0–255 and Y 0–191, with vertical inversion. Input capture preserves a single active pointer, while cancellation and lost capture release the native contact.

Direct mouse or touch drawing remains valid without holding the modeled pen. This is important for accessibility and testing: the decorative pickup workflow should not become an unexplained prerequisite for the actual touchscreen. Conversely, moving the held visual off the LCD must not produce out-of-bounds contact coordinates.
Contact edges must survive asynchronous delivery

DsTouchQueue stores down, move and up samples. Consecutive move samples can replace one another, but contact edges remain separate. After each dispatched sample, the queue waits for nextFrame, preserving observable transitions across native polls. A generation counter invalidates stale work after cancellation; cancellation also releases a previously dispatched down contact immediately.

The queue implementation (src/ds-touch.js:11) and unit cases (tests/unit/ds-touch.test.mjs:16) distinguish edge preservation from throughput. Coalescing an entire quick tap into a final unpressed sample would be efficient but wrong: the native game might never observe contact.
Figure MD15.2. Move compression is safe only when the beginning and end of contact remain independently observable.
MD15-R01 Retry under an oblique locked pose

Change the assumption from a flat front-facing display to a rotated body with a partially folded lid. A constant screen-space offset may appear correct at the center yet drift at the corners. The corrected approach keeps using a camera ray, obtains the actual hit point and solves the tip offset in world space. Do not repair drift with a hand-tuned X/Y cursor correction.

Refresh camera and root matrices immediately after pose or viewport changes. The scene update boundary (src/scene.js:495) explicitly avoids waiting for another GPU paint before projection and touch rays become current. When debugging, separate stale matrices from a wrong UV map: the first shifts intersections; the second shifts pixels after a correct intersection.

The browser orientation scenarios (tests/browser/ds.spec.mjs:413) cover locked orientations, zoom and high-DPI touch. They were read, not rerun here. Historical commit 0fdd81b introduced the pickable pen; that history supports feature provenance, not a universal accuracy guarantee.
Debug the pen with three separate errors

Recommended diagnostic procedure. Record visual-tip error, hit-point error and native-pixel error independently. Visual-tip error is the distance between the projected nib anchor and pointer. Hit-point error asks whether the ray reached the intended visible surface. Native-pixel error compares the accepted UV conversion with the game-space location. A correct-looking pen can still draw at the wrong pixel, and correct drawing can coexist with a visibly misplaced pen.

To isolate the first error, hold a deterministic quaternion and scale and test the tip reconstruction formula without a raycaster. To isolate the second, remove only the held clone from consideration and record the first real DS hit. To isolate the third, log accepted UVs and converted coordinates without introducing a hand-tuned cursor offset. These are proposed diagnostic steps, not operations performed during this authoring task.

The pen's cloned material references also deserve care. The model separately clones stylus plastic from the button material, which isolates hover treatment from console buttons. Cloning the object hierarchy does not imply a fresh independent material for every descendant. A later extension that recolors only the held pen should inspect material sharing first rather than assuming scene ownership guarantees material ownership.

At pointer exit, the held visual may disappear while its held state remains available for return. That is distinct from a native pressed contact, which must be released when the input path no longer has a valid lower-LCD hit. Treat visibility, pickup state and contact state as separate booleans in a debugging log. Otherwise an invisible cursor can be misdiagnosed as a stuck native press.

For touch cancellation, verify the release edge as well as the final queue contents. Emptying pending samples alone does not release a contact already dispatched to the runtime. The generation mechanism and immediate release in cancel() address that distinction. This is a reusable principle for any modeled tool whose visual movement is more frequent than the native consumer's polling: preserve semantic edges even when intermediate motion is compressed.
MD15-Q01 Exercise: why keep an invisible docked pen?

A proposed optimization removes the docked pen from the DS hierarchy while held and reparents it to the scene. The camera then changes framing as the pointer moves. Explain the coupling and choose a safer visual strategy.
MD15-A01 Explained answer

The pose-bounds calculation traverses geometry in the DS hierarchy, including geometry whose visibility may be false. The original implementation deliberately retains the docked geometry as a stable part of that envelope and moves only a scene-owned clone. Reparenting changes the envelope; moving a still-parented held pen can make the envelope chase the pointer. Neither effect is desirable for stable gameplay framing.

Keep the original docked transform, hide its visual during pickup and move the non-pickable clone. Return paths should restore visibility, release contact and reset cursor state. This is not a general claim that invisible meshes never matter: here they remain relevant to the specific bounds traversal. Read ownership and consumers together before deleting apparently redundant geometry.
