MD16 / CARTRIDGE INSERTION AND LOADING CHOREOGRAPHY
Cartridge insertion and loading choreography
There are three different loading stories

Selecting a file begins application work, not merely a mesh animation. The console must become visible while identification is pending; a loading LCD must communicate progress or waiting; a card prop may move toward its seated position. Native startup is a fourth boundary whose completion is not determined by the prop's position.

Implemented evidence. load() closes DS tools, selects the DS and enters play before awaiting ROM identification. It calls loadingStatus('READING LOCAL ROM') before the expensive asynchronous work. Only after identification and retained-state lookup does it clear the old session, retain the new file and configure card insertion. The load ordering (src/ds-controller.js:345) is the authoritative workflow, not a generic “load then show console” sequence.
Figure MD16.1. Presentation begins before slow file work, while native readiness remains a separate success condition.
Model the card and identify the correct opening

The root-owned card group starts at (1.4, .44, −.02) and is hidden until needed. Its dark shell is 1.46 by 1.56 by .13, with a smaller raised label and two procedural text lines. It is not a detailed scan of a commercial cartridge. The card geometry (src/ds-handheld.js:239) uses the same rounded-box and text vocabulary as the console.

The nearby rear DS game-card slot sits at X 1.4, Y .1, Z −.02. The front navy expansion opening sits near Y −4.842 and has a different orientation. The modeled bottom/front expansion slot is not the actual original hardware's rear DS-card slot. Describing the animated DS card as entering the bottom opening would conflate two separately authored features.

The card translates along root-local Y, from 3.1 toward .44. Depending on the root quaternion, that is not necessarily world-down, room-back or screen-down. The scene pose constants (src/scene.js:18) show why a direction must name its coordinate space. A camera-facing image can be useful evidence of presentation, but not proof of a mechanically exact connector path.

The slot is a dark rounded box, not a fully modeled socket with contacts, retention spring and collision-tested internal cavity. The card visibly approaches a representative slot region. If an extension requires physical insertion tolerances, it needs new cavity topology and clearance tests rather than stronger adjectives for the existing animation.
DS insertion uses painted updates

When motion is allowed, load() places the card at Y 3.1 and creates {elapsed: 0, lastPaint: null}. Reduced motion seats it directly at .44 and creates no insertion motion. During controller paint(), elapsed time increases by the nonnegative difference from the previous paint; the first call adds zero. Fraction is clamped at elapsed/1800, eased with f²(3−2f) and used to interpolate Y.

The DS animation code (src/ds-controller.js:624) is called after the scene's eligible-paint gate. Read the scene scheduling boundary (src/scene.js:1339). It is inaccurate to call this an unconditional wall-clock timer independent of rendering.

The nuance is equally important: elapsed differences between painted calls can include a long real-time gap. The DS path does not reserve a midpoint boundary inside its 1800 ms slide. A sparse subsequent paint can therefore advance a long way. “Paint-driven” does not guarantee every intermediate pose is shown.
Do not borrow the GBA's timing contract

The shared cartridge-motion.js helper belongs to the scene's other cartridge path. It defines 850 ms framing and 1350 ms sliding, preserves elapsed time when paint is not due, and clamps advancement at a framing boundary before allowing seating. transition-motion.js similarly reserves a painted midpoint for desk transitions.

The cartridge helper (src/cartridge-motion.js:4) and transition helper (src/transition-motion.js:1) explain the repository's broader sparse-paint strategy. They do not make the DS card use those exact durations or boundaries. Reusable-agent documentation must identify which caller owns a helper before transferring its guarantees.
MD16-W01 Calculate the DS halfway position

Assume the first eligible DS paint records time 100 ms and elapsed remains zero. A later paint at 1000 ms adds 900 ms. Fraction is .5, and smoothstep easing is also .5. The card position is 3.1 + (.44−3.1) × .5 = 1.77. Another 900 ms of painted-call interval reaches elapsed 1800, Y .44 and the seated dataset state.
Original arithmetic recipe:

Assumptions are the current DS endpoints and duration, not a physically measured insertion speed. The zero derivative at both ends reduces abrupt starts and stops in the displayed motion. It does not simulate friction, a latch click or card mass. The expected result is a reproducible root-local position at a chosen interpolation fraction.

For comparison, a 450 ms elapsed value gives fraction .25 and ease .15625, producing Y 2.684375. Equal time steps do not produce equal travel distances. This is useful when checking captures: a slowly moving initial card can be correct easing rather than a stalled loader.
The loading LCD is an illustration, not a progress meter

paintLoading() chooses one of twelve frames with floor(time/160) % 12; reduced motion fixes frame zero. It draws an original card and slot illustration, text and three cycling dots onto the lower status texture. Its card Y is 52 + min(frame/8,1) × 148, with clipping around the illustrated slot.

The loading painter (src/ds-controller.js:310) does not measure bytes downloaded or native initialization percentage. Calling its loop “90% complete” would invent information. It communicates that the application is working and names the current phase: reading a local file or starting DeSmuME.

Canvas generation uses the shared texture helper (src/handheld.js:68), while native success replaces status maps with separate 256-by-192 outputs. The visual card loop and 3D card can coexist without being synchronized mechanical representations of the same event.
Figure MD16.2. The loading illustration signals a phase, while real native startup determines when live display textures replace it.
MD16-R01 Retry with a rejected replacement file

Change the assumption: an existing session is running and the replacement file is invalid. loadingStatus() avoids replacing active screen materials when running is true, although it still records loading state. Identification occurs before clear(). A rejection therefore need not destroy the previous source, frame or game identity.

The browser upload scenario (tests/browser/ds.spec.mjs:116) explicitly checks retained session objects and restored native pixels after an invalid replacement. It also checks reduced-motion loading and cancelled startup separately. These assertions were read, not rerun here.

A corrected retry preserves the prior session until a new file passes identification, clears loading state in the finalizer and surfaces the existing error UI. Do not equate a failed file read with successful replacement merely because the 3D prop reached its seat. Conversely, do not erase the old game at the first upload event just to simplify the visual state machine.

Documented history. Commit e1896ce moved visible DS feedback ahead of slow identification. The immediate-loading task (TODO/115_DS_IMMEDIATE_LOADING.todo:5) records the motivating sidebar delay. That history supports the ordering explanation, not a fresh startup-performance measurement.
Validate choreography without private content

Recommended diagnostic procedure. Use the repository's original homebrew integration fixture or synthetic phase control when validating presentation; do not introduce private cartridge images merely to make the loading path look authentic. The browser cases deliberately hold the upload read so the immediate UI transition and changing LCD can be observed before native startup. This isolates an ordering property that a fast local file might conceal.

For a purely geometric check, inspect the card shell and slot bounds in root space at staged fractions. Their construction uses the same centered extrusion helper (src/handheld.js:19), so nominal width and depth are not necessarily final outer bounds. A card fitting within the nominal slot width does not establish a physically valid cavity when the slot itself is represented by a dark solid.

For timing, record the sequence of eligible paint timestamps, not only the upload timestamp and a final screenshot. An 1800 ms nominal interpolation duration describes elapsed differences consumed by DS paint calls. A blocked or skipped interval can change which intermediate positions are actually visible. That observation should be reported as scheduling evidence rather than rounded into a guaranteed smooth frame rate.

The loading illustration's twelve-frame loop has another important limit: its phase can jump when time advances. It is an animation frame selector, not a queue that must display every preceding illustration. Reduced motion selects a static frame by policy. A static image under reduced motion is therefore expected behavior, while a static image under ordinary motion needs investigation of loading state, frame selection and texture upload.

Cancellation deserves its own evidence record. A failed runtime launch should remove the pending frame, clear loading and busy state, and surface a retryable explanation through the established operation path. A rejected replacement while an old session is running has a different preservation requirement. Combining those into a single “error case” hides whether the application retained or discarded the right state.

Keep proposed refinements separate from implemented guarantees. A future DS-specific midpoint reservation could make a sparse paint show a staged insertion pose before seating, but that is not present in the current controller's slide loop. It would require explicit new tests and should not be inferred from the neighboring shared GBA helper.
MD16-Q01 Exercise: can seated mean ready?

A proposed UI hides Cancel as soon as the card reaches Y .44. The native runtime is still fetching and has not sent its started message. Explain why this couples unrelated completion conditions and choose the proper readiness evidence.
MD16-A01 Explained answer

Seating is visual interpolation completion; readiness is a validated native display handoff. The controller checks framebuffer layout and retained drawing-buffer support before installing output canvases and setting running. Cancel belongs to the pending launch callbacks, not to the mesh's Y coordinate. A seated prop can accompany a slow or failed native launch.

Keep the loading state and error recovery until native success or failure resolves the operation. Preserve the 90-second startup timeout and explicit cancellation rather than inventing readiness from animation duration. This separation makes the model choreography useful feedback without allowing it to misrepresent actual application state.

MD17 / INSPECTION, CAMERA AND MANIPULATION
Inspection, camera and manipulation
A good model needs a truthful viewing instrument

A procedural assembly can be correct and still look broken if its camera crops the lid, places the shell outside the lamp's useful region or leaves projected controls aligned to an old pose. Inspection is therefore part of the modeling workflow. It must expose geometry without rewriting the object merely to flatter one view.

Implemented evidence. The DS camera uses articulated geometry bounds, not a hard-coded flat-screen rectangle. Body rotation and hinge edits are separate actions; an optional gameplay lock preserves both. The Inspect controls and pose setters (src/scene.js:460) define those ownership rules. The constructor supplies a root and a lid, so the camera must respect two transform spaces rather than pretending the whole object is rigid.
Figure MD17.1. Pose editing must update geometry envelopes and input matrices, not merely the rendered root rotation.
Evaluate a candidate pose without flattening its hierarchy

dsPoseBounds(rotation, hinge) first updates current world matrices. It composes a candidate root matrix at the shared play position and calculates a root delta relative to the current root matrix. It separately composes the candidate lid transform, then derives a lid delta relative to the current lid world matrix.

For each geometry object, the traversal determines whether its ancestry reaches the lid or root first. It computes a geometry bounding box when needed, applies the appropriate delta multiplied by the object's current world matrix, then unions the transformed box into an assembly envelope. The bounds implementation (src/scene.js:502) preserves nested local details while evaluating a different overall pose.

This is conservative box geometry, not an exact silhouette or a minimum-volume oriented hull. Rotated boxes can include empty corners. The advantage is predictable fitting and inexpensive computation across many separate meshes. The limitation is extra framing space around some oblique poses. Do not describe that slack as a mesh defect without checking the actual rendered silhouette.

Visibility is not filtered in that traversal. Hidden card or stylus geometry can still contribute to the envelope. This is especially relevant to the held stylus: its docked original remains in the DS hierarchy while only a clone moves in the scene. The controller clone rationale (src/ds-controller.js:25) deliberately preserves stable bounds.
Fit width, height and depth with interface reservations

The DS camera path gets the candidate envelope, then lifts the focused target so its minimum world Y is at least 2. It extracts size and computes a distance using field-of-view tangent, aspect ratio, width padding, height padding and half-depth. Narrow Inspect viewports reserve more top space for controls.

The fit formula (src/scene.js:940) uses top reservation 260 for phone Inspect and 90 otherwise; bottom reservation is 140 below width 600 and 120 otherwise. A minimum usable height prevents division by an arbitrarily tiny content area. A minimum width envelope of 12 also participates, so the formula is not merely the tightest possible fit to visible shell vertices.

The look target shifts vertically to account for asymmetric top and bottom reservations. The camera then sits along positive world Z from that target. Changing the object quaternion changes the evaluated bounds, not necessarily the camera's world viewing axis. This separation is useful when comparing front, back and three-quarter diagnostic poses.

Figure MD17.2. Parent-supplied neutral-studio constructor diagnostic for thickness and articulated relationships; the verified capture pose belongs to the parent render, not to an inferred native room or gameplay camera.
MD17-W01 Work a camera-fit term by hand

Assume a hypothetical candidate envelope of width 9, height 10 and depth 3, a 960-by-720 viewport, a 40-degree vertical field of view, Inspect mode and zoom 1. These are teaching assumptions, not a claim about a captured production camera. Aspect is 4/3, and tangent of half-FOV is about .36397.

The width term is max(12, 9+1.2)/(4/3) = 9. With top 90 and bottom 120, usable height is 510, so the height term is (10+.8) × 720/510 ≈ 15.2471. Height wins. Distance is approximately 15.2471/(2×.36397) + 1.5 ≈ 22.45. This demonstrates why leaving room for UI can dominate a shell-only fit.
Original arithmetic recipe:

Expected output is about 22.45 model units under those assumptions. The real path additionally applies zoom and the gameplay play-zoom factor. A fit calculation should report those multipliers rather than silently treating every mode as Inspect.
Input matrices cannot wait for an expensive paint

reframeDsPose() marks visuals and reflections dirty, updates camera targets, moves the root to the play target, copies the camera and look positions, then calls updateViewMatrices(). That function runs lookAt, refreshes camera and active-model matrices, and projects controls immediately.

The matrix-update contract (src/scene.js:494) explicitly decouples input correctness from the next eligible GPU paint. Under rendering backpressure, waiting for another painted frame could leave rays using a previous camera pose. The correct repair is not a permanent cursor offset; it is current transform data.

Research guidance. Current Object3D documentation distinguishes local and world matrices, and current Raycaster documentation specifies normalized-device coordinates and nearest-first hits. Both were consulted 2026-11-07. They support this diagnostic method, while the repository's pinned Three.js 0.186.1 code remains the version-specific implementation authority.

The controller's projected HTML buttons also have explicit limits. They use anchor world positions, a root-derived facing normal and a distance-based size estimate, with minimum sizes of 44 pixels for power and 14 for other controls. They test lid occlusion but are not exact projected cap polygons. Read the projection implementation (src/ds-controller.js:684) before calling it physically exact.
Lighting diagnosis begins with position, not paint

A dark metallic shell is not automatically a bad material. The model uses roughness, grain, clearcoat and environment reflections; its appearance depends on actual room geometry and emitters. Moving the focused console outside the lamp's emitting region can make the front unreadable even though the same paint looks good on the table.

The upright-lighting history (TODO/116_DS_UPRIGHT_LIGHTING.todo:25) records an initial lighting improvement at (−2,5.1,−2) that failed rotation clearance, followed by the final shared target (−2,5.1,−8). Commit 9be851e grounds that correction. These are historical measurements, not readings repeated during chapter authoring.

The lesson is causal: inspect which surface a sample ray actually hits, then inspect light direction and object placement. Increasing emissive intensity or global exposure can hide the symptom while breaking dark-room behavior and active-screen comparisons. Material tuning belongs after spatial diagnosis.
MD17-R01 Retry on a phone-sized Inspect viewport

Change the example to a 390-by-844 viewport in Inspect. Aspect drops sharply and the top reservation becomes 260, while bottom becomes 140. Reusing the desktop distance can crop the stylus or force the hinge controls over the display. Recompute the same envelope under the new reservations rather than reducing renderer resolution or shrinking the physical model.

Then verify actual picking at the lower-screen corners. A fit that includes the whole object does not guarantee that the lid leaves the touchscreen exposed. Also check the projected power target after resizing; its minimum touch size and anchor alignment are separate from the shell's visibility. The browser phone and hinge scenarios (tests/browser/ds.spec.mjs:1063) encode those expectations. They were read, not rerun here.
Figure MD17.3. Responsive fitting preserves geometry and pixel resolution while changing the viewing envelope and projected interaction layout.
Keep inspection instruments calibrated

The model's nominal dimensions depend on the shared centered rounded-solid helper (src/handheld.js:19). That helper's bevel expansion is one reason the camera measures generated geometry rather than rebuilding an envelope from a table of nominal dimensions. If a future toolkit change increases bevel thickness, an unchanged DS constructor can still need a different fitted distance.

Recommended diagnostic procedure. Record the candidate envelope before applying camera padding. This separates a larger geometry envelope from a larger UI reservation. If the model suddenly looks smaller on screen, compare those intermediate values: the shell may be unchanged while the viewport's reserved region grew, or an unexpectedly moved hidden child may have enlarged the measured bounds.

Also separate body rotation from camera orbit. The existing inspection interaction rotates the active model; a different tool might orbit the camera around a fixed model. Both can produce similar images, but their effects on world-space lighting and picking are not identical. A camera-relative highlight change is not interchangeable with rotating a metallic shell relative to a fixed lamp.

Avoid reusing local normals as world directions. A normal (0,0,1) on the control deck must be transformed by the root matrix before comparing it with the vector toward the camera. The controller performs that transformation for its broad facing check. A diagnostic that compares the untransformed vector can label a rear-facing console as front-facing after root rotation.

For a proposed alternative camera, preserve immediate matrix updates and rerun corner rays after resize, zoom and hinge edits. Then check scene clearance separately. A camera can fit an object that physically overlaps a companion, and collision-free placement can still be cropped. Combining those as one generic “framing pass” makes it difficult to identify which constraint failed.

Finally distinguish a stable mathematical fit from a pleasing composition. The source formula reserves interface space and fits conservative geometry, not an art-directed photographic composition for every angle. A proposed manual diagnostic camera may choose a tighter crop, provided its caption states that scope and does not present it as the native application's default view.
MD17-Q01 Exercise: why does fitting not prove accessibility?

A folded DS fits entirely inside the camera frustum. The author concludes that every control should remain enabled because no geometry is cropped. Explain the missing visibility test and identify the correct behavior for a hidden lower LCD.
MD17-A01 Explained answer

Frustum inclusion only means the assembly envelope lies within the view. It says nothing about one component occluding another. The lid can cover the lower display while both remain inside that envelope. Projected controls must respect lid intersections, and touch must accept only a first relevant hit on the lower LCD.

Do not force hidden controls to remain clickable by searching through occluders. That would make the model visually truthful but behaviorally false. Preserve the lower-screen hit gate (src/ds-controller.js:494) and teach operators to open the hinge or change pose. Inspection is useful precisely because it exposes such constraints rather than concealing them.

MD18 / THE DS MODEL REGRESSION ATLAS
The DS model regression atlas
An atlas records questions, not just attractive images

A useful model atlas explains what each observation can establish. A front image can reveal a control overlap; an underside ray can establish that branding faces outward; a unit test can establish a bounded D-pad target. None alone proves the whole console is correct. The goal is to preserve independent evidence channels so a later agent can diagnose a changed model without confusing appearance, geometry and native behavior.

Evidence status for this part. Source, selected TODO histories, scoped commit diffs and test assertions were read at cutoff 1e4ef518d6943ab1af39cef3b4d558f209a17891. This authoring task did not rerun browser or unit suites, produce production renders, inspect supplied images, publish or establish owner approval. Parent-supplied constructor PNGs are diagnostic illustrations with a separate verified capture pose; they are not native-runtime or historical-development proof.
Figure MD18.1. Independent checks narrow the failure boundary; an attractive final image does not replace the earlier measurements.
Establish a minimal constructor baseline

The constructor baseline should identify the root quaternion, lid rotation, camera, lights, renderer and material initialization stage. Without those facts two images can disagree even when the factory source is identical. In particular, a bare factory has hidden branding and initial unlit screens; the controller later loads the supplied emblem and selects reflective powered-off glass.

The factory return interface (src/ds-handheld.js:273) identifies the stable diagnostic handles. The controller initialization (src/ds-controller.js:196) and power-off material state (src/ds-controller.js:266) explain why a constructor image is not the same fixture as a running application.

For an open diagnostic pose, set the returned lid.rotation.x to degToRad(35), corresponding to a 145-degree opening under the scene convention. This is a safe value within the scene's supported 30–180-degree opening range, not a factory-enforced constraint. The factory exposes no setter; direct diagnostic assignment bypasses the application's guards and reframe logic.

The shared rounded-solid helper (src/handheld.js:19) must also be pinned. Changing its bevel behavior can change many apparent dimensions without editing the DS file. A regression atlas that records only ds-handheld.js can therefore miss a real geometry dependency.
Geometry atlas: surfaces, envelopes and ownership

The browser placement scenario combines several distinct checks. Rear rays hit the two inset floors and intact shell between them. The underside emblem is root-owned, faces outward and clears the battery cover. Face-cap and socket bounds clear the actual beveled touchscreen bezel and remain inside the deck. Four pads are square, matte and hittable from the rear; shoulders have the intended top-edge location and press normal.

The surface and bound assertions (tests/browser/ds.spec.mjs:1347) are a compact regression specification. Notice the measurement diversity: names from rays, parent identity, axis-aligned gaps, material properties and transformed normals. They are not redundant ways to prove the same fact.

MD18-W01 Design a regression for a wider Y socket

Assume a proposed edit increases only face-socket radius from .220 to .250 while keeping the Y center at X 2.75. Its left bound moves from 2.530 to 2.500. The current beveled bezel right bound is approximately 2.451667, leaving .048333. That falls below the existing greater-than-.05 requirement even though the cap radius remains .195 and the cap itself still appears clear.

The correct regression selects both cap and socket, calculates their boxes in root coordinates and compares against the generated bezel, not the nominal width alone. It should report which named part failed and the measured gap. Then it should check the outer A-side deck margin before accepting any outward correction.
Original pseudocode, assuming a browser fixture with current world matrices:

for part in all_face_caps_and_sockets:
  b = rootSpaceBounds(part)
  innerGap = b.minX - bezel.maxX
  outerGap = deck.maxX - b.maxX
  report part.name, innerGap, outerGap
  require innerGap > .05
  require outerGap > .10

Expected result under the changed assumption: the enlarged Y socket fails the inner criterion. Do not weaken the threshold to accommodate the edit. The threshold expresses a preserved model contract, while the proposed radius is the variable under evaluation. An implementation change can be rejected without treating the existing test as an obstacle.
Pose atlas: fixed references and editable poses coexist

An atlas needs both reproducible reference poses and varied interaction poses. A fixed historical lighting pose supports color comparisons; an unlocked default play pose supports everyday usability; a 30-degree opening tests occlusion; a tilted lock tests preserved articulation. Substituting one for another can make an otherwise valid photometric expectation fail for the wrong reason.

The hinge setter and bounds path (src/scene.js:467) define allowed edits and candidate evaluation. The camera-fit formula (src/scene.js:935) includes viewport reservations and desk lift. Record those conditions before interpreting a crop or brightness difference as a model defect.

Current Object3D documentation, consulted 2026-11-07, supports explicit world-matrix reasoning. Current Raycaster documentation, consulted the same day, supports nearest-first hit and face-orientation diagnostics. These are researched recommendations, not evidence that a different current Three.js release was used to author the pinned model.
Input atlas: measure behavior independently of artwork

The D-pad unit test uses a lightweight fixture and checks signed physical edge heights, diagonal magnitude, opposite-direction cancellation, exact rest return and idle-settled behavior. It also checks that the cap surface remains above the deck. The unit cases (tests/unit/ds-controls.test.mjs:49) are valuable arithmetic evidence but do not instantiate the complete shell.

The touch queue tests separately preserve quick down/up edges, coalesce drags and cancel stale work. Their fixture and expectations (tests/unit/ds-touch.test.mjs:29) establish asynchronous sequencing, not native-game success. The implementation is DsTouchQueue (src/ds-touch.js:28).

Browser scenarios then connect the pieces: real dual-screen startup, scene/runtime keyboard focus, stylus placement, quick taps, rotated poses and resize under deferred painting. Read the scenario inventory and native case (tests/browser/ds.spec.mjs:168) as integration intent. Reading an assertion is not observing its current pass status.
Pixel atlas: choose the material state first

The active-LCD invariant applies to unlit, non-tone-mapped status or native textures. Reflective powered-off glass is expected to change with lighting. The upright-lighting browser case explicitly installs static status LCDs, verifies sampled shell hits and compares LCD RGB values across lamp, dark and room states. That fixture avoids confusing a legitimate reflection with a pixel-presentation regression.

The pixel and material assertions (tests/browser/ds.spec.mjs:1455) require actual surface identity as well as color. Sampling a nearby background pixel can produce a plausible brightness number with no evidence about the shell. Keep the ray-hit name in the diagnostic output.
MD18-R01 Retry after a slow integrated browser case

Change the failure condition: an overpacked browser scenario times out after several correct native direction checks. Do not immediately reverse D-pad signs, reduce rendering quality or add retries. First inspect which checks completed and whether the deadline expired before the remaining independent behaviors were exercised.

The D-pad historical task (TODO/97_DS_DIRECTIONAL_DPAD.todo:40) records splitting scene keys, runtime keys, diagonal/opposite holds and mixed-source cleanup into independently booted scenarios while retaining assertions and deadlines. That is historical failure isolation, not evidence that every timeout has the same cause.
Figure MD18.2. Recovery changes the diagnostic arrangement only after evidence identifies the boundary; it must not silently relax the model contract.
Build a reusable evidence packet

Proposed agent procedure. For each model edit, retain a small packet containing the exact source cutoff, parameter delta, relevant constructor names, expected invariant, test selection and actual execution status. Add diagnostic images only when their fixture is known. A packet with fewer but well-scoped observations is more useful than many unlabeled screenshots.

For geometry, include generated bounds and the coordinate frame in which they were measured. For ray evidence, include origin, direction, first-hit name and relevant distance. For motion, include input state and timestamps or interpolation fraction. For pixel evidence, include the material state, light state, sampled surface identity and viewport. These fields make a failure reproducible without requiring the next agent to infer hidden conditions.

Keep source-read status distinct from execution status in the packet. “Assertion exists at this line” is a useful fact. “Passed locally on a historical commit” is another useful fact. Neither means “passed now.” Likewise a successfully produced constructor image does not establish native framebuffer readiness. The atlas should preserve those categories rather than flatten them into one completion badge.

When updating documentation after a model change, recalculate arithmetic examples as well as replacing images. A moved Y button changes the worked socket gap; a new lid offset changes the pivot example; a new screen dimension changes pixel scale and illumination metadata. Leaving old arithmetic next to a fresh image can make a handbook internally inconsistent even when every individual source link still resolves.

The same principle applies to coverage. This part covers the DS shell, hinge, controls, screens, card, stylus, markings and interaction boundaries actually discussed. It does not claim exhaustive explanation of save formats, emulator internals, all renderer code or every source line. A precise boundary lets a future extension add missing topics honestly instead of accidentally inheriting an impossible completeness claim.
MD18-Q01 Exercise: write an honest atlas conclusion

You have read a geometry test, produced a neutral-studio front image and found a historical task reporting local passes. You have not run the current browser suite or inspected native drawing. What can the coverage record claim, and what must remain unverified?
MD18-A01 Explained answer

It can claim source construction coverage, an identified assertion contract and a separately described diagnostic image. It can report the historical result explicitly as historical, with its source. It cannot claim fresh integration success, hosted qualification, native touch accuracy in the current environment or owner approval.

The coverage JSON for this part therefore names models, source symbols, components, chapters and tests read, then records limitations and unverified work. It is not a claim that every source line was explained or every hardware detail reproduced. This restraint makes the handbook reusable: a later agent can see exactly which evidence to regenerate rather than inheriting an inflated green status.

MD19 / PEAR BOY: THE PARAMETRIC BODY
Pear Boy: the parametric body
Evidence boundary and construction objective

Implemented behavior. Pear Boy is authored by createPearBoy, not imported from a sculpting package. The factory assembles a lathed shell, projected facial geometry, simulated rope limbs, decorative stem and leaf, contact shadow, and interior lights. This chapter reconstructs the shell first because its sampled profile becomes the geometric authority for both facial depth and rope collision. The implementation baseline is commit 1e4ef518d6943ab1af39cef3b4d558f209a17891; measurements below are model units, not inferred manufacturing dimensions. See factory and profile (src/pear-boy.js:5).

Design interpretation. A broad lower body and narrower upper neck can read as soft, stable, and toy-like. That is an interpretation of the silhouette, not proof that a user approved it or that a physical silicone prototype exists. The useful procedural objective is more concrete: preserve a continuous, rotationally symmetric shell whose front surface can be sampled consistently by independent features.
Build the profile before the surface

The profile starts as ten radius-height pairs in the XY plane. The endpoints are (0,.16) and (0,6.85). Intermediate radii grow through 1.6, 2.5, and 2.85, then taper through 2.8, 2.5, 1.95, 1.6, and 1. The widest authored control point is therefore at height 1.3, not at the middle of a generic sphere. The control-point list is interpolated with CatmullRomCurve3, sampled with getPoints(96), converted to Vector2, and clamped to nonnegative radius. This produces 97 sampled profile points.

There are two distinct resolutions: 96 curve divisions describe the vertical silhouette; 64 lathe segments describe angular sampling. Increasing one cannot repair undersampling in the other direction. A coarsely sampled profile can produce a stepped shoulder despite a smooth circular cross-section. Conversely, a fine profile with too few radial segments can look polygonal from above. Do not silently replace getPoints with evenly spaced arc-length samples: that would change the correspondence used by the downstream height lookup. The actual choices appear together at shell construction (src/pear-boy.js:66).
Figure MD19.1. One sampled profile supplies the lathe and the later shell queries; those consumers must not drift into independent approximations.
Derive the shell coordinates

For explanatory purposes, let r(y) denote the radius interpolated between neighboring sampled profile points. A rotational shell can be described by x=r(y) sin(theta) and z=r(y) cos(theta). This is a derivation of the surface of revolution, not a transcription of Three.js's internal vertex ordering. Positive Z is the authored face direction. At each fixed height, the ideal cross-section satisfies x²+z²=r(y)².

The code does not solve the original spline analytically for height. radiusAt finds the first sample after index eight with height at least the requested value, then linearly interpolates its radius against the preceding sample. The index guard avoids the beginning of the rounded base. Its validity depends on the authored profile behaving sensibly over the queried heights. A proposed profile with loops or decreasing height needs a new lookup contract; the existing function is not a general spline inversion algorithm.

This distinction explains why a visually plausible replacement sphere is insufficient. The face and collision code would continue asking the old profile for radii. A faithful rebuild must retain one authority, or deliberately update every dependent consumer and its tests.
Topology, normals, and ownership

The body uses LatheGeometry(profile,64) and a MeshStandardMaterial. The factory does not manually recalculate its normals after construction. Do not describe the body as a subdivision surface, voxel remesh, or normal-map sculpt: none of those stages appears here. The mesh helper marks the object with userData.pearBoy, sets receiveShadow, and adds it to the root. The root owns model placement; the body geometry remains in local coordinates.

Researched guidance. Current Three.js BufferGeometry documentation distinguishes indexed shared vertices from non-indexed triangles and explains that normal recomputation behaves differently for each. That reference was consulted on 2026-11-07; it is not an immutable description of this repository's dependency internals. If a proposed extension edits lathe positions directly, inspect its actual index and normal attributes before deciding how to rebuild shading. Updating positions alone is not a complete geometry-editing policy.

The material's cream base, roughness .65, warm emissive color, and intensity 77 are factory defaults. They suggest a luminous toy surface but do not implement subsurface scattering or elastic shell deformation.
Keep decoration separate from shell authority

The brown stem is a curved tube through heights 6.8, 7.55, and 8.02, with radius .22. The leaf is a planar Bézier outline extruded .08, with .04 bevel size and thickness. Its root translation is (0,7.5,.2); the vein is another small tube. These parts extend the recognizable silhouette without changing radiusAt. See stem, leaf, and vein (src/pear-boy.js:285).

That separation matters in collision interpretation. A profile-radius query describes the pear shell, not the leaf or every decorative protrusion. Conversely, an object-wide box can include protrusions that are not intended as physical support. Neither representation replaces the other. The source uses several envelopes for different jobs; treating all of them as the literal surface would produce contradictory dimensions.
Figure MD19.2. Actual original-factory diagnostic under neutral studio lighting; useful for silhouette comparison, not proof of native-room illumination or animation.
MD19-W01 Reconstruct a cross-section consistently

Begin with the exact control points, create the 97-point profile, and select height 4.5, the facial anchor height. Locate the same bracketing samples that radiusAt uses. Compute t=(4.5-a.y)/(b.y-a.y) and then r=a.x+t(b.x-a.x). Do not substitute the radius of a neighboring control point: the sampled interpolant is the implemented surface authority.

Next choose a test horizontal coordinate .66, matching one calm eye center. Derive its shell depth as sqrt(r²-.66²) and add the feature's chosen offset. Repeat with negative .66. The two depths should match because the shell is rotationally symmetric. Their X coordinates differ; their Y and Z values should not. This checks both symmetry and the sign convention without needing a rendered screenshot.

Finally compare the derived point with the factory's front result and check that all coordinates are finite. A useful observable recipe is to create the factory in its normal browser environment, inspect the named black eyes, and compare their neutral local positions. The texture helper needs a document canvas, so do not claim a bare Node factory run works without a canvas adapter. The helper's actual environment requirement is visible at canvas creation (src/handheld.js:68).
MD19-R01 Widen the belly without breaking dependents

Proposed extension. Change the 2.85 control radius to 3.1 in an isolated experiment, retaining its height and the sampling counts. This retry changes geometry, not only material color. Rebuild the shell and derive radii at limb attachment heights and the face height. A local belly change can influence adjacent spline intervals; do not assume the effect ends exactly at the edited control point.

Diagnose three consequences separately. First inspect the silhouette for a new shoulder kink. Second compare projected facial depths using the new shared profile. Third settle the ropes against the new radius function. The rope constraint pushes points outward using body radius plus cord or tip radius, as implemented in body contact (src/pear-rope.js:140). A rope that intersects the widened shell is not repaired by increasing render order.

Also re-evaluate body movement bounds. PearMotion has a deliberately simplified box, not a runtime extraction of every new profile vertex. Widening beyond its half-width can invalidate collision expectations even when the visible mesh is excellent.
Movement and clearance are different contracts

The motion controller bounds Pear by (-3,0,-3) to (3,8.1,3), with root workspace from (-22,0,-11.5) to (24,25,7.5). Those values govern upright body motion; they are not a promise to enclose every hanging foot. See PearMotion configuration (src/pear-motion.js:150).

The factory additionally computes an object box and expands its horizontal reach to at least ±4.5. Scene clearance starts with that envelope and unions current children except the contact plane. That arrangement protects broader limb reach while avoiding a fake shadow becoming solid furniture. Scene envelope assembly (src/scene.js:797) and the separate placement solver (src/desk-clearance.js:3) explain why a new body shape needs integration checks, not merely a neutral-front capture.
Figure MD19.3. A silhouette edit propagates into three geometric contracts before the model can be considered safely placeable.
Preserve useful invariants during reconstruction

A practical reconstruction should record three independent measurements before experimenting: the shell's local vertical span, sampled radius at the face anchor, and full assembly bounds after settling. The first describes body geometry, the second supports attachment math, and the third describes scene participation. Combining them into one “size” number throws away the distinction that makes later failures diagnosable. The factory exposes both body and bounds, while motion supplies another explicitly configured envelope (src/pear-boy.js:375; src/pear-motion.js:150).

For a proposed lower-resolution version, reduce only one sampling direction at a time in an isolated copy. Compare front silhouette, top circularity, and projected face clearance under the same coordinates. A lower polygon count is not automatically a valid optimization if broad expression patches start intersecting a coarser shell. Likewise, a higher count is not evidence of a better design if it changes nothing visible at the intended desk scale. The relevant tradeoff is observable quality against geometry cost, with the attachment contract retained.

The existing rope tests offer a useful numerical counterpart to silhouette inspection: finite coordinates, pinned attachment, controlled length error, and correct edge support. Keep the tests' synthetic constant-radius fixture distinct from the actual pear profile. Passing that fixture validates solver mechanics, not every authored radius sample. A profile-specific extension should sample its own critical heights rather than copying the fixture's constant 2.8 as if it were the entire body's radius. The fixture and its assertions are explicit in (tests/unit/pear-rope.test.mjs:6).
MD19-Q01 Choose the right failure detector

A rebuilt Pear looks correct from the front, but its hand enters the shell after a lateral pickup. Should the first repair change shell roughness, add more radial lathe segments, or inspect the shared radius/contact contract? Explain what additional observation would distinguish a bad collision radius from an incorrectly transformed rope.
MD19-A01 Separate shape, contact, and coordinate failures

Inspect the radius/contact contract first. Roughness changes shading, and radial segments change the polygonal approximation; neither necessarily changes the constraint's requested clearance. Compare each rope point in world coordinates against the body-local radius evaluated at point.y-origin.y. Then check that painting subtracts the root position exactly once. A consistent radial shortfall suggests wrong radius or tip clearance; a displacement that follows root translation suggests a coordinate conversion error.

The failure boundary is important: the rope only collides with the pear and desk, not arbitrary scene props. Existing rope unit cases exercise body contact and stale-momentum removal, but do not prove a future profile is safe at every possible point. Use them as regression contracts, then add focused negative controls for the changed shape. This handbook is a reproducible reconstruction aid, not a recovered internal design memory.

MD20 / PROJECTING A FACE ONTO A CURVED SHELL
Projecting a face onto a curved shell
Why a flat face fails on a rounded body

Implemented behavior. The Pear face is real mesh geometry attached to a curved shell. It is not a texture decal and does not use a camera-facing billboard. Its placement function derives Z from the same sampled radius profile that builds the body. The important dependency is therefore geometric: a facial feature must remain outside a shell whose depth changes with both height and horizontal coordinate. See profile, front projection, and patches (src/pear-boy.js:66).

Design interpretation. Keeping the markings close to the surface can make them read as part of a soft lamp rather than floating accessories. That reading does not establish a physical printing process. The procedural problem is simply to balance surface clearance against conspicuous separation, including when the face moves.
Derive the front projection and its domain

At a chosen height, the ideal section satisfies x²+z²=r². Selecting the front half gives z=sqrt(r²-x²). The code adds a positive offset, named inset, although numerically it pushes the point outward along positive Z. Its default is .03. A literal inward normal displacement would have a different meaning; use the actual equation rather than interpreting the name as a physical direction.

The function clamps the square-root argument to zero. This prevents a negative radicand from generating NaN when |x|>r, but does not make such a point a correct surface attachment. It would sit beyond the valid circular section with depth equal to the offset. Nor does front include the explicit height guard present in radiusAt; an out-of-range height can fail while selecting its interpolation pair. Valid feature authoring must respect both domains.

For a broad patch, it is not enough to project only its corners. A triangle connects projected vertices with planar edges. Across a convex shell that flat chord can cut inward between samples, burying its interior even when the vertices are individually clear. This is the reason to examine tessellation before increasing offset.
Form expressions in two dimensions first

facePatch constructs a ShapeGeometry with curve-segment argument 16, converts it to non-indexed triangles, copies its positions into vectors, and disposes both intermediate geometries. It then performs two triangle subdivision passes. Each triangle becomes four by introducing edge midpoints. After two passes an original triangle contributes sixteen triangles. Only then are all vertices projected using front.

This ordering is the central lesson: shape placement happens in its XY description before projection. Translating an already projected patch vertically does not re-evaluate the shell radius at the new height. A mouth can consequently enter a region of greater shell depth and disappear behind the body; movement toward a narrower region can instead leave it floating. The implemented anger mark follows the safer pattern too: it adds .42 to the authored Y coordinate before calling front, rather than moving the finished tube afterward. See anger mark construction (src/pear-boy.js:215).
Figure MD20.1. Subdivision precedes projection so the filled interior follows the rounded shell rather than remaining a large cutting plane.
Tubes, patches, and small solid features

The calm eyes are scaled spheres at x=±.66, y=4.5, with scale (.18,.22,.09). The smile samples seventeen points from X -.5 to .5, using a sine depression of .32 from height 3.96, then forms a tube of radius .055. These solids have their own thickness; they are not equivalent to a zero-thickness patch with the same center coordinate.

Expression eyes, cheeks, mouth fills, and tongue use different offsets. Typical patch clearance is .06; the white angry-eye interior and tongue use .085; rosy cheeks use .025. These layers should be understood relative to their projected surface, not as absolute world depths. The mesh helper initially adds meshes to the model root, after which adding them to a face group reparents them. Their coordinates were already authored in model space, and those face groups start with identity transforms.

Researched guidance. Current BufferGeometry documentation states that absent indices, successive triples form triangles. That supports the patch's setFromPoints construction. The returned patches do not explicitly compute normals or retain UV coordinates; their MeshBasicMaterial colors do not require the same lighting response as the standard-material shell.
Move around the body axis, not the face center

face.root is a group at the body origin, containing both expression groups and permanent freckles. Horizontal tracking rotates this group about Y. Because its geometry is already located near the shell's front, that operation moves features around the body axis. Rotating a group newly centered at the face anchor would instead turn markings around their own center, an entirely different trajectory.

Vertical tracking translates the group and scales X and Z by radiusAt(4.5+dy)/radiusAt(4.5). This is a shared center-height approximation, not a per-vertex reprojection at every feature height. It preserves a coherent face while accommodating the narrowing shell. The fixed anchor is a separate object attached directly to the model root, so pointer normalization does not chase the moving face. See anchor and transform update and gaze transform (src/pear-boy.js:248).
MD20-W01 Derive lateral motion of a marking

Take a neutral point (x,y,z) on the face. Let the horizontal normalized gaze be one, so the implemented yaw is .55 radians. Under the conventional Y rotation, its new horizontal coordinate is x cos(.55)+z sin(.55). This includes a contribution from shell depth. An eye can therefore move substantially farther than a simple .55-unit lateral translation would suggest. The angle is approximately 31.5 degrees; it is not a screen-pixel distance.

Now set upward gaze to one. The implemented Y offset is .75 model units, not .75 radians. Compute the radius ratio at heights 5.25 and 4.5. Apply that ratio to local X and Z before yaw. The exact numerical result must come from the sampled profile, not from assuming a spherical head.

For an observable reproduction, compare world positions of both named black eyes at neutral and extreme gaze after updateWorldMatrix(true,true). Keep the root position unchanged and separately project the fixed anchor. The browser regression requires upward eye movement over .65 world units and five screen pixels, with an unchanged anchor. It also checks smile and freckle movement. See pointer assertions.
MD20-R01 Move a broad mouth toward the shoulder

Proposed extension. Raise an expression mouth's XY control points by .3 before constructing its shape. Rebuild its triangulation and projection; do not translate the finished mesh. The changed condition is increased shell curvature and a smaller radius at the new height. Inspect the patch center as well as its perimeter, because corner-only tests miss chord penetration.

If the interior disappears, first verify subdivision and the resulting vertex depths. Increasing offset may restore visibility but can leave a floating outline in three-quarter views. Increasing tessellation better approximates curvature, at a geometry cost. Replacing the fill with a texture is another tradeoff, but it would introduce UV and texture-resolution contracts absent from the implemented expression pipeline.

Do not assume DoubleSide fixes buried geometry. It can expose back faces, but the shell can still occlude the patch. Current Raycaster documentation also distinguishes back-face behavior from closest-hit ordering. Diagnose the actual surface intersection instead of using material settings as a substitute for correct placement.
Visibility means foremost appearance

The freckle test casts toward each dot and selects the nearest intersection whose entire ancestor chain is visible. A dot's own visible=true is not sufficient if its parent is hidden. Nor does a visible flag prove the body or another eye is not in front of it. The test examines all nine gaze combinations for four expressions, requiring all six foremost names to be the freckle name. See visibility filtering.
Figure MD20.2. A geometric visibility check rejects hidden ancestors and intervening surfaces before accepting a facial marking.
Integration constraints beyond the face

The same model root also carries moving limbs and lights. Rope painting converts simulated world positions back to root-local coordinates; it must not inherit face-group yaw. Body motion is separate again, using DeskMotion integration rather than facial interpolation. These ownership boundaries are explicit in limb painting, rope origins (src/pear-rope.js:48), and body integration (src/pear-motion.js:59).

Scene pointer normalization projects the immutable anchor and clamps gaze to [-1,1], independent of the current markings (src/scene.js:1326). Texture color-space setup is centralized in the canvas helper (src/handheld.js:68), whereas face patches use direct basic colors. Those distinctions explain why changing emission or the canvas gradient is not a repair for a buried mouth.
Depth offsets are a layered budget

The patch and solid-feature offsets form a small but important depth budget. An angry eye's white interior at .085 sits farther forward than the black outline's default .06; the tongue uses the same larger offset against its mouth fill. Blush at .025 is intentionally closer to the shell than many ink features. These are source values, not universal safe distances. Their relative arrangement is visible in the expression constructors (src/pear-boy.js:136; src/pear-boy.js:202).

When adapting a feature, first identify which layer should be foremost and whether it is a tube, flattened sphere, or triangulated fill. A tube radius contributes additional geometric depth around its centerline, whereas a patch has no comparable thickness. Equal center offsets therefore do not imply equal front surfaces. This explains why moving every feature to the same Z offset can introduce new occlusion even if it removes shell penetration.

A useful proposed diagnostic is to cast separate rays toward the intended foreground layer, its surrounding outline, and a point just beyond the feature. Record object identity, not only hit distance, because two parts can be nearly coplanar while belonging to different expressions. Repeat after upward and horizontal gaze, then compare the same local layer ordering. This extends the existing freckle-center method without pretending it already tests every mouth pixel. If a repair requires disabling depth testing, stop and re-examine geometry: the current implementation's lesson is to construct surface-following features, not to draw facial colors over unrelated objects.
MD20-Q01 Diagnose a face that vanishes only upward

A new cheek fill is visible at neutral gaze but becomes partly hidden looking up. Its object and parent are visible, and its corner vertices are outside the shell. What should be measured next, and why is rotating the whole lamp an invalid repair?
MD20-A01 Inspect interior sampling and transform ownership

Measure interior triangle clearance at the changed height, then inspect the group's center-height scale approximation. Large planar triangles may penetrate between clear vertices; a shape extending far above the anchor may also exceed the approximation's useful range. Rebuild with more appropriate sampling or change its authored XY extent before projection.

Rotating the whole lamp changes body, ropes, lights, and desk collision relationships. It conceals the local error by changing the viewing condition. The failure boundary is that the current face transform is designed for the authored range, not arbitrary expressions spanning the entire pear. History records wider gaze and later upward travel, but those commits do not prove every proposed larger face is safe. Extend the geometric test grid and inspect actual appearance rather than converting historical qualification into universal approval.

MD21 / EXPRESSIONS, GAZE AND SIX VISIBLE FRECKLES
Expressions, gaze and six visible freckles
Separate where the face looks from what it expresses

Implemented behavior. createPearBoy builds four expression groups beneath one movable face root: calm, scared, angry, and sad. The public expression labels are curious, scared, angry, and sad; the final sad appearance is a squeezed-eye pout, not the earlier glossy worried face. Gaze moves the shared face root, while visibility selects the expression. This separation prevents each expression from implementing slightly different tracking. Face ownership (src/pear-boy.js:43) is the authoritative hierarchy.

Design interpretation. The compact eyes, short brows, blush, and puckered mouth can communicate a gentler reaction than large wedges. “Cuter” is a design interpretation and historical task vocabulary, not a measurable shader property. This chapter instead makes the mechanics reproducible: which geometry appears, what triggers it, how long it remains eligible, and which markings never belong to a temporary expression.
Permanent freckles are structural, not duplicated decoration

Each side creates three dots at positive-coordinate pairs (1.05,4.25), (1.16,4.03), and (.92,4.04), mirrored in X by the side sign. Each dot is a sphere of radius .055, with ten width and eight height segments, flattened in Z by .4. The material is orange MeshBasicMaterial with tone mapping disabled. All six are attached directly to face.root, not to calm or scared. See freckle creation (src/pear-boy.js:160).

This ownership makes six a persistent inventory invariant. Duplicating the dots into four groups would multiply maintenance points and could accidentally leave two sets visible. Attaching them outside the moving root would preserve their count but break whole-face tracking. Neither error is caught by simply counting named objects in the entire model; both hierarchy and actual foremost visibility must be checked.
Gaze math and a fixed reference

The scene projects an immutable anchor at the original face center, converts cursor displacement into fractions of twenty percent of viewport width and height, and clamps each axis to [-1,1]. Upward screen movement reverses the usual screen-Y direction. The anchor is separate from the animated face group, avoiding a feedback loop in which the target moves because the face already moved. See scene normalization (src/scene.js:1326).

The gaze interpolation blend is 1-exp(-12*delta), or one for reduced motion. For a constant target, the remaining error after elapsed time t behaves like exp(-12t) until the snap threshold is reached. The characteristic time is about .0833 seconds. A squared error below 1e-7 copies the target exactly, preventing perpetual microscopic changes.

Horizontal gaze produces Y-axis rotation up to .55 radians. Positive vertical gaze produces up to .75 model units of rise; negative gaze produces down to -.18. These are deliberately different dimensions. A radius ratio scales X and Z to follow the changing shell width. It is not a .75-radian pitch.
Figure MD21.1. Gaze is derived from a stationary reference and applied once to every expression and permanent dot.
Expression state and paint acknowledgment

showExpression switches group visibility, restores the wobbly scared mouth, hides the open scream mouth, resets elapsed time, and clears presented. setFaceLifted selects scared or curious unless an impact reaction currently owns the face. A reset or new lift clears that reaction. reactToImpact ignores speeds below ten and ignores another impact while already reacting. State setters (src/pear-boy.js:224) establish these rules.

While reacting, angry lasts at least .9 accumulated seconds and sad at least 1.25, but transitions additionally require presented=true. The scene sets that flag after submitting the main room render. Consequently a stalled renderer cannot silently consume the entire reaction sequence before any expression was submitted. This is a visibility contract layered over elapsed time, not a promise of exact wall-clock dwell on every device.

When lifted without a reaction, the two scream mouths alternate after .9 seconds only if the current mouth was presented. Reduced motion suppresses that alternation and forces the wobbly mouth if the open one was visible. Recovery can still progress through static expressions. See face update.

Add .31 seconds: the accumulated .91 crosses .9, so the open mouth becomes visible and presented resets.

Without another acknowledgment, advancing time does not authorize another switch. After acknowledgment, repeat the .6 and .31 pair. The deterministic browser test records [false,true,true,false,false], where the final false comes from a reduced-motion update forcing the closed variant. This recipe distinguishes state timing from automation latency and does not require loosening any screenshot deadline.

Then test a hard impact separately: set lifted false with reset, call reactToImpact(20), and inspect the expression label. Advance beyond .9 without acknowledging paint; angry should remain. Acknowledge, update, and observe sad. Repeat beyond 1.25 to return to curious if no longer lifted. The actual browser timing and visibility fixture provides an existing executable model for this separation.

If all expressions disappear immediately into curious, inspect whether a caller set presented before rendering or bypassed the state setter. Do not conclude that large deltas inherently require skipping intermediate states. The implementation explicitly preserves them until presentation.

Next enable reduced motion. Gaze should snap rather than ease; mouth alternation should stop; impact recovery remains eligible after its timing and presentation conditions. Rope motion has a different accommodation: it settles constraints immediately instead of swinging. See reduced-motion limbs and the settling procedure (src/pear-rope.js:34). Reduced motion is therefore not a global instruction to freeze every state variable or teleport a dropped body home.

The browser fixture iterates X and Y values -1, 0, and 1 under each expression, casting rays from a point in front of the Pear toward each dot. It filters intersections whose object or any ancestor is invisible, then requires the closest remaining object to be the freckle. Thirty-six combinations times six dots provide 216 center-ray checks.

This is stronger than visible=true, but narrower than a complete perceptual proof. It checks centers, not every silhouette pixel or every possible camera angle. Antialiasing, tiny projected size, and color contrast still affect appearance. Current Raycaster guidance supports nearest-first intersections and explains mesh face orientation; the repository's explicit ancestor filter supplies its visibility policy.
Figure MD21.2. Hard-impact recovery requires time and submitted presentation; permanent freckles remain outside this expression selection.

Documented history. Commit 1510777ff05b82414e8e1b5958e8c76e446a0eaa replaced large angry-eye shapes and glossy recovery eyes, and changed scream dwell from .24 to .9. Commit 44b5dc2213bcf9ee464357cfa68ee44b8c1d9bbe widened yaw from .22 to .55. Commit dd269dea6f5cc6ada0038a2245b0ec3a420768c5 increased only positive vertical travel from .18 to .75. Their scoped source diffs establish those changes; the task records describe observed failures and qualification. They do not recover private deliberation or imply aesthetic approval. The numerical changes are recorded at (TODO/118_PEAR_BOY_FACE_TRAVEL.todo:23) and (TODO/121_PEAR_BOY_UPWARD_FACE_TRAVEL.todo:22); the approval boundary is explicit at (TODO/113_PEAR_BOY_CUTER_RECOVERY.todo:22).

Geometry makes each reaction readable

The scared face uses squeezed tube eyes, projected pink cheeks, and either a wobbly line mouth or a filled open scream. The wobbly mouth samples 33 points across width 1.2, with a cosine oscillation of amplitude .075 and six half-turns across the normalized parameter. Its geometry is fixed; the visible tremble impression comes from its contour and alternation, not continuous random vertex motion. The open mouth is a distinct curved patch (src/pear-boy.js:186).

Angry uses compact ellipse-based black outlines and smaller white interiors, short curved brows, lower blush strokes, a filled shouting mouth, a pink tongue, and an anger mark built higher on the forehead. Sad uses squeezed eyes, small frustrated brows, rosy cheeks, and a narrow alternating-X pout. These are different geometric vocabularies, not merely recolored calm eyes. When reconstructing them, preserve the XY coordinates before projection; raising a complete already-projected patch can bury it in the tapering shell.

A proposed alternative based on a single animated texture could reduce mesh inventory, but would introduce atlas coordinates, texture filtering, and expression-frame lifecycle concerns. The pinned assembly instead makes individual features inspectable by name and allows ray-based occlusion checks. Neither approach is categorically superior; the reusable lesson is to state which representation owns expression identity and how its visibility is proved.
Keep acceptance layers separate

The historical task records distinguish technical qualification, public deployment, and aesthetic approval. Repeating a recorded “passes” statement does not execute a test in a new checkout. This authoring pass reads the fixtures and history; the parent owns rendering and publication. Another agent should retain that boundary rather than treating prose as an invisible test run.

For a new expression, preserve permanent-dot count and hierarchy, test both reduced-motion and ordinary timing, then instrument actual room submissions for state order. Only after those mechanics pass should visual review decide whether the reaction reads as intended. A six-dot center-ray result still does not establish that a tiny dot is perceptually readable on every display. The failure boundary includes projected size, contrast, camera angle, and unreviewed combinations beyond the existing nine-point gaze grid.

Remaining angry is expected while presented is false. The purpose is to avoid consuming an expression entirely between submitted paints. After the main room render calls acknowledgeFacePaint, a subsequent eligible update can advance to sad, whose own presentation must also be acknowledged before recovery completes.

A genuine failure would be a submitted angry frame followed directly by curious without the sad state being presented, or an acknowledgment from an unrelated reflection render that incorrectly unlocks progression. The boundary is main-room submission, not proof of physical monitor scanout. Preserve that distinction when instrumenting tests. The painted-drop browser case samples the actual renderer call and expects scared, angry, sad, curious in order, rather than using animation callbacks alone as evidence (tests/browser/pear-boy.spec.mjs:496).
